placeStudy.title: Nalanda and Tamralipti: two textual settings
placeStudy.description: Approximate locators distinguish Nalanda from the Tamralipti/Tamluk region named in the translated account. The coast is a modern generalized outline, not a reconstructed seventh-century estuary. No journey line or complete route is implied.

points.label: Nalanda — monastic and scholastic remains
points.text: The locator orients the Bihar site. It does not identify an exact seventh-century room or make the protected boundary the full historical complex.

points.label: Tamralipti / Tamluk region — a different monastery
points.text: Takakusu identifies Tamralipti with Tamluk. Pages 63–65 describe this setting before turning to Nalanda. The rounded point is regional, not an ancient harbor survey or the exact Bha-ra-ha monastery.

place-work.text: A drinking cup’s named owner and proposed courtly use differ from an excavated household’s provisioning evidence. Ceramic work, patronage and exchange can be compared across these contexts without turning a regional attribution into a findspot or assigning this cup a maker from another object.

participation.text: An elite owner’s name and imagery connect rank with food and fertility; other voices are less directly represented.

evidence.text: The proposed regional origin rests on comparisons rather than a documented excavation of this vessel.

subjects.name: A Maya drinking vessel: text, food and rank
subjects.place: Mesoamerica; proposed Tabasco association
subjects.geographicPrecision: Broad hypothesized region; no precise excavated findspot is claimed.

interval.label: Seventh–eighth centuries CE
interval.note: Catalogue object range; not a lifespan for Maya peoples, who continue today.

subjects.question: What can a name on a cup tell us—and what does it leave open?
subjects.summary: A made container joined food, imagery and a named owner. Its courtly interpretation becomes more useful beside evidence for ceramic making, attributed painters and household provisioning elsewhere. Each source keeps its own date, place and limits.

sections.title: A container joined several kinds of work
sections.text: This large ceramic cup brings making and representation together. Fine incised outlines run across its pale surface, while the catalogue proposes a painted-stucco finish near the rim. Doyle’s wider account describes Maya potters forming vessels by hand and choosing clay, additives and surfaces before firing. Such choices made containers durable and gave artists a working surface. They supply a production context for this cup, while its particular clay recipe, workshop and maker remain unrecorded.

citations.locator: Artwork Details; Description: incisions and rim ornamentation; existing photograph

sections.title: Naming a relationship
sections.text: The museum reads the short text as identifying a drinking cup belonging to Baje(?) Kaan, or Chan, Took’, a ruler or noble. Part of that reading remains uncertain. It makes ownership a visible social relationship: a named person could be connected with a container used for serving and display. The figure and signs also share the same composition. The catalogue considers it possible that the seated figure represents the named owner; the text supplies no polity.

citations.locator: Description: ownership text; text-image relationship; polity paragraph

sections.title: Food, display and exchange
sections.text: Doyle relates the cup’s form to cacao preparation scenes on other vessels, where pouring makes froth. Shared dipping is a proposed reconstruction of use. The museum reads imagery of agricultural fertility as connecting the represented ruler with food and renewal. In the wider Classic-period account, finely made vessels also served as diplomatic gifts between courts and governors. Their circulation could carry skilled work and messages about relationships, without establishing a particular gift event for this cup.

citations.locator: Cacao preparation and presumable shared dipping

sections.title: Makers and patrons can enter the record
sections.text: Some other vessels allow the maker-patron relationship to be studied more closely. Princeton’s account attributes an Ik’ dish around 755 CE to Mo?-n Buluch Laj and names Yajawte’ K’ihnich as patron. It also describes signed cups from that courtly setting. These records make skilled people visible beside their patrons. They do not supply a maker for the selected vessel or prove that its owner made it.

sections.title: Other households produced and exchanged
sections.text: A separate excavated village, Cerén in present-day El Salvador, brings households into view. Sheets describes people producing food and goods for their own use, making surplus through part-time specialties and exchanging products with neighbors or at elite centers. Groundstone tools, painted gourds and plant fibers enter that account. A later botanical study documents productive gardens and outfields. This evidence explains daily work beyond courtly imagery; it does not locate this museum cup at Cerén.

citations.locator: Exposed publisher abstract: three provisioning domains
Exposed primary abstract: gardens and outfields

deeperReading.title: An argued origin is different from a findspot
deeperReading.text: The Tabasco association rests on comparisons in the museum’s account: a similar name on a Comalcalco brick and incised cylinders described from Jonuta. The original brick edition and Berlin study were not consulted here. The cup’s appearance in Europe in 1961 and a Swiss collection notice in 1964 belong to its modern documentary history. Those notices neither record its excavation nor establish a complete ancient itinerary. The current provenance-tab text was not exposed.

citations.locator: Description: Comalcalco/Jonuta hypothesis and 1961/1964 publication history

deeperReading.title: Ownership, contents and making ask different questions
deeperReading.text: Doyle explains that texts on other vessels can name their type, contents, owner or giver. This cup’s short ownership statement does not provide all those answers. An artist signature would address another relationship again. Distinguishing these statements keeps the named owner from becoming an invented maker and the broader cacao interpretation from becoming a translation of a word absent from the supplied ownership reading.

deeperReading.title: Preservation shapes the household comparison

subjects.name: Mali: pilgrimage, trade and historical voices
subjects.place: Western Sahel; locator at Timbuktu, Mali
subjects.geographicPrecision: Regional orientation at a scholarly/trade center, not a certain imperial capital or border.

interval.label: Mali political frame, c.1230–1600 CE
interval.note: Broad exhibition convention; political influence and local autonomy changed. This is not an exact founding or extinction date.

subjects.question: How do oral history, foreign images and material evidence change one another?
subjects.summary: Mali’s rulers depended on a landscape of farming, fishing, making and exchange. The resources displayed by a court came through many people’s work. Oral histories, excavated fragments and foreign depictions preserve different parts of that world. Mansa Musa’s pilgrimage is one dated episode within changing political networks, not the origin of West African urban life or its only important story.

sections.title: Begin below the royal throne
sections.text: The supplied atlas detail makes a seated ruler and a gold-colored object prominent. Ordinary work is largely absent. Berzock’s archaeological synthesis instead describes unglazed pots used for cooking, storing food and carrying commodities such as grain and fish. Iron tools, metalworking and regional exchange supported daily life. A rare imported fragment is striking, but the common broken vessel can be more direct evidence of repeated household tasks. Neither should be discarded because it lacks a royal name.

citations.locator: Printed pp. 26–29: domestic ceramics and materials

sections.title: Cities had histories before this empire
sections.text: Jenne-jeno developed long before the conventional Mali frame. Archaeology identifies a diverse urban population and specialized work without an obvious royal palace at its center. This challenges a story in which urban life arrived only with foreign traders or a named conquering king. It does not establish one uniform political system across all places later associated with Mali. A settlement’s local organization and an empire’s wider claims operate at different scales.

citations.locator: Ancient Mali and Middle Niger Civilization; Archaeology

sections.title: Exchange required relationships and could impose violence
sections.text: River-basin production and pastoral movement linked different environments. Saharan exchange added longer connections, including salt, cloth, metals and gold. Muslim merchants and scholars participated in relationships that also crossed religious differences. These were not exclusively equal or voluntary exchanges: enslaved people were transported through the same wider networks. Goods circulating and rulers prospering do not establish the security or freedom of all those doing the work.

citations.locator: Printed pp. 27–28: accounts, slavery and material evidence

sections.title: A pilgrimage and a later map have separate dates
sections.text: Mansa Musa passed through Cairo on pilgrimage in 1324. The atlas, conventionally dated about 1375 and attributed to Abraham Cresques, was made in Majorca. It presents him with a crown, a throne and gold. Those signs make wealth and rulership legible to a foreign court audience. They are not a portrait made from life, an inventory of his treasury or a neutral map of political boundaries. The image tells us how news of Mali could be selected and pictured elsewhere.

sections.title: Remembering also involved living work
sections.text: Mande jeliw have carried genealogies, praise and Sunjata narratives through performance. These living traditions changed with audiences and circumstances. They should not be treated as a single frozen transcript of the thirteenth century, or dismissed because they are oral. Compare their purposes with foreign accounts and archaeological contexts before deciding what a particular claim can establish.

Keeping those qualifications does not make the image unusable: it makes an interpretation more precise. The accompanying text’s claim of extraordinary wealth belongs to the map, not to an audited modern ranking.

deeperReading.title: Context changes what a fragment can say
deeperReading.text: A pot fragment with a documented excavation context can connect material, use and date. An object removed without a record loses part of that relationship. Berzock’s chapter places common wares alongside rare imports to avoid making distant commerce the whole economy. This does not let us assign every sherd to a Mali royal workshop. A regional archaeological assemblage and a named ruler’s reign must be joined by evidence, rather than by sharing a place on a modern map.

deeperReading.title: A broad interval contains uneven changes
deeperReading.text: The case keeps its approximate 1230–1600 exhibition frame. It does not announce an exact foundation or sudden extinction. The rise of Songhay overlapped later Mali histories; every settlement did not change allegiance on a single year. Likewise, the Met’s exhibition labels Musa’s passage through Cairo in 1324, while its later interview describes the pilgrimage as 1325. Here 1324 remains the Cairo anchor; the source wording difference stays documented rather than silently replacing the original case date.

subjects.question: Can urban life be studied without assuming a centralized state?
subjects.summary: A skilled clay figure and an excavated city answer different questions. Looking closely reveals a maker’s choices; settlement layers reveal food, building and craft work without recovering the figure’s lost biography.

sections.title: A maker’s choices remain visible
sections.text: A clay body bends around a raised knee; the head rests sideways, and arms draw the composition together. The back view shows raised oval forms and rows of small depressions. These are choices made in shaping a terracotta figure. Its maker gave a compact object a complicated posture. The museum dates it to the thirteenth century, but neither posture nor markings identify a named sitter, a feeling, an illness or a particular ritual. The broad Inland Niger Delta attribution does not supply a controlled excavation context.

citations.locator: Artwork Details; actual front/back images; interpretive limits

sections.title: Food and materials supported urban life
sections.text: Jenné-jeno’s archaeology reaches far earlier than this object. Roderick and Susan McIntosh’s 1981 article describes a town growing among other settlements, with an urban high point around 750–1100. Its account connects rice, fish and fish oil with the region’s economy, alongside exchanged materials. People sustaining a town needed food as well as objects arriving from elsewhere. This makes cultivation, fishing and provisioning part of the urban story; imported valuables alone do not explain how a large community lived.

citations.locator: Exposed Extract: settlements, staples and exchange

sections.title: Places for work changed
sections.text: Later excavation reporting distinguishes domestic, burial and craft uses in different places and periods. Houses and granaries point to building and storage; furnace concentrations mark work involving heat. Dating showed that the sampled furnace areas were not all used together. A present-day scatter therefore cannot simply become a picture of simultaneous specialist neighborhoods. Reading the sequence helps recover people making and remaking places, rather than freezing the region at the date of the figure.

citations.locator: PDF pp. 4–7: changing uses and non-simultaneous activity

sections.title: Organization is a question to investigate
sections.text: The Met’s Sahel essay presents McIntosh’s interpretation of urbanism without centralized state hierarchy. That is an argument to assess, not proof that everyone was equal or that leadership was absent. A figure, a household deposit and a settlement survey offer different scales of evidence. Keeping those scales distinct makes room for forms of cooperation that a single royal biography could obscure.

deeperReading.title: What survives affects the comparison
deeperReading.text: The excavation report found limited variation in imported materials across sampled units and considered what that might mean for wealth. The authors also note that valuable textiles might not have survived. Erosion removed parts of the later occupation. A measure made from surviving imports cannot settle every kind of inequality, and an absent deposit may reflect loss rather than an unused place. The report’s proposed connection between Jenné-jeno’s decline and Djenné’s growth likewise remains a hypothesis, not an established movement of every household.

He also calls for critical comparison between oral histories and archaeological remains. His published account was translated and edited from French. It offers an attributed perspective on how research should work, not a statement made by every community or an explanation of this particular figure. The Met’s 1981 purchase credit adds a modern acquisition date; it does not reconstruct the object’s earlier custody or an ancient owner.

subjects.name: Angkor: water, temples and a living landscape
subjects.place: Siem Reap region, Cambodia
subjects.geographicPrecision: Angkor Wat orientation within a wider group of capitals and settlements; no empire outline.

interval.label: Successive capital landscapes, ninth–fifteenth centuries CE
interval.note: Broad archaeological frame, not one city plan, one reign or an exact date of universal abandonment.

subjects.question: What is missing when a city is pictured as only a temple?
subjects.summary: Angkor was a landscape of temples, settlements, fields and water works built and altered over centuries. Stone monuments survive conspicuously; traces of less durable buildings and infrastructure require other ways of looking. Satellite observation, lidar, excavation and network models help us ask how the city worked, why it changed, and why the story cannot end with an empty jungle.

sections.title: Begin outside the famous temple
sections.text: Angkor Wat belongs to a much larger settlement landscape. UNESCO includes reservoirs, canals, roads and successive capital plans within its account of the site. The water works mattered alongside ceremonial buildings: they connected places, helped manage seasonal water and supported cultivation. Different rulers added or altered projects. A modern visitor sees remains from many phases together, so the visible landscape must not be mistaken for a single design built in one reign. Our map separates several locations to make those relationships easier to investigate.

sections.title: How a water network works
sections.text: Reservoirs store water; channels move it; embankments and control points influence where it goes. The 2018 study describes a system serving flood regulation and agriculture, accumulated through repeated construction and modification. Connections matter as much as individual structures. A reservoir cannot supply a place if its connecting channel no longer functions. Maintenance is therefore part of urban history: excavation, clearing and repair are recurring work, not just the exceptional achievement of building a monument. Religious and political importance does not remove these material demands.

citations.locator: Angkor’s water distribution network; modeling framework

sections.title: Seeing traces beneath vegetation
sections.text: Many buildings were made of perishable materials, leaving subtler traces than stone temples. The 2013 lidar study used airborne laser scanning to model ground surfaces beneath vegetation. Roads, ponds, occupation mounds and organized layouts became easier to recognize. Lidar does not directly show the people who once lived there or tell us the year of every feature. It changes what can be mapped, then archaeology has to connect those forms to activities and dates. A seemingly isolated temple can become part of a much larger urban pattern.

citations.locator: Introduction; airborne laser scanning and urban landscapes

sections.title: Stress can travel through connections
sections.text: Penny and colleagues tested a model derived from archaeological mapping. At a branching channel, stronger flow can erode one branch and attract still more water. Another branch receives less, deposits sediment and loses capacity. In the model, sufficiently large disturbances can produce cascading changes elsewhere in the network. This is a possible mechanism linking unusual water flows to infrastructure damage. It does not reproduce every historical decision or establish that water damage alone caused political change. The authors argue for a contributing vulnerability, in combination with climatic variation.

sections.title: Transformation did not empty the landscape
sections.text: The history of particular places complicates a single abandonment date. Excavations around Angkor Wat found changing occupation of its habitation mounds, while inscriptions and modifications attest to the temple’s continuing importance. Political relocation, religious change, trade and climate belong in the discussion together. UNESCO also describes villages and cultivation in the present heritage landscape. The end of a capital phase is not the end of everyone’s relationship with a place. Asking what continued is as important as asking what failed.

citations.locator: Timing and Tempo of Collapse; occupation layers

deeperReading.title: A mechanism is not a complete cause
deeperReading.text: A model is valuable because it makes assumptions explicit enough to test. Here channels become connections in a network, and changing flow alters their capacities through erosion and sedimentation. That abstraction allows researchers to examine how local change might spread. It also leaves out much of social life: who organized repairs, how communities responded, and how political priorities changed. The historical interpretation is strongest when the modeled mechanism is tested against independently dated archaeological and environmental evidence. It is weaker if the model is retold as a witnessed sequence of events.

deeperReading.title: Four instruments, four questions
deeperReading.text: The satellite image is a modern view of surface patterns. Lidar models ground elevation and exposes subtle forms beneath vegetation. Excavation investigates deposits and material remains in selected places. A network model tests the behavior of a simplified system. These approaches complement one another precisely because they do different work. Seeing a rectangular reservoir from space does not date its construction; finding an occupation layer does not map every household. Begin with the question, then choose the evidence suited to answering it.

deeperReading.title: Do not turn 1431 into an on/off switch
deeperReading.text: The Angkor Wat study places local changes within a much longer sequence and cautions against treating conventional political chronology as a universal date of abandonment. People could leave one precinct, continue worship at another and alter the use of surrounding mounds. Our broad ninth–fifteenth-century frame organizes a capital-era investigation; it is not a claim that the settlement was created in 800 or emptied in 1500. Continuing communities belong to the history of the place, not only to an epilogue about modern tourism.

subjects.question: Can objects and paintings embody competing views of an ordered world?
subjects.summary: Song institutions joined court service, commercial activity and skilled production. A tea bowl makes material work visible; a proposal about crop loans exposes a different relationship between officials and farming households. Neither stands for everyone’s experience. Northern and Southern Song had different capital settings, while neighboring states and changing borders prevent a single unchanging picture of China.

sections.title: A bowl begins with work, rather than a dynasty label
sections.text: This Jian-ware bowl is stoneware with a dark, streaked glaze conventionally called hare’s fur. Its catalogue date is the eleventh–twelfth century, a range spanning more than one political phase. Forming a vessel and controlling its fired surface required practical skill. The photograph shows a finished object; it does not identify its potter, fuel supply, purchaser or a shipment to the capital. A name for a ware is not a complete workshop history.

citations.locator: Artwork details, accession 91.1.226 and supplied image

sections.title: Market exchange depended on other people’s tasks
sections.text: The Columbia teaching account describes markets spreading through cities and the countryside, specialized producers and water transport for bulky goods such as grain. Growing for sale linked a household’s choices to buyers and prices. Boats still needed loading, routes and provisioning. Commercial activity therefore involved several kinds of work, beyond making a fine bowl. The presence of markets does not by itself establish that every cultivator became wealthier or had equal bargaining power.

citations.locator: Robert Hymes excerpt; grain transport and cash-cropping passages

sections.title: A proposal tried to alter the timing of debt
sections.text: In the 1069 crop-loan memorial, the fiscal commission proposed using public reserves to lend before harvest and accept repayment with later tax instalments. It also described buying grain when prices were low and selling when high to moderate price swings. For a household, receiving resources before a crop was ready could matter as much as an annual total. This is the policy’s stated rationale. Whether officials made borrowing voluntary, and how repayment worked after poor harvests, require evidence beyond the proposal.

citations.locator: Longer selection: 1069 memorial, reserves, loans and repayment

sections.title: Court culture did not exhaust government
sections.text: The Met essay contrasts imperial painting patronage with scholar-official expression. Such cultural differences help explain competing ideals, but offices also collected taxes, kept records and provisioned military forces. Hartman argues that accounts focused only on elite literati leave other political workers out. Read the bowl, a court ideal and a fiscal proposal together without making them interchangeable evidence. A ceramic surface cannot tell us whether a named loan was repaid.

citations.locator: Introduction pp. 3–5: political actors and fiscal/military work

sections.title: The southern court belongs to a later phase
sections.text: The conventional Northern Song frame ends in 1127, when the court lost its northern capital to the Jurchen Jin. Southern Song government was centered at Hangzhou; it ended with the Mongol conquest in 1279. These transitions changed political geography. They did not make a bowl’s broad date exact or turn the whole region into one uninterrupted jurisdiction.

claims.text: The selected tea bowl is eleventh–twelfth-century Jian ware, separate from the full Song dynastic frame.

deeperReading.title: Follow a reserve through the proposed cycle
deeperReading.text: The memorial joins three things often separated in a summary: grain stocks, cash and the timing of tax collection. Loans used reserves to address a seasonal shortage, then brought repayment into an official collection cycle. It also allowed delay after disaster. The diagram maps these proposed relationships, not a measured flow of grain or money. A government’s justification explains why its authors wanted a measure adopted. Local accounts, petitions and disputes would test what a particular household actually faced.

citations.locator: Longer selection: kinds of reserves, tax instalments and disaster deferral

deeperReading.title: A capital move does not date a ceramic
deeperReading.text: Keep the dynasty’s phase labels separate from the object’s range. The catalogue’s eleventh–twelfth-century description remains useful even without assigning the bowl to one side of 1127. Kaifeng and Hangzhou are approximate capital-area locators; neither point is the bowl’s documented findspot or production kiln. Nor does selecting a year on the atlas narrow the museum’s date. This distinction allows a material investigation to sit within a longer political account without supplying missing provenance.

deeperReading.title: Who appears in a history of government?
deeperReading.text: Hartman’s introduction reviews sharply different modern interpretations of Song governance. His own argument broadens attention to clerks and military officials, as well as the monarch and literati. This is an interpretive intervention, not a settled vote among historians. It prompts a practical question: whose work disappears when the surviving voices belong mostly to highly educated officials? A household budget or a clerk’s register could answer questions that a painting or policy defense leaves open.

citations.locator: Introduction pp. 1–5: contending interpretations and political participation

evidenceReading.title: Distinguish a proposal, an object and an interpretation
evidenceReading.introduction: The sources do different jobs. None supplies a census of ordinary experience.

items.interpretation: This explains intended timing, not the observed debt or consent of every household.

items.interpretation: Material and date attribution do not identify the maker, buyer or loan used to make it.

items.text: Hartman challenges a political history limited to emperor and literati.
items.interpretation: An attributed interpretation helps frame questions without becoming a contemporary Song witness.

evidence.text: A regional comparison is more secure than a precise itinerary or named maker.

obligation.text: Rotating service, resettlement and textile work were distinct arrangements. Provisioning does not establish equal choice or returns; the selected tunic cannot be assigned a particular obligation without provenance.

subjects.name: Inca weaving: skill across highlands and coast
subjects.place: Peru; highland technique and coastal comparisons
subjects.geographicPrecision: Broad Peruvian regional locator; no precise findspot or full itinerary is asserted.

interval.label: Tunic catalogue range, 1450–1550 CE
interval.note: A broad object range crossing the C6/C7 boundary and Spanish conquest; not the lifespan of the Inca state.

subjects.question: How can the way cloth is made reveal connections?
subjects.summary: An Inca-attributed tunic joins skilled textile work to a larger question: how did households, specialists and state demands fit together? The finished garment and its broad date do not identify a worker’s obligations. Roads, stores, later accounts and household archaeology provide other evidence. They also expose differences between what authorities claimed, what people supplied and what particular communities could do.

sections.title: Start with the garment’s construction
sections.text: The Met describes two woven pieces sewn together, camelid hair, striped areas and a jagged design. It interprets parts of that design as added by needle darning rather than woven into the structure. Making cloth involved several decisions and skills, not decoration alone. The catalogue compares highland techniques with central-coast traditions. This is an attribution based on features; it does not provide the maker’s name, an exact findspot or the garment’s recorded path between regions.

sections.title: Work could be demanded in different ways
sections.text: Museum accounts explain mit’a as rotating labor required by the state. Agricultural work, road building and military tasks drew on people whose households also needed continuing care and production. Textile work could involve domestic makers and specialists; an obligation should not be imagined as the same job for everyone. The conceptual diagram separates household work, state demands and provisioning. It does not identify which arrangement produced this particular tunic.

sections.title: Roads and stores joined movement to authority
sections.text: NMAI describes official travelers, messengers and work parties using the roads, with ordinary travelers requiring permission. Flores Ochoa and Matos explain stores holding food and textiles as well as tools and weapons. Collecting, keeping and distributing supplies required continuing labor. Such arrangements could support workers and military forces while concentrating control. An institutional explanation is not proof that all households consented, received equal returns or avoided hunger.

sections.title: Household evidence complicates a total-control story
sections.text: At Yanawilka, a settlement of resettled laborers near Vilcashuamán, researchers studied starch on stone tools from four domestic structures. Their results include foods that could not all have grown locally. These traces indicate wider food connections even in an area of strong state presence. The authors leave open whether some foods moved through direct exchange or controlled traffic. This is a particular archaeological study, not the selected tunic’s excavation or a diet for every Inca subject.

sections.title: The object range crosses a political rupture
sections.text: The tunic’s 1450–1550 catalogue range extends across the Spanish invasion. It remains an object date, rather than the empire’s full lifespan or an exact production year. Later Indigenous criticism also matters: Guaman Poma’s manuscript addressed colonial exploitation and proposed reform. Its early-seventeenth-century perspective cannot be relabeled an eyewitness account of every preconquest textile workshop.

claims.text: The museum gives a 1450–1550 object range and interprets highland technique alongside coastal comparisons.

deeperReading.title: Rotating service and resettlement are different
deeperReading.text: The Yanawilka study distinguishes mit’a, involving turns of service, from mitmaqkuna, communities resettled away from ancestral homes. Both could support imperial goals, but their consequences for household life differed. A temporary absence and a long-term relocation are not interchangeable. The article also discusses women assigned to textile and food work through state institutions. These categories help ask about constraint and skill without assigning a biography to an unprovenanced garment. Regional investigation is still necessary.

deeperReading.title: A plant trace is not an itinerary
deeperReading.text: The researchers analysed 53 stone tools; nine were tested in both recovery rounds. Those repeat analyses do not add nine independent tools. Starch identification uses modern comparison material, with possible indirect contact and contamination discussed explicitly. The interpretation of non-local foods concerns access, not a traced journey or a named trader. Even the authors’ conclusion leaves alternatives for how food moved. Archaeological observations can test an account of restricted travel while still leaving mechanisms unresolved.

deeperReading.title: Indigenous authorship belongs in its own context
deeperReading.text: Guaman Poma wrote and drew under colonial rule, criticizing exploitation and addressing proposals to a Spanish king. The Royal Danish Library describes Spanish text with Quechua passages. That audience and purpose shaped the work; Indigenous authorship does not make it a transparent transcript of earlier life. Here the library introduction has been consulted, not the entire manuscript. Reading selected original pages with appropriate language expertise is a next research task, rather than an achievement claimed by linking a digitization.

evidenceReading.title: Separate skill, obligation and observed household traces
evidenceReading.introduction: The garment, institutional explanations and a local excavation are related questions, not one continuous provenance.

items.label: A constructed textile

items.interpretation: These features support discussion of skill, not identification of a worker’s consent or labor category.

items.label: Turning service into supplies
items.text: Museum accounts describe rotating work and stores used for several kinds of goods.
items.interpretation: Provisioning and obligation belong together, but equal returns cannot be assumed.

items.label: Food beyond the local environment
items.text: The Yanawilka authors identify non-local foods through starch analysis.
items.interpretation: They leave direct exchange and state-controlled movement as alternatives. The tunic has no demonstrated connection to this site.

subjects.name: Voyaging to Aotearoa: knowledge at sea
subjects.place: East Polynesia and Aotearoa New Zealand
subjects.geographicPrecision: Destination-region locator; no exact reconstructed canoe track.

interval.note: Te Ara synthesis of arrival/settlement evidence. Not an exact first landfall or the beginning/end of Māori identity.

subjects.question: How can practiced knowledge leave evidence without a stone monument?
subjects.summary: Reaching Aotearoa depended on boats, provisions and learned judgment at sea. Archaeological dates investigate settlement; attributed accounts of teaching and practice explain knowledge that need not take the form of a written chart. Those sources have different purposes, and modern voyaging has its own history.

sections.title: Preparation made sailing possible
sections.text: A canoe needed more than a destination. Taonui describes food taken aboard, water stored in gourds and rain caught during a voyage. Preparing and managing supplies made a continuing journey possible. His account also describes directions held in memory or song and departure bearings judged against land and stars. These are connected tasks: making a seaworthy vessel, provisioning it and learning how to keep a course. They explain practical work without assigning one cargo, crew size or departure point to every ancestral voyage.

sections.title: Keeping direction was practiced judgment
sections.text: The Polynesian Voyaging Society describes modern wayfinding as planning a reference course, tracking movement and finding land near the destination. Its account brings stars, sun and swells together, rather than treating one sign as an infallible instruction. It also names teachers: Mau Piailug of Satawal guided Hōkūleʻa to Tahiti in 1976; Nainoa Thompson learned with him and later navigated voyages. This documented modern practice shows knowledge being taught and used. It does not reproduce a particular medieval journey to Aotearoa.

citations.locator: Modern Methods: teaching history and three components

sections.title: A small trace can test a large date claim
sections.text: Wilmshurst and colleagues investigated an earlier-settlement argument by redating rat bones and comparing gnawed and intact seed cases. Their 2008 study linked introduced-rat presence around 1280 with human arrival. The material, its context and its preparation mattered to the conclusion. A 2022 analysis by Bunbury, Petchey and Bickler incorporated marine and terrestrial dates and distinguished modeled settlement windows for the North and South islands. Research can refine chronology while leaving the exact first landing, named crews and individual experiences unresolved.

citations.locator: PDF pp. 2–3: materials and settlement windows

sections.title: Knowledge continues through people
sections.text: In a 2022 account, Māori researcher Haki Tuaupiki describes examining waiata, proverbs and other narratives in te reo Māori, alongside work with navigator Jack Thatcher. He explains environmental and seasonal knowledge and sharing research at hui and marae. This makes language, teaching and community relationships part of the explanation, beyond a list of stars. A separately dated profile describes Thatcher joining Te Aurere in 1992 and being invited to train as a navigator. These are attributed perspectives and histories, rather than one account speaking for every Pacific community.

citations.locator: Narrative research; Thatcher; sharing at hui/marae

claims.text: Te Ara dates Polynesian settlement of Aotearoa to about 1250–1300 CE. Navigators learned to steer by stars and ocean swells.

deeperReading.title: A chronology depends on its materials and assumptions
deeperReading.text: The 2022 paper does not simply average every published date. It screens contexts and materials, uses calibration curves and compares models. Its North Island 1250–1275 and South Island 1280–1295 windows are highest-probability-density intervals, normally reported at 68%, with model ages rounded to five years. They should not become certain years of departure and arrival. The authors also caution that small rat datasets and traces not directly associated with human activity need careful interpretation. This later analysis and the 2008 rat study are related evidence streams, not identical methods or interchangeable claims.

citations.locator: PDF pp. 2–3: settlement/rat discussion; p. 7: Bayesian Analysis

deeperReading.title: Relationships do not become a simple calendar
deeperReading.text: Te Ara explains how converting generations to years depends on assumptions about their length and selection. A changing calculation need not erase the relationships or meanings carried by a tradition. Tuaupiki’s account instead shows a scholar working through language, scattered records and conversations with a practicing navigator. Only that published account was consulted here: no complete waiata or tribal history has been independently translated. A reader should ask who is speaking, how the knowledge is transmitted and what question an archaeological date can actually answer.

Literature, language expertise and work with Thatcher

deeperReading.title: Modern success is evidence with its own date
deeperReading.text: The 1976 voyage demonstrates the working possibility of learned wayfinding under documented modern conditions. It is not a medieval crew list or proof of one ancestral route. Thompson’s Hawaiian star compass is a particular teaching system; its maker requires permission for reproduction. No compass is copied here.

evidenceReading.title: Practiced knowledge, a proxy and a dated model
evidenceReading.introduction: These are editorial paraphrases of selected publications, not a new translation of an ancestral narrative or a reanalysis of archaeological samples.

items.label: A rat-gnawed seed is a dated material, not a voyage log
items.text: The 2008 study compares dated rat bones and seed cases and infers introduced-rat arrival around 1280.
items.interpretation: The human-arrival inference depends on the relationship between transported rats, deposits and measured ages. The trace does not identify a crew, exact landing, canoe or course; later studies can revise the model.

items.label: A range belongs to a specified model
items.text: The 2022 analysis separates North and South Island settlement windows and normally reports 68% highest-probability-density intervals.
items.interpretation: The intervals are probabilistic estimates from selected material and assumptions. They are neither exact event dates nor a measured travel time between islands. The complete 1250–1300 case remains unchanged.

items.label: A named account makes teaching visible
items.text: Tuaupiki describes researching narratives in te reo Māori, working with Thatcher and sharing knowledge through community meetings.
items.interpretation: This published account supports a particular explanation of practice and transmission. It is not a complete oral corpus, universal community position or permission to reproduce cultural knowledge, and it does not imply approval of this atlas.

steps: Read the supplied capsule together. Write four cards: preparing supplies; practicing navigation; dating a seed; interpreting a model.
Match each card to a question: how can a voyage be sustained; how can direction be judged; when was a material alive; what settlement window does the analysis support?
Separate the approximate medieval settlement window, the 1976 modern voyage and the 2008/2022 study dates. Explain why a paper’s date is not a canoe’s date.
Name a familiar skill learned through practice in your own family or community. What could another person observe, and what would they still need to learn from a teacher?
familyActivity.explanation: Source capsule — editorial paraphrase: Taonui describes preparing food and water and using remembered stars and swells for navigation. The Polynesian Voyaging Society records Mau Piailug navigating Hōkūleʻa to Tahiti in 1976, and later teaching. A 2008 study used rat bones and gnawed seeds to infer introduced-rat arrival around 1280. A 2022 study modeled different North and South Island settlement windows. Practice, a dated trace, an inference and a modern voyage are different kinds of evidence; none supplies one exact ancestral crew or route. The task uses the supplied text, not an absent image. It does not teach navigation at sea, copy a star compass or reenact a cultural performance. A dated seed informs a chronology only through context and interpretation; a practicing person can explain a working skill without supplying an exact medieval event date.

review.reviewer: Codex selected source consultation and internal author QA; not independent historian or Māori/community approval
review.scope: Five new selected sources, two explicitly retained-and-renewed source scopes, layered explanation, a source-qualified reference and text-supplied family inquiry. The 1250–1300 interval is an estimate for settlement. The 4 November claim review separates the dating evidence from evidence of navigation. No new map, media, annotation, source figure or reconstructed voyage is added.
limitations: Only selected 2008 HTML and selected 2022 PDF text were consulted. Supplementary samples, calibration/code and original excavations were not independently reanalysed; PDF screenshots failed, so no figure pixels are claimed inspected.

The complete ancestral narratives, original waiata, restricted knowledge and full research/recording corpus were not read, translated or performed. Attributed contemporary accounts are not all-Polynesian consensus or community approval.
Modern PVS and Thatcher accounts retain their own periods. No single Great Fleet, exact ancestral course, named medieval crew, universal provisions or precise first landing is recovered.

There is no existing image in this dossier. Te Papa’s Te Aurere page was encountered principally in te reo Māori, and source captions identify modern voyages/photos; no unverified translation, exposure date, reuse licence or new asset is adopted.
PVS expressly requires permission to reproduce Thompson’s Hawaiian star compass. No source compass or geometry is copied or supplied as an ancient Aotearoa chart.
The selected reference does not end voyaging or Māori identity at 1300. Independent historical/community review, real family use, screen-reader/device behavior and physical print remain open.

work-organization.text: Textile work linked machine operation with homes, subsistence and schooling. Statutory protection depended on covered categories, usable records and investigation. A complaint, an inspection power and a completed improvement are different evidence; neither one complaint nor one reported benefit measures every workplace.

production.text: Textile production involved children’s labor and contested regulation.

participation.text: A written restriction required inspection and implementation, whose success needs evidence.

subjects.name: Factory reform: a law and the work of enforcement
subjects.place: British textile factories; locator near Manchester
subjects.geographicPrecision: Regional industrial anchor, not a location for every inspector’s report.

interval.label: Act in 1833; inspector evidence in 1836
interval.note: Selected law-and-enforcement investigation, not the beginning/end of industrialization or child labor.

subjects.question: Does passing a law mean a workplace has changed?
subjects.summary: Textile production joined machinery with skilled tasks, household needs and children’s time. The 1833 Act created obligations and inspection powers; later records let us investigate their operation. Protection required evidence and continuing work, with results that cannot be read directly from the date a law passed.

sections.title: Threads and machines still required people
sections.text: Spinning turned cotton into yarn, but machinery still needed people to repair broken threads and clear waste. The Science Museum’s account describes skilled work within a hot, noisy production process. Quarry Bank supplies a particular background: the National Trust describes cotton spinning brought under one roof, with a water wheel powering machinery and a steam engine later assisting it. This organized power, materials and workers together. The history of one mill helps explain production without making every textile process or workplace identical.

citations.locator: General spinning, repair and cleanup explanation

sections.title: Work and household arrangements were connected
sections.text: At Quarry Bank, apprentices received lodging, clothing and food in exchange for work; their lives included shared housing, chores and learning. Mill cottages linked other workers’ homes with the industrial community. These were arrangements that organized daily life as well as production. Children’s earnings were also politically contested. In 1836 Charles Villiers argued that restricting work could remove means of subsistence from families. His speech identifies a household-income argument, not proof that every family wanted the same work or hours.

citations.locator: Apprentice housing, cottages and Child labour

sections.title: The Act created a system of obligations
sections.text: The Act dated 29 August 1833 named powered textile processes and regulated children and young persons. Different provisions began at different times, with industry exceptions. The Act used certificates for defined age groups and school-attendance vouchers for children within its schooling provisions. Employment therefore depended on specified documents as well as a spoken promise. Parents or guardians had a role in choosing a school, with provision for an inspector to act when needed. Keeping records and providing schooling therefore became part of making protection operate. The statute supplied requirements; its existence did not establish that every certificate was accurate or every lesson useful.

citations.locator: Clauses I, VII–VIII, XI–XIII and XVIII–XXI

sections.title: An inspector had to investigate what happened
sections.text: The law empowered inspectors to enter operating mills, question people and require records. In the extract identified as an 1836 report, an inspector describes boys at Taylor, Ibbotson & Co. reporting work from Friday morning into Saturday afternoon, with breaks. He says he repeated his questions and went to look at the time book, then stated that he intended punishment. That sequence reveals investigative work. The extract does not give the book’s findings or a completed prosecution, so an intention cannot be counted as an enforced penalty.

citations.locator: Lesson PDF, printed p. 9, Source 1 transcript

sections.title: Results needed comparison
sections.text: A reported complaint does not prove that protection achieved nothing. In the 1836 Commons debate, Hindley quoted Inspector Howell describing instances of benefit, particularly stopping children’s night work. These reported observations also fall short of a national success rate. Read together, the records turn a legislative milestone into an inquiry about institutions, particular workplaces and outcomes.

claims.text: The archival investigation pairs the 1833 law with an 1836 inspector report to test enforcement.

citations.locator: Teacher’s Notes, p. 3, and Source 1, pp. 8–9

deeperReading.title: Read a provision before making a headline
deeperReading.text: The statute’s categories and exceptions matter. Clause VII’s restriction on younger children excepts silk manufacture, while further coverage is phased. Certification clauses refer to a child’s strength and appearance, rather than supplying a modern independently verified birth record. The selected scan itself requires care: clause VIII’s body says Nine Hours, while its marginal heading says Eight Hours. This account keeps that difference visible and avoids turning an uncertain shorthand into a single universal daily limit. Further edition and legal-history collation remains open.

deeperReading.title: Follow the chain from testimony to outcome
deeperReading.text: The boys reach us through an inspector’s selected report. Their consistent answers are evidence he says he collected, while looking at a time book is an action he reports taking. Neither tells us the book’s contents, the boys’ ages or what a court eventually did. The extract also leaves meal-break lengths incomplete, so it cannot support an exact net-work calculation. A conviction record, follow-up inspection and later testimony could answer different questions about enforcement. They have not been consulted here and must not be invented.

citations.locator: Questioning, time book, breaks and intended punishment

deeperReading.title: Parliament selected evidence for an argument
deeperReading.text: Hindley quoted inspectors while opposing a proposed alteration; Villiers emphasized family subsistence. Their choices explain political purposes without making either speaker the voice of all workers. Howell’s reported benefits and the particular complaint remain different observations. The museum’s much later 1927 spinning mule supplies general process interpretation, not an image or workplace record from 1833.

evidenceReading.title: A rule, an investigation and evidence of change
evidenceReading.introduction: These are editorial paraphrases of selected sources. The statute, the inspector’s account and the parliamentary quotations do different jobs.

items.label: A statutory obligation describes what should happen
items.text: The Act empowers inspection and the keeping of employment and school-attendance records. Its named processes, exceptions and phased provisions define its scope.
items.interpretation: This supports a claim about the institutional design of protection. It does not establish that a workplace complied or a document was accurate. The body/margin hours discrepancy is preserved in deeper reading, rather than hidden inside a universal summary.

items.label: Checking a book is not the same as reporting its result
items.text: The inspector says he questioned the boys, heard consistent accounts, looked at a time book and intended punishment.
items.interpretation: The extract makes his method and judgment visible. It does not state what the book contained, prove every age-specific breach or report a completed penalty. More evidence is needed to connect investigation with outcome.

citations.locator: Lesson PDF, printed p. 9, Source 1 transcript

items.label: One complaint and one reported benefit have different limits
items.text: In the Commons debate, Hindley quotes Howell reporting instances where limiting work and ending night work benefited children.
items.interpretation: That is evidence quoted within a political argument, not a complete national measurement. It prevents equating the particular Taylor, Ibbotson complaint with zero improvement everywhere, while leaving the extent and durability of change open.

familyActivity.title: A rule is the start of a test
steps: Read the source capsule with an adult. Make cards headed Rule, Investigation and Outcome still to check.
Sort the power to examine records, the inspector’s questioning of boys, his looking at a time book and his intention to punish. Explain which are reported actions and which are powers or intentions.
Name one record that could help establish what happened afterwards. Say what you would look for in it, without inventing its contents.
Write a conclusion that allows both the reported complaint and instances of benefit to remain visible. Explain why neither measures every workplace.
familyActivity.explanation: Source capsule — editorial paraphrase: the 1833 Act gave inspectors powers to question people and require records in covered workplaces. In the extract dated 1836, an inspector says he heard boys’ consistent accounts of prolonged work, looked at a time book and intended punishment. The extract does not tell us the book’s findings or a completed penalty. In a separate parliamentary debate, Hindley quoted Howell reporting instances of benefit, especially stopping night work. The activity asks what each record establishes; it does not require an exact hours calculation, graphic reenactment or an invented child’s diary.

The Act’s passage, staged commencements, particular report and debate are different evidence; the 1927 museum machine is later.

work-organization.text: Photographic investigation and publicity could expose a disputed workplace scene. Applying age and hour rules required a separate system of reliable records, certificates and inspection. Neither a reform image nor the existence of a statute alone proves workers’ ages or effective protection.

subjects.name: A child in a cotton mill: photograph and caption
subjects.place: Newberry, South Carolina, United States
subjects.geographicPrecision: Named mill town from Hine’s caption, not the child’s home address.

interval.label: 3 December 1908
interval.note: Date of photograph and caption; not a known birth date, age or whole working life.

subjects.question: What does a photograph show, and what does its caption claim?
subjects.summary: A photograph, its caption and an inspection report reveal different kinds of work. Hine’s mill scene became part of a reform campaign; the caption reports an overseer’s denial. Later officials checked age evidence and inspected workplaces to apply particular rules. Neither the child’s age nor effective protection follows from the image alone.

sections.title: Machinery, a person and a chosen view
sections.text: A young figure stands in an aisle between long rows of spinning machinery. The repeated machine parts fill much of the image, while windows light one side of the room. Comparing the person’s height with the equipment makes the setting’s scale visible. Hine chose where to stand and when to expose the photograph. The supplied view documents this arrangement at one moment; it does not let us watch a complete task or reconstruct a working day.

sections.title: Investigation also required circulation
sections.text: The National Child Labor Committee employed Hine for investigative and photographic work from 1908. Photographs travelled through reports, the organization’s publications, newspapers, slide shows and exhibits. Making a case involved recording conditions and arranging evidence for audiences who might never enter the workplace. The Library of Congress describes Hine taking charge of the exhibits department in 1913. Photography belonged to a continuing campaign, alongside writing and display work; one image cannot measure the campaign’s reach or its effects.

citations.locator: Background and Scope: hiring, distribution and exhibits

sections.title: A caption records a contested explanation
sections.text: The selected caption says the child was tending her sides of the machinery, then reports an overseer saying, “She just happened in.” That is a conversation recorded in the campaign’s account, rather than speech audible in the photograph. Another Mollahan caption, dated the same day, identifies a group as spinners and doffers and names Sara R. Hine as witness. Together these records make a small evidence series: they show how work was described, without verifying ages or counting every child employed.

citations.locator: Indexed caption title: reported conversation; 3 December 1908
Indexed caption title: group, date and named witness

sections.title: A rule needed records and inspectors
sections.text: The 1916 Keating-Owen Act addressed interstate and foreign shipment of specified products made under prohibited age or hour conditions. It authorized workplace inspections and provided for age certificates. The act took effect in September 1917. The Children’s Bureau’s later administration report explains why issuing a certificate was a job of checking evidence: a paper approved on unreliable information could leave inspectors having to establish age again. A statutory limit, a document and a verified fact were different things.

sections.title: Inspection gives a bounded comparison
sections.text: In its spring 1918 South Carolina inspections, the Bureau reported twenty children under fourteen employed in nine of sixty-four establishments visited. It separately recorded missing federal certificates. These are findings from an inspected sample, not a statewide census or identification of this child ten years earlier. The act was declared unconstitutional in June 1918; later visits and state arrangements did not simply disappear. Following changes in working conditions therefore requires dated inspection evidence as well as photographs and the text of a law.

claims.text: The catalogue dates the photograph to 3 December 1908 and identifies its caption as an NCLC caption card.

subjects.returnPrompt: Write one observation from the image and one claim that depends on the caption.

deeperReading.title: The caption is evidence with its own history
deeperReading.text: The Library of Congress transcribed titles, places and dates from caption cards received with the NCLC collection. Its collection account does not establish precisely who compiled every card. Typed strips, handwritten additions and later institutional annotations could share the same surface. Some cards were prepared after the photograph, or described a later revisit. The selected account credits a witness and preserves a reported denial, but neither feature independently checks every statement. The child’s own explanation, a verified age record and a complete employment history remain absent. Reading the caption critically does not require discarding it; it means naming whose account supplies each claim.

citations.locator: The Photo Captions: compilation, witnesses and accuracy
Indexed caption title; earlier catalogue consultation retained

deeperReading.title: A series expands questions without becoming a census
deeperReading.text: A second caption can identify another kind of view or another description of work. It cannot turn a deliberately assembled reform collection into a random sample. The Library’s discussion of Hine’s technique also draws attention to choices of framing and focus across other photographs; those examples are not measurements of this image’s camera settings. Finefield’s later account shows students combining photographs with other records to investigate questions. Here, the enforcement report supplies a different source series with stated places, dates and administrative categories. Its authors were describing their own institution’s work, and missing papers were not automatically proof of underage employment. Comparing these sources reveals how claims were made and checked while keeping their populations, purposes and dates distinct.

citations.locator: Indexed caption title only; image not inspected

evidenceReading.title: A scene, related captions and an enforcement record
evidenceReading.introduction: The following are visible observations and editorial paraphrases of identified records. The companion photograph itself is not supplied or newly inspected; its indexed caption title forms the second written record.

items.label: Visible machinery; a reported conversation
items.text: The supplied photograph shows a young figure beside spinning machinery. Its caption reports the overseer saying, “She just happened in,” after the picture was taken.
items.interpretation: The machinery and relative scale can be examined directly. The denial depends on the caption’s account of a conversation. Neither provides a verified birth date, wage, full working day or the child’s own testimony. The caption’s argument should not become an invented biography.

citations.locator: Actual local photograph; indexed caption title, Hine 358

items.label: A second caption gives a group description
items.text: LOC item 2018674903 describes spinners and doffers at Mollahan Mills, dates the caption 3 December 1908 and names Sara R. Hine as witness.
items.interpretation: This supplies a related, separately identified record; it does not establish that the selected child appears in another view. A title naming occupations is evidence of how the group was described. Its assertion about other small workers does not verify their ages or establish a workforce count. Only indexed caption text was accessible in this consultation.

items.label: A legal standard and an observed sample answer different questions
items.text: The 1916 act authorized inspection and age certificates. The Bureau’s 1921 report records underage employment and missing federal certificates as separate findings in its spring 1918 South Carolina inspection sample.
items.interpretation: The law establishes a prescribed rule; the report describes particular administrative findings. Their difference makes enforcement assessable. Neither retrospectively proves the selected child’s age or that one photograph caused legislation. The report was read in HTML transcription; its linked PDF was unavailable.

Its caption reports that an overseer denied the child was working. A separate caption describes a group at that mill as spinners and doffers. These records do not verify this child’s exact age or hours. A later Children’s Bureau report explains that age certificates based on unreliable evidence could require inspectors to check ages again. A dated birth record could help investigate age; a dated work or inspection record could help investigate hours. None is supplied for this child.

work-organization.text: Reeling joined trained handwork with machinery; sericulture, teaching and cold storage solved different practical problems. Learning could spread while the conditions and protection of workers remained unequal and source-specific.

production.text: Imported machinery worked within local farming, training and construction networks.

evidence.text: Industrial heritage documents a production system more directly than every worker’s experience.

subjects.name: Tomioka: adapting an industrial system
subjects.place: Gunma Prefecture, Japan
subjects.geographicPrecision: Mill-site locator within a regional production system.

interval.label: Model mill opened October 1872
interval.note: Opening event; the mill and associated techniques continued afterward. This is not an endpoint for Japanese industrialization.

subjects.question: What does it take to move a technology between places?
subjects.summary: Tomioka’s imported machinery depended on trained women, local building work and people raising silkworms. Later teaching, adaptation and storage extended the inquiry beyond the model mill; evidence of working conditions and legal protection needs its own dates and places.

sections.title: A machine still needs practiced hands
sections.text: When the government mill opened in October 1872, machinery arrived within an existing silk-producing region. Japanese carpenters constructed buildings that joined French design with local timber, brick and plaster work. Inside, women learned demanding operations. Sashinami describes sorting cocoons, finding and drawing their filaments from hot water, joining them into raw silk and winding at the speed of powered machinery. Reliable output depended on attention and practice. A reel could organize motion without making the worker’s judgment unnecessary. French instructors and Japanese women trained by them helped others acquire these skills.

citations.locator: Tomioka Silk Mill; Women Mill Workers

sections.title: Workers carried knowledge elsewhere
sections.text: One learner became a teacher. The National Diet Library records Wada Ei(ko) at Tomioka from April 1873 to July 1874, followed by instruction at another mill and, in 1878, a prefectural appointment. Her career makes women active participants in moving techniques. At the separate Rokkōsha mill in Matsushiro, imported arrangements were reworked using local materials. Nakamura and Molteni explain how other mills also replaced expensive components and combined different technical models. Adaptation involved decisions about construction, power and handling, rather than simply copying a complete French factory. Wada’s remembered comparison was written much later.

sections.title: The crop has its own timetable
sections.text: Silk work also depended on keeping silkworms alive and producing cocoons. The region’s farmhouse experiments managed airflow, warmth and humidity. Takayama-sha became a school in 1884, joining teaching with practical rearing. Arafune’s first cold-storage units began operating in 1905. Cooling delayed eggs hatching; marked cards, testing, labels and catalogues helped organize storage and return. Such work changed when a living crop could be raised. The four heritage components therefore explain connected functions with different beginnings. They are not four parts opened together in 1872, nor proof of one recovered shipment between them.

sections.title: Training and protection are different questions
sections.text: Learning a valuable skill did not settle who controlled working time. Tomioka’s institutional account describes dormitories and trainers. Broader evidence from Suwa concerns other workplaces and must stay located there. The Factory Act was promulgated in 1911 but implemented only in September 1916. Its initial scope and exceptions matter when asking what protection meant in practice. Buildings, production and a model institution’s aims cannot alone tell us whether every worker could rest, leave or benefit equally.

claims.text: The mill opened in October 1872, combining French technical input with Japanese construction and regional silk expertise.

deeperReading.title: A recollection has more than one date
deeperReading.text: Wada’s experience and its publication are separate evidence. The NDL says that she began writing memories in 1907; an edited book appeared in 1931. Nakamura and Molteni’s 1994 English chapter quotes a later Japanese edition when discussing her visit to Rokkōsha. Their chapter calls her Wada Hide, while the NDL uses Ei(ko). Here the biographical and technical accounts remain attributed to their sources. The original Japanese memoir and those editions have not been independently read or translated. The comparison shows what one remembered about adapting materials, without becoming a contemporary inspection of every reel.

deeperReading.title: Implementation is not a completed outcome
deeperReading.text: The National Archives separates the 1911 law from its 1916 implementation. Nakamura and Molteni describe provisions allowing extended hours in silk-reeling. They also mediate a woman’s recollection of long days at an Okaya mill in 1917, the year after implementation. Their note leads to a 1981 publication; that original interview volume was not read here. The factory-inspection annual they cite is another record, not this woman’s own speech. Together these materials make a useful question: what happened after a rule existed? They do not supply a complete compliance history for Tomioka or speak for every worker. A model mill, a law and a worker’s retrospective account each require a different kind of interpretation.

evidenceReading.title: Hands, memories and rules
evidenceReading.introduction: These are editorial paraphrases of selected passages. A training account, a later recollection and an institutional legal caption answer different questions.

items.label: Technical skill is part of production
items.text: Sashinami’s exposed introduction describes women learning to sort cocoons, join filaments and reel at machine speed, then teaching other women.
items.interpretation: Machinery and human practice worked together. The passage does not count every trainee, recover each woman’s consent or establish every factory’s conditions.

items.label: A memory can explain a comparison
items.text: The NDL dates Wada’s Tomioka employment to 1873–74 and her memory-writing from 1907. The 1994 chapter uses her later account when comparing materials at Rokkōsha.
items.interpretation: Experience, remembering, editing and translation have different dates. The original Japanese memoir was not freshly read, and Rokkōsha’s equipment is not silently transferred to Tomioka.

items.label: A law needs an implementation history
items.text: The National Archives gives 1911 promulgation and September 1916 implementation. The labor chapter discusses exceptions and a later recollection of long working days at Okaya.
items.interpretation: The legal dates establish different steps. The recollection supplies a particular remembered experience through a later publication, rather than proving uniform compliance or violation at every mill.

familyActivity.title: What would a machine still need?
steps: Use the supplied capsule to name three jobs: tending silkworms, reeling silk and keeping egg cards in cool storage. Explain why one machine could not do all three.

If the contemporary mill print is included, find two rows of people and equipment, and the roof supports. Describe what is drawn. If it is not available, use the capsule’s description of those features.

Sort two questions: What arrangement does the artist show? Could every worker leave or rest when she wanted? Decide which needs more evidence, then return to the opening question about moving technology.
familyActivity.explanation: Source capsule — editorial paraphrase: Tomioka opened in October 1872. Reeling required women to handle filaments and learn machine-paced work; other tasks included raising silkworms. Takayama-sha became a practical sericulture school in 1884, and Arafune’s first cold-storage units operated in 1905. Cooling helped delay hatching, while labels and catalogues organized egg cards. The NDL’s contemporary interior print arranges workers and equipment in two receding rows beneath roof supports. It is an artist’s published representation, not a photograph, payroll or complete account of freedom and rest. The NDL brackets its impression [1872]; MAFF dates a comparable impression 1873. The date match is mill/1872, school/1884, storage/1905. The image can support observations about its drawn arrangement; questions about workers’ choices require appropriate records and attributed accounts.

participation.text: Enslaved people’s resistance and differing revolutionary interests shaped independence.

evidence.text: A declaration establishes a political statement; other records are needed for the lives of its many participants.

subjects.name: Haiti: freedom fought for in a plantation world
subjects.place: Saint-Domingue/Haiti, Caribbean
subjects.geographicPrecision: Gonaïves declaration-region locator; the revolution involved many places and changing alliances.

interval.label: Revolutionary investigation, 1791–1804
interval.note: Uprising to independence; not the end of the consequences of slavery or colonial power.

subjects.question: Who made freedom, and why was it contested?
subjects.summary: Enslaved people’s resistance broke the plantation order, but emancipation, control of work and independence were distinct struggles. Regional research, a leader’s letter and constitutional rules show people making different political choices. The 1804 declaration severed French rule while also establishing authority; it does not speak directly for every household.

sections.title: Resistance grew through different local struggles
sections.text: Sugar and coffee production depended on coerced work. In 1791, enslaved people challenged that order in the northern plantation region. Sabine Manigat’s research distinguishes this uprising from different conflicts in the West and South. Insurgent groups, free people of color, colonists and competing armies formed shifting alliances rather than one stable camp. War and negotiation created openings for people seeking liberty. Regional differences help explain how a struggle could change direction without assuming everyone began with the same plan for an independent nation.

sections.title: Emancipation had to be defended and interpreted
sections.text: Provincial emancipation measures in 1793 preceded the French Convention’s 1794 colonial abolition decree. Deputies carried events in Saint-Domingue into metropolitan politics. Louverture, a formerly enslaved leader, offers one particular political voice. His 1797 letter asks Vincent to defend him before the Directory, rejects racist accusations and affirms attachment to France. The argument makes sense within that moment’s commitments. It does not turn him into the spokesman for every cultivator, nor make independence the inevitable meaning of all earlier resistance.

citations.locator: Le débat: provincial measures, delegation and decree

sections.title: Ending slavery did not settle control of work
sections.text: The 1801 constitution prohibits slavery and calls people free and French. It also insists that cultivation continue. Articles 15–16 picture an estate as a family led by its owner or representative, promise cultivators a share of revenues and treat changes of residence as a threat to production. The governor receives police powers to regulate them. This language connects agricultural output with political control: freedom from enslavement and freedom to leave a workplace were not treated as identical questions. The rules are evidence of a governing project, not proof that workers consented or received what was promised.

sections.title: Independence created another political settlement
sections.text: The French expedition of 1802 renewed the threat to emancipation and met resistance. Independence was proclaimed in 1804. The Acte records assembled generals renouncing France; its claim of agreement concerns that gathering. Armitage and Gaffield distinguish the official printed pamphlet and broadside from a lost manuscript stage. They also identify an accompanying oath making Dessalines governor general for life. Political separation and the defense of liberty therefore came with a new concentration of authority. Other records are needed for landholding, work and participation beyond the leaders’ declarations.

claims.text: The printed pamphlet dates Dessalines’s address at Gonaïves on 1 January 1804.

citations.locator: Printed p. 7 (digital leaf 8), final dateline above Dessalines’s name
