Maya selected renewal, 2026-10-29: Visible Description through the 1961/1964 publication-history paragraphs, byline, Artwork Details and Public Domain statement for accession 1992.4. The Provenance heading appeared but complete tab contents were not supplied; no comprehensive renewed custody-chain consultation. Baje(?) and Kaan (or Chan) Took’ remain uncertain, the seated figure is only possibly the owner, and no polity is named. The proposed Tabasco association uses a similar Comalcalco name and Jonuta ceramic comparisons, not a newly established excavation. Cacao use/dipping is comparative interpretation, not a residue result. Original 1369×1600 local image pixels actually inspected and bytes retained; no new remote-image parity or photography-date verification. Met eligible-image CC0 policy read separately; copyrighted article rollouts/drawings not reused.

sources.title: Seated figure
sources.scope: Prior consultation (2026-10-26) retained: Accession 1981.218; Description, Artwork Details, provenance and Public Domain image statement. Selected 29 October 2026 Middle Niger renewal: Visible opening description, Artwork Details, Public Domain label and selected Met Open Access introduction read on 29 October. Thirteenth century, terracotta, Inland Niger Delta/Mali, accession 1981.218 and the 1981 purchase credit were confirmed. The narrative’s Jenne-jeno attribution is not a controlled excavated locus or contextual association for this specimen. Anxiety/prayer and illness are interpretive possibilities, not an adopted biography, diagnosis or established function. Actual unchanged front/back images and thumbnail were inspected and hashed; no remote-original byte parity or modern exposure date established. Provenance/reference tab contents and full audio were not freshly read; transcript unavailable. Direct raw HTML returned 429 and was not retried or bypassed; the official API web request was inaccessible. Earlier provenance consultation is retained separately. Existing CC0-image rights remain; no new image or catalogue-prose reuse claimed.

sources.title: Tea bowl
sources.scope: Current object details and existing supplied image inspected: accession 91.1.226, eleventh–twelfth century, stoneware with hare’s-fur glaze, Jian ware, Public Domain. No maker, exact kiln, buyer or shipment inferred. Existing image bytes retained.

sources.title: Tunic
sources.scope: Full main description and artwork details read; existing image inspected. Accession 1979.206.954, camelid hair, two woven pieces, seams and interpreted needle-darned patterns, 1450–1550 range. Highland/coast feature comparisons are attributions, not exact findspot or proven travel. The catalogue’s upper/lower terminology is not transferred into visual orientation claims; no state work order, maker identity or link to Yanawilka inferred; original image bytes retained.

sources.title: The Severan Dynasty (193–235)
sources.scope: Museum essay consulted: dynastic representation, military patronage and the citizenship grant. A broad grant did not erase differences in wealth, gender or legal condition.

sources.title: Roman Art: A Resource for Educators
sources.scope: Search-indexed PDF text consulted, printed pages 130 and 149: occupations, agriculture, legal status and freed people. Direct PDF download returned a verification page; no complete-volume consultation claimed.

sources.title: Chao Cuo: Memorial on the Encouragement of Agriculture
sources.scope: Indexed five-page teaching PDF consulted; introduction and translated memorial, especially pp. 3–5. Translation from Sources of Chinese Tradition (1999), pp. 355–357. A Western Han policy argument dated 178 BCE, not an Eastern Han census. The earlier PDF URL returned 404. On 4 November the university’s full HTML teaching edition was retrieved and read, including the final paragraph of the longer excerpt on grain, rank and pardons. Its edition and page range match the previous consultation.

sources.title: A Record of the Debate on Salt and Iron
sources.scope: Full teaching page consulted: introduction and translated excerpts from Sources of Chinese Tradition (1999), pp. 360–363. Literary record of a court debate in 81 BCE; neither verbatim audio nor a direct account of conditions in 200 CE.

sources.title: Uncovering archaeological landscapes at Angkor using lidar
sources.scope: Full article consulted: abstract, methods, urban landscapes and figures. DOI 10.1073/pnas.1306539110. Lidar reveals ground topography; interpretation and dating require other evidence.

sources.title: The demise of Angkor: Systemic vulnerability of urban infrastructure to climatic variations
sources.scope: Full article consulted: water distribution network, model, results and discussion; especially Figs. 1–2. DOI 10.1126/sciadv.aau4029. A model of network vulnerability supports a contributing mechanism, not a complete causal explanation. CC BY-NC 4.0.

sources.title: Temple occupation and the tempo of collapse at Angkor Wat, Cambodia
sources.scope: Publisher-indexed article sections consulted: life history of the temple, timing of change, and occupation of excavated mounds. Findings concern specific excavations; they are not a census of all Angkor.

sources.title: Angkor Ruins
sources.scope: 2004 ASTER image and caption consulted for the relative positions of Angkor Wat, Angkor Thom and the barays. A modern observation, not a medieval city plan. Image use follows NASA educational media guidelines with the full supplied credit.

sources.title: Oral Histories
sources.institution: The Partition Museum, Amritsar and Delhi
sources.scope: Public written summaries consulted for Sunil Chandra Ghosh, Hamida, Ila Banerjee and Ijaz Khan. Full interviews were not independently transcribed or translated; the atlas explicitly uses the museum summaries.

sources.title: Punjab boundaries and a Sikh boundary demand, 1947
sources.scope: Teaching image and supplied transcript consulted; CO 1054/76, source 3a. The solid and dashed lines distinguish an awarded border and a demand. The atlas links to the original scan. The National Archives requires Image Library permission for public reproduction.

sources.title: Naskah Sumber Arsip Presiden RI: Sukarno
sources.scope: 2015 archival volume: indexed description identifies Sukarno’s handwritten proclamation draft on printed p. 7 (PDF p. 13), ANRI Teks Proklamasi I. Description and attribution consulted through the web PDF; direct download returned 403 and the screenshot service did not return viewable pixels. The separately credited typed facsimile was visually inspected. This volume is not used as a general biography or a complete history of the revolution.

sources.title: Soevereiniteitsoverdracht Indonesië, 1949
sources.scope: Full Dutch archival teaching page consulted: 1945 proclamation, disputed sovereignty, negotiations, federal settlement and 27 December 1949 transfer. The archive’s transfer vocabulary describes the Dutch legal act; it does not replace Indonesia’s 1945 proclamation date. Exact Linggajati signing day is not adopted from this summary.

sources.title: 1945–1949: Van Nederlands-Indië naar Indonesië
sources.scope: Full Dutch military-history timeline consulted, especially 1945, July 1947, December 1948, May/December 1949 and 1950. An institutional account of Dutch operations and diplomacy, not a survey of Indonesian civilian experiences. Colonial euphemisms are identified rather than used as neutral labels. Additional consultation 4 November: Selected Dutch timeline entries 21 July 1947 and 1950 end of federal structure reconsulted. Military/administrative record not a full civilian history.

sources.title: 70 jaar soevereiniteitsoverdracht aan Indonesië
sources.scope: Full account consulted for the 27 December 1949 federal transfer and explicit exclusion of Netherlands New Guinea. No modern territorial boundary is reconstructed.

sources.title: History of Parliament
sources.scope: Full institutional history consulted for changing legislative representation, the 1951 assembly, independence in 1957 and the 1960 republic. Its national institutional perspective is paired with a contemporary debate and a later historical synthesis.

sources.title: Biography of Osagyefo Dr. Kwame Nkrumah
sources.scope: Full commemorative biography consulted for UGCC, CPP, Positive Action, imprisonment and the move to government. The institution commemorates Nkrumah; its account is not treated as an independent assessment of all his policies.

sources.title: Legislative Assembly Debates, 4–5 March 1957: Government Policy Statement
sources.scope: Original scan downloaded successfully and visually read: cover, printed columns 7–8 and 23–26 (PDF pp. 12, 20–21). Nkrumah’s policy statement is dated 5 March, before midnight independence; it is not the separate outdoor independence speech. Only those pages are used. No whole-volume OCR or transcription is claimed.

sources.title: Ghana: A Country Study
sources.institution: Federal Research Division, Library of Congress
sources.scope: LaVerle Berry, editor, 1995. Historical Setting, printed pp. 26–36 (PDF pp. 70–80), consulted for organizing, regional opposition, constitutional change and repression. Later US government synthesis with dated terminology and interpretive judgments; used alongside Ghanaian institutions and primary records. No unqualified “first independent African country” claim is adopted. Additional consultation 4 November: Table A, printed xv–xvi, and selected Historical Setting paragraphs on 1900 Asante resistance, 1947 UGCC and 1950 Positive Action rechecked against preserved PDF text. No fresh whole-volume review.
sources.author: LaVerle Berry, editor

sources.title: Address at the mural celebrating adoption of the new constitution, 8 May 1996
sources.institution: Office of the President; Department of Justice, South Africa
sources.scope: Both pages consulted. Issued speech text marked “check against delivery”; this is the May adoption celebration, not the December signing. Used as a statement of political purpose, not measured outcomes or proof of verbatim delivery.

sources.title: Certification of the New Constitution: procedure for objections
sources.scope: A. Chaskalson, 20 May 1996, both pages consulted: 34 principles, written objections, languages, deadline, copies and limits of certification jurisdiction. This procedural statement alone does not establish the Court’s later judgment.

sources.title: The path to a Government of National Unity
sources.institution: Nelson Mandela Foundation, The Presidential Years
sources.scope: Full account consulted for negotiations, interim arrangements, the 1994 government, May 1996 adoption and October amendment after Constitutional Court review. Not an account of every negotiating party or all political violence.

sources.title: History of Constitution Hill
sources.scope: Full heritage-site account consulted for apartheid-era imprisonment, resistance and the later decision to locate the Court at the former prison complex. The present Court building opened in 2004, outside this atlas’s 2000 endpoint; it is not shown as the site of 1996 hearings.

sources.title: Proklamasi.png: typed proclamation facsimile
sources.scope: File page and actual 399 × 268 image inspected. Typed facsimile with Sukarno/Hatta signatures; different from the handwritten ANRI draft. Record asserts Indonesian government-work public-domain status. The digital upload date is not the document date. Low-resolution copy; no invented restoration.

sources.title: Ghana Independence overprint on Gold Coast 1s stamp, 1957
sources.scope: File page, public-domain UK government-work rationale and 611 × 460 scan inspected. Overprint dated 6 March 1957; cocoa-pod scene and Elizabeth II remain visible underneath. Scan uploaded by Philafrenzy, 2016; no inference of a particular worker’s identity or earnings.

sources.title: Mandela voting in 1994
sources.scope: File page, permission record and 538 × 800 photograph inspected. Paul Weinberg, official IEC photographer; Ohlange School, Inanda near Durban, April 1994. Used under CC BY-SA 3.0 with credit and licence link, not labelled public domain.

sources.title: Uruk (Warka): excavation results
sources.scope: German Ergebnisse section consulted: emphasis on monumental architecture; late-fourth-millennium buildings, later residential excavations and third-millennium walls. Later house and palace evidence is not backdated to the selected tablet. No full excavation-volume review or fourth-millennium household census.

sources.title: Dholavira site plan, January 2020
sources.institution: Archaeological Survey of India; World Heritage nomination map
sources.scope: PDF p. 1: indexed labels and component key consulted, including C1/C6/C7, C5 (Stage VI), B2, M3, East/South reservoirs and D1. Direct download returned 403 and the web screenshot supplied no viewable pixels. Used for labelled components, not traced geometry or a measured reconstruction. The teaching diagram is an original schematic; this map is linked, not reproduced.

sources.title: Archaeological studies at Dholavira using GPR
sources.institution: Indian Institute of Technology Gandhinagar; Current Science 114 (2018), 879–887
sources.scope: Silky Agrawal, Mantu Majumder, R. S. Bisht and Amit Prashant. Downloaded nine-page paper; pp. 879–880 and 884–886 read, Fig. 1 and interpretation/conclusion inspected. Excavated East Reservoir is distinct from proposed buried water structures requiring excavation. Opening chronology ends at c1700 BCE, unlike UNESCO’s c1500 endpoint; neither is a precise abandonment date. Conflicting survey-area totals in the paper are not adopted.

sources.title: Earliest hydraulic enterprise in China, 5,100 years ago
sources.scope: Publisher HTML consulted: Defining the Liangzhu Hydraulic Landscape, chronology, construction/labor discussion, Conclusion, Methods and figure captions. Article text is accessible despite PMC/Europe PMC full-text retrieval failures. No downloaded PDF, supplement or figure-pixel inspection claimed. Calibrated BP uses 1950 as present; diagram is conceptual, not a traced figure. Reservoir capacities must use the 2018 correction. Labor totals are modeled estimates, not a census.

sources.title: Correction: Earliest hydraulic enterprise in China, 5,100 years ago
sources.scope: Full publisher correction consulted. Replaces the two reservoir-capacity estimates on p. 13641 with about 14.98 and 50.72 million cubic metres, respectively. These are modeled capacities, not measured ancient annual supply; the original HTML still displays the superseded values.

sources.title: Ḫattuša/Boğazköy: the Hittite capital
sources.scope: German project overview consulted: capital/cult and administrative centre c1650–1180 BCE, temples, palace, archives and later occupation. Broad orientation, not a map of one simultaneous phase or a complete institutional history.

sources.title: The Excavations at Boğazköy-Hattuša in 2015
sources.scope: Abstract only: northern Lower City residential excavation, three construction layers from kārum into Hittite periods, housing and an official building. No house plans or full excavation text consulted; Roman remains discussed in the abstract are not backdated.

sources.title: Ulu Burun: 1990 Excavation Campaign
sources.scope: Original issue downloaded. Printed pp. 8–11 read and inspected: recovered cargo, hull, joints, anchors, weights, slope movement, excavation and tentative identifications. An interim field report; partial totals and contemporary dating are not silently substituted for the later project account. Research PDF and photographs are not redistributed in the atlas.

sources.title: Tin from Uluburun shipwreck shows small-scale commodity exchange fueled continental tin supply across Late Bronze Age Eurasia
sources.institution: Wayne Powell and colleagues; Science Advances 8 (2022), eabq3766
sources.scope: Full body retrieved through PMC: Introduction, Results, Discussion subsections and Methods consulted. Chemical/isotopic comparison and source assignments are interpretations. Central Asian/Anatolian allocations are contested by Berger et al. (2023); no reconstructed trade route or percentage allocation is adopted as settled.

sources.title: Why Central Asia’s Mushiston is not a source for the Late Bronze Age tin ingots from the Uluburun shipwreck
sources.institution: Daniel Berger, Kai Kaniuth, Gerhard Brügmann and Ernst Pernicka; Frontiers in Earth Science 11 (2023)
sources.scope: Publisher abstract consulted; full critique body and figures not inspected. Challenges the 2022 source assignments and proposes alternatives; its preferred sources are not converted into a confirmed itinerary.

sources.title: From Land’s End to the Levant: did Britain’s tin sources transform the Bronze Age in Europe and the Mediterranean?
sources.institution: R. Alan Williams and colleagues; Antiquity 99 (2025), 708–726
sources.scope: Nineteen-page primary paper downloaded. Printed pp. 717–719, especially p. 718 on Uluburun, read with the lead/trace-element discussion. Contamination and possible remelting complicate Uluburun lead provenance; findings for other wrecks are not automatically assigned to this cargo. No supplement review or decisive ore-source assignment claimed.

sources.title: Yin Xu
sources.scope: Description and Brief synthesis consulted: selected late capital c1300–1046 BCE, Huan River, palace/ancestral shrine and royal tomb areas, Fu Hao, oracle bones and burial assemblages. Human remains are described as interpreted sacrificial victims. Universal priority claims and praise are not adopted.

sources.title: Making Sense of the Future: The Oracle Bone and Shang Dynasty Divination
sources.institution: Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art
sources.scope: Indexed museum lesson passages consulted: materials, rain/hunt topics and distinction among introduction, charge, prognostication and verification. Direct page retrieval failed and direct download returned 403. Its collection fragment and the separate translated hunt example are not the selected Met bone. No full-page or original object inspection claimed.

sources.title: Wine pouring vessel (Gong), 43.25.4
sources.scope: Description, Artwork Details, public-domain image label and audio transcript consulted. Bronze, 13th–11th century BCE, Henan Province, possibly Anyang; no secure excavated findspot asserted. Primary image visually inspected. Transcript discusses multiple vessels; details of another turquoise-inlaid vessel are not assigned to this gong.

sources.title: Mausoleum of the First Qin Emperor
sources.scope: English Description, Brief synthesis and criterion iv consulted for Lishan mausoleum, construction from 246 BCE, death in 210 and relationship to the capital Xianyang. No superlative, exact worker total, surveyed capital plan or imperial boundary adopted.

sources.title: Inscriptions of Asoka: Girnar II and Dhauli Separate I
sources.institution: Archaeological Survey of India; Clarendon Press; Internet Archive copy
sources.scope: Hultzsch 1925 edition: OCR read for Girnar II (printed pp. 3–4), Dhauli Separate I (pp. 95–97) and introduction on regional versions. Exact source scans of p. 4 and pp. 95–96 retrieved and visually inspected. Editorial translation and ancient message are separate. No complete volume audit; this edition predates the Kandahar Greek/Aramaic discoveries. Scans remain private research, not public assets.
sources.author: E. Hultzsch, editor and translator

sources.title: The Athenian Constitution, parts 26, 42–43
sources.scope: Kenyon English translation: parts 26, 42 and 43 consulted for the parentage rule, male enrollment scrutiny and institutional procedure. A late-fourth-century account attributed to Aristotle’s school, not a contemporary report of the selected Archaic vase. The c330 BCE orientation follows Forsdyke rather than the older MIT page header. No claim to have verified the original papyrus or every legal rule.
sources.author: Attributed to Aristotle; translated by F. G. Kenyon

sources.title: Slave Agency and Citizenship in Classical Athens
sources.institution: Symposion 2017; Österreichische Akademie der Wissenschaften; author copy at University of Michigan
sources.scope: Downloaded author PDF with volume front matter. Printed pp. 345–349 read; p. 348 citizenship passage visually inspected. Argument about status claims and networks, 451/0 and 403 BCE law and c330 treatise context. Selected legal evidence does not provide a reliable frequency of successful passing or represent every enslaved person.
sources.author: Sara Forsdyke

sources.title: Ancient Agora of Athens
sources.institution: Hellenic Heritage; archaeological site and museum
sources.scope: Historical description consulted: Agora’s mixed public uses, Bouleuterion, Tholos and State Archives, and Assembly place on the Pnyx. Modern visitor information is not used as ancient evidence. Approximate locators only; no street itinerary, exact building boundary or universal political participation inferred.

sources.title: The Tax Law of Palmyra: Evidence for Economic History in a City of the Roman East
sources.institution: Journal of Roman Studies 74 (1984), 157–180; available excerpt hosted by Ostia Antica
sources.scope: Publisher opening extract consulted. An eight-page original-paper excerpt, printed pp. 173–180, was downloaded; pp. 173–175 and selected tariff passages read, p. 175 visually inspected. Local economy, council decree, Greek/Palmyrene versions and editorial supplements; not the whole 24-page article, original stone or a new translation. The municipal tariff is not a list of every caravan journey.
sources.author: J. F. Matthews

sources.title: The Legacy of Ancient Palmyra: Ancient Palmyra
sources.scope: Trade, inscriptions, funerary sculpture and Roman/later sections read. Caravan honorific inscriptions, bilingual public writing, and the separate 272/273 sieges are used. No population total, universal religious tolerance, willful language-suppression claim or direct travel from every network endpoint adopted. Images/maps linked, not reproduced.
sources.author: Frances Terpak and Peter Louis Bonfitto

sources.title: The Brother and the Sister, the Tablet, the Epitaph, and their Tutor
sources.institution: Centre for the Study of Manuscript Cultures, University of Hamburg; Artefact of the Month 31
sources.scope: Full illustrated essay read. It concerns Berlin 27/65, a different relief with Yarhai and Mainat. Hypothetical literacy/education readings and the ambiguous tutor/guardian/steward term retain their qualifications. Neither the tablet, names nor proposed schooling are transferred to Met 02.29.1. Source photographs are not reproduced.
sources.author: Łukasz Sokołowski

sources.title: Bactrian Historical Inscriptions of the Kushan Period
sources.scope: Five-page original PDF downloaded. Introduction and translated inscriptions, especially Rabatak and Surkh Kotal, read; pp. 77 and 79 visually inspected. An editor’s English translations, not a new original-language reading. Uncertain words, possible year-six reference, disputed absolute chronology and versions remain explicit. No imperial polygon or universal language/religious policy reconstructed. The earlier foundation-host download failed; the university copy succeeded.
sources.author: Nicholas Sims-Williams

sources.title: “Ethiopia” and the World, 330–1500 CE: introduction and early Aksum
sources.institution: Cambridge University Press, Elements in the Global Middle Ages
sources.scope: Publisher’s eight-page excerpt downloaded and read, especially pp. 3 and 5–8; p. 6 visually inspected. Greek/Ge’ez and three-script distinction, first-century Periplus/Adulis, uncertain Zoskales identity, and separate Adulis monuments/transmission. Not the full 88-page book, Casson’s complete edition, an original manuscript or a fresh translation. Broad ancient names are not mapped onto modern national borders.
sources.author: Yonatan Binyam and Verena Krebs

sources.title: Beta Samati: discovery and excavation of an Aksumite town
sources.scope: Original nineteen-page PDF and publisher HTML downloaded. Site/chronology, excavation methods, Area A, selected Area B material and Discussion/Conclusions read. Figures 3 and 4 inspected; Figure 4 is reproduced under the article’s CC BY 4.0 licence with figure credit. Food preparation, small-scale metal/glass work, mixed coin dates and dated deposits remain distinct. Original radiocarbon data/supplement and every stratigraphic association were not independently reanalysed. The author-repository PDF returned 403; the publisher copy succeeded.
sources.author: Michael J. Harrower, Ioana A. Dumitru and colleagues

sources.title: Chang’an (Xian)
sources.institution: University of Washington, Silk Road Seattle
sources.scope: Full university essay downloaded and read, including the distinct Han/Sui sites, Xuanzang’s return, later pagoda rebuilding and the 845 persecutions. Waugh’s synthesis is not Xiong’s full monograph. No population total, exact modern/ancient city identity or blanket religious tolerance adopted; images not reproduced.
sources.author: Daniel C. Waugh

sources.title: Cityscape of the Ordinary in Tang period Chang’an
sources.institution: National University of Singapore, East Asian Institute, In Focus seminar summary
sources.scope: One-page indexed PDF text read in the web tool. Direct download returned a 212-byte challenge page, not a PDF; screenshot failed. Summary of Heng Chye Kiang’s seminar, not the full 2014 article or his reconstruction files. Used for walled wards, gates, curfew and explicit conjectural reconstruction limits; no density/household totals or measured plan adopted.
sources.author: Seminar summary reporting Heng Chye Kiang

sources.title: Abbasid Ceramics: investment, production and centres of innovation
sources.institution: Ashmolean Museum, University of Oxford, Islamic Ceramics Online
sources.scope: Course page downloaded; investment/production, dating frameworks, centres and lustre technique passages read. Mariam Rosser-Owen’s 2000–2001 teaching synthesis draws on Hallett and others; their full theses were not consulted. Kilns, skill, fuel and costly failures support an original conceptual diagram. Court sponsorship and a single production centre are hypotheses, not settled facts. The page’s erroneous Red Sea description of Basra and speculative invention narrative are not adopted. No source figure copied.
sources.author: Mariam Rosser-Owen

sources.title: Early Islamic Basrah (Iraq)
sources.institution: Fondation Max van Berchem, archaeological project report
sources.scope: Full project page downloaded; settlement/topography, ceramics and 2017–2018 survey sections read. Early Basra near al-Zubayr is distinct from modern Basra. Report qualifies reported kiln finds, competing production centres and surface evidence; no precise ancient canal or boundary traced and no analysis transferred to the selected Met bowl.
sources.author: Andrew Petersen

sources.title: Petrographic analysis of ceramics from Murwab, an early Islamic site in Qatar
sources.institution: Proceedings of the Seminar for Arabian Studies 51 (2022), 55–70
sources.scope: Sixteen-page original PDF downloaded. Summary, introduction/methods and conclusions read: study of 134 selected common generally unglazed sherds, not the Met lustre bowl. Provenance is preliminary and concerns sampled material from Murwab, Qatar. The paper reports petrography in detail; chemical data are preliminary, not a fully published chemical dataset. The paper does not prove the selected Iraq-attributed bowl’s workshop or route. Figures are not reproduced.
sources.author: José C. Carvajal López, Alexandrine Guérin and Myrto Georgakopoulou

sources.title: A Record of the Buddhist Religion as Practised in India and the Malay Archipelago (A.D. 671–695)
sources.scope: Original 1896 English edition downloaded. Selected introduction and printed pp. 62–65, 154–155 and 176–177 read; pp. 65, 154 and 177 visually inspected. Yijing’s seventh-century account through Takakusu’s translation and textual notes, not a fresh Chinese reading or a whole-book review. Tamralipti’s guest/room rules on pp. 63–64 are not transferred to Nalanda. Nalanda resident totals have textual variants; no exact census or eight-hall match to today’s ruins is asserted.
sources.author: Yijing; translated and annotated by J. Takakusu

sources.title: Nalanda Ruins (41): photographer’s record
sources.institution: Wikimedia Commons; original work by Sumit Surai
sources.scope: Original 3280×2464 image downloaded and visually inspected. Record gives 9 October 2023, Sumitsurai and CC BY-SA 4.0; categorised as Monastery 1. It documents conserved brick remains, not an occupied seventh-century room, an original roof or an independently dated teaching space. No individual brick dated from appearance; copyright licence is separate from UNESCO description licence.
sources.author: Sumit Surai / Sumitsurai

sources.title: “Preparing Medicine from Honey”, from a Dispersed Manuscript of an Arabic Translation of De Materia Medica
sources.scope: Description and artwork details read: accession 57.51.21, ‘Abdullah ibn al-Fadl, dated 621 AH/1224 CE, attributed to Baghdad. Used as a later manuscript example of copying/illustration, not an eighth-century original translation, observed hospital, clinical recommendation or proof of universal literacy. Image linked, not reproduced. The page’s first-century BCE dating of Dioscorides is not adopted.
sources.author: The Metropolitan Museum of Art

sources.title: Memorial on the Crop Loans Measure, 1069: selected translation
sources.institution: Columbia University, Asia for Educators; Sources of Chinese Tradition
sources.scope: Short and longer selections, editorial conclusion and translation attribution read. The longer selection dates the fiscal commission memorial to 1069; this date is used without adopting the introduction’s appointment chronology. English translation from de Bary and Bloom, 2nd ed., vol. 1 (1999), pp. 617–618, not the Chinese original or full book. Policy justification and reported adoption do not measure voluntary participation, debt or harvest outcomes. No translation or source figure reproduced.
sources.author: Wang Anshi / fiscal administration commission; English selection edited by Wm. Theodore de Bary and Irene Bloom

sources.title: The Song Dynasty in China: Commercialization
sources.scope: Main commercialization page read, including Robert Hymes excerpt, market/guild, cash-crop and water-transport passages. Selected teaching synthesis, not a household dataset or the full 1997 course. The Marco Polo passage concerns the Yuan period and is not adopted as Song traffic evidence. No universal prosperity, world ranking, market volume or scroll image is adopted.
sources.author: Asia for Educators; includes Robert Hymes, 1997 course excerpt

sources.title: Structures of Governance in Song Dynasty China, 960–1279 CE: introduction excerpt
sources.scope: Publisher’s ten-page excerpt available; introduction pp. 1–8 read through the opening political-economy discussion. Not the full monograph. Hartman argues against limiting government to an emperor and elite literati, emphasizing clerks, military institutions, taxation and competing historical narratives. His interpretive model is attributed, not presented as scholarly consensus. Revenue percentages and claims of a world-first fiscal state are not adopted; no source illustration reproduced.
sources.author: Charles Hartman

sources.title: Caravans of Gold, Fragments in Time: An Introduction
sources.institution: Princeton University Press / The Block Museum of Art
sources.scope: Fifteen-page publisher chapter excerpt available; printed pp. 23–30 read, particularly pp. 26–29 on domestic ceramics, local/interregional work, fragmented evidence and slavery. Not the entire exhibition book or excavation reports. The foreign map’s wealth language is attributed, not a measured ranking. No gold tonnage, population estimate or precise empire boundary adopted. No copyrighted chapter figures reproduced.
sources.author: Kathleen Bickford Berzock

sources.title: Catalan Atlas: supplied detail depicting Mansa Musa; image and rights record
sources.institution: Wikimedia Commons; Bibliothèque nationale de France, MS Espagnol 30
sources.scope: Original 3712×2647 JPEG downloaded and visually inspected. The file is already a detail of the atlas, not the complete panel. Commons attributes Abraham Cresques and conventional 1375 date; attribution retained as uncertain. Record marks a faithful reproduction of public-domain two-dimensional art with PD-Art / Public Domain Mark 1.0, with jurisdiction caveat. BnF/Gallica original catalogue fetch returned 403; no full catalogue consultation or global CC0 grant claimed. Derivatives only resize and encode the supplied detail, with no further crop, retouch or invented legibility.
sources.author: Attributed to Abraham Cresques; BnF / Gallica digital reproduction

sources.title: Atlas of Maritime Charts (The Catalan Atlas), object 26
sources.institution: The Block Museum of Art, Northwestern University, Caravans of Gold
sources.scope: Complete short object page read. Attribution is Abraham Cresques (?) and the commission is qualified as possible. Used for Majorcan production, conventional 1375 date, foreign court audience and the interpretation of royal gold imagery. Translated wealth caption is paraphrased as the map’s claim; neither a portrait made from life nor an audited fortune is asserted. Physical panel dimensions are not transferred to the supplied image detail.
sources.author: The Block Museum of Art, Northwestern University, Caravans of Gold

sources.title: Building the Road: Mit’a and Ayni—Labor and Reciprocity
sources.institution: Smithsonian National Museum of the American Indian
sources.scope: Building-the-road page and Mit’a/Ayni paragraphs read as a public exhibition synthesis. Used for rotating state labor, roads and provisioning in a reciprocal idiom. Universal language about every household and balanced exchange is not adopted as a measured outcome. No identical work term, universal consent or assurance of welfare inferred. No image, audio or original chronicler text reproduced.
sources.author: Smithsonian National Museum of the American Indian

sources.title: Who used the Inka Road?
sources.institution: Smithsonian National Museum of the American Indian
sources.scope: Complete short text read: official travelers, messengers, work parties and permission for ordinary travelers. A statement of regulated access is not proof that all actual movement was controlled. No traffic count or road-length total adopted.
sources.author: Smithsonian National Museum of the American Indian

packs.title: Communities, cities and the evidence of work
packs.question: How do we know about early communities, work, exchange and political organization?
packs.orientation: Begin with things people made and places they built. A grain account, a tomb wall, a reservoir, a carved jade and a stone household preserve different kinds of human activity. Some societies built large cities; others organized life differently. Their histories are contemporary without forming a single ladder toward civilization.
packs.geography: Move among southern Mesopotamia, the Nile Valley, Gujarat, the lower Yangtze, coastal Peru and Orkney. River systems, arid landscapes and island settings invite different questions. The selected object’s place attribution is kept separate from the location of a wider society.
packs.limits: This is a selective investigation of archaeological and institutional evidence. Many communities beyond these places are absent. Large monuments and durable materials survive unevenly; they cannot stand for all early human life.

Americas.reason: Caral now has settlement, food-evidence and construction-renewal explanation with phased context. One Supe study and selected project pages do not complete wider American or household histories.

Africa.reason: The selected Saqqara wall now connects to a bounded source-based account of provisioning, Giza institutions and changing cult service. Wider Nile farming, households, gender and provincial histories remain selective.

Europe.reason: Skara Brae now has household/landscape interpretation, source-qualified phases and an original feature guide. Wider Neolithic Europe, measured plans and independent archaeological review remain open.

West/Central Asia.reason: Expanded Uruk account with distinct urban chronology, accounting diagram and source interpretation. Later residential evidence is not backdated; wider Mesopotamian and household histories remain open.

South Asia.reason: Expanded Dholavira water/work inquiry separates excavated components from proposed radar features. The regional seal has no asserted Dholavira findspot. Wider Indus reference history remains open.

East Asia.reason: Expanded Liangzhu account joins rice, waterworks and jade while preserving separate dates and corrected capacity estimates. Household relations and wider East Asian histories remain open.

Southeast Asia/Oceania.reason: A sourced Kuk reference supplies a highland New Guinea agricultural setting from about 2400 BCE. Earlier C1 dates and mainland Southeast Asian settings still need research. The later Lapita dossier is a comparison, not contemporary C1 settlement evidence.

investigations.title: Accounts, reservoirs and rice
investigations.question: What evidence connects everyday work with a city’s organization?
investigations.orientation: Follow three investigations in thematic order. This is a comparison of evidence, not a travel route, a claim of contact or a sequence of stages toward one civilization. Read each source interpretation before deciding what the works reveal about people.
investigations.geography: Southern Mesopotamia, Khadir island and the lower Yangtze. Existing site locators orient the inquiry; original diagrams explain components and tasks without invented political borders or connecting routes.
investigations.limits: Three expanded investigations within the six-case chapter. Household detail and independent archaeological review remain open; Egypt, Caral, Orkney and missing regional frameworks are not completed by this batch.

investigations.title: Homes, provisions and renewal
investigations.question: What recurring work kept a place usable, and which records reveal it?
investigations.orientation: Follow three investigations in thematic order: preparing food, renewing built space and maintaining a home. They are comparisons of work and evidence, not a travel route, a claim of contact or stages toward one origin of civilization. Each place retains its own chronology and institutions.
investigations.geography: Saqqara/Giza/Memphis, the Supe Valley and Orkney: distinct site and regional locators, not an ancient connecting route.
investigations.limits: These three expansions preserve different periods and institutions. Broader household/recruitment research, the measured Skara site-plan task and independent/human acceptance remain open.

packs.title: Networks, resources and disruption
packs.question: How did regional societies interact, depend on resources and respond to disruption?
packs.orientation: Copper, tin, pottery, food and stories moved through particular networks. Communities also depended on landscapes, institutions and skilled work. Around 1200 BCE some eastern Mediterranean political centers changed dramatically. That regional investigation belongs beside other histories, with evidence for both disruption and continuity.
packs.geography: The main network case lies in Anatolia and the eastern Mediterranean. Move separately to the Nile, China, Mesoamerica and island Oceania. Earlier Caral and Dholavira contexts remain accessible where their occupation ranges overlap this window. Poverty Point adds a separate Lower Mississippi Valley investigation of earthworks, food and materials.
packs.limits: This chapter is selective. It does not establish one universal Bronze Age, a single cause of political change, or a global event in one exact year. European, inland South Asian and African regions beyond the selected Nile case need fuller accounts.

Americas.reason: Olmec and Poverty Point now have layered accounts, distinct phased contexts, geographic locators and material/source interpretation. These selected communities do not complete Gulf Coast, Lower Mississippi or wider American histories.

Africa.reason: Kerma-Egypt exchange and craft evidence; other African regions require separate histories.

Europe.reason: A sourced reference compares selected Aegean centres and British farms. There is not yet a standalone European dossier in this chapter; Uluburun remains a separately dated cargo comparison in West/Central Asia.

West/Central Asia.reason: Expanded Hattusha and Uluburun accounts distinguish capital phases, Gordion drought proxy, wreck association and contested tin provenance. These do not supply a full eastern Mediterranean or inland Asian reference history.

South Asia.reason: Dholavira’s later occupation provides an overlap with C1; it is not a full account of regional change after urban transitions.

East Asia.reason: Expanded Shang account separates the conventional period, Yin Xu late capital, ritual/casting practice and object-specific attribution. Household and wider regional coverage remain limited; no shared Anatolian collapse is inferred.

Southeast Asia/Oceania.reason: Lapita now joins pottery-making, provisioning and source-qualified island sequences, with a modern cast, original action guide and a correctly wrapped regional locator. Archaeological and linguistic reconstruction stay distinct; this is not a complete Pacific reference framework.

investigations.title: Institutions, shipments and ritual
investigations.question: How far can a record take us from materials to people?
investigations.orientation: Read a wreck, a capital and ritual objects in thematic order. Their evidence reveals work and power in different ways. This is not a confirmed route between the three cases or a single worldwide collapse story.
investigations.geography: Keep the documented wreck off southwestern Anatolia, the central Anatolian capital/Gordion proxy and the Chinese objects’ qualified attributions distinct. No connecting route is drawn.
investigations.limits: Three expanded inquiries within a wider selective chapter. Domestic histories, detailed phase maps and independent/human acceptance remain open. Kerma, Olmec, Lapita and other regional reference frameworks are not completed by this batch.

investigations.title: Clay, work and local histories
investigations.question: How can clay reveal practical work and connections?
investigations.orientation: Compare heating objects, a small represented body and the making of patterned pottery. Each investigation connects materials with practical work and its own local history. This thematic order is not a travel route, a claim of contact between these places or a single sequence of civilizational stages.
investigations.geography: Gulf Coast reference centres, selected Pacific island settings across 180° and two Lower Mississippi sites: source-qualified locators, with no invented interregional route.
investigations.limits: The three expansions retain their own case and reference dates. Abstract-only food/material sources, archaeological models, measured regional histories and independent/human acceptance remain qualified. Kerma and broader C2 regional frameworks remain open.

packs.title: States, ideas and everyday voices
packs.question: How did power, techniques and systems of thought change across different regions?
packs.orientation: Different materials preserve different voices. Royal texts, ritual objects, household work and portable images make an uneven archive. Compare the purposes and audiences of those records while keeping each region’s chronology distinct.
packs.geography: Move from Mesopotamia to South Asia, Athens and the Nile, then across Andean and island worlds. These are comparisons; no connecting line is inferred from contemporaneity.
packs.limits: Selected contexts offer depth rather than a catalogue of all empires or philosophies. Achaemenid, Greek, Indian and Chinese intellectual histories extend well beyond these cases.

Americas.reason: Chavín textile, Olmec and Colima material histories; not all American regions.

Africa.reason: Taharqo now has temple, production and funerary-labor explanation with a distinct phased context, original figure, inspected workshop photographs and local source-qualified references. Kerma offers a separately dated comparative bridge, not an unbroken polity or a complete African framework.

Europe.reason: Expanded Athenian account separates Archaic image, changing civic eligibility, public work and later constitutional description. Other Greek and European histories remain outside this bounded set.

West/Central Asia.reason: Nimrud now pairs royal imagery with a primary settlement claim, a later captive-provision letter and a licensed composite palace plan. These distinct sources deepen work and authority without completing Assyrian social or regional history.

South Asia.reason: Expanded Ashoka account distinguishes regional versions, audiences, practical instructions and unmeasured outcomes within a separate Mauryan frame. Wider South Asian coverage remains selective.

East Asia.reason: Expanded Qin account separates measuring devices, prescriptions, excavated Liye practice and their distinct dates. Broader Chinese institutions, households and intellectual histories remain limited.

Southeast Asia/Oceania.reason: Dong Son material and Lapita cultural traditions with uncertain functions and distinct dates.

investigations.title: Rules, messages and public work
investigations.question: Who carried a rule into everyday life?
investigations.orientation: Compare Qin administrative work, Ashoka’s regional messages and Athenian public life in thematic order. These different places and dates are not one political ladder, a travel itinerary or evidence of contact.
investigations.geography: Locate a capital and a county archive, separate regional inscriptions, and Athenian public places. The maps are approximate locators with no connecting transmission route or reconstructed borders.
investigations.limits: Three expanded cases within a wider selective chapter. Qin legal provenance, regional reception and diverse Athenian work/status histories remain open; this does not complete global first-millennium BCE coverage.

investigations.title: Makers, supplies and royal claims
investigations.question: Who made and supplied things for powerful places?
investigations.orientation: Compare a carefully finished vessel, a palace environment and royal funerary objects. Each place depended on materials, skills and provision, but the evidence gives different views of work and authority. This thematic inquiry crosses separate centuries and institutions; it is not a journey, a single tradition of kingship or proof of contact between these particular cases.
investigations.geography: A Nubian capital and the beaker’s Egyptian findspot, selected Assyrian royal centres and separate Nuri/Sanam settings. Thematic comparison across different times; no connecting route or reconstructed border.
investigations.limits: Three bounded expansions preserve their case, reference, object and source dates. A composite small-source palace plan, mediated royal translations, the later archive letter and broad workshop chronology retain their limits. Wider labor histories and independent/human acceptance remain open.

packs.title: Contemporary worlds
packs.question: What did distant societies share—and which connections can we demonstrate?
packs.orientation: Around 200 CE, cities, farms, ports and households existed within many different political and cultural settings. Some regions were linked through specific networks of trade and movement. Elsewhere, a useful comparison does not imply contact. Begin with real objects, locate their date ranges, and ask what each can support.
packs.geography: Locate the Mediterranean, Red Sea, Central and South Asia, China, Vietnam, Mexico and northern Peru. Dots are regional or city locators, not boundaries. Objects retain their catalogue ranges, including later phases. Ohio’s Hopewell networks add an eastern woodland comparison without asserting contact with the other pilot societies. A separately dated Bering Strait object opens an Arctic inquiry.
packs.limits: An anchor year is a way into a changing world. This chapter is selective, especially for Africa beyond Aksum, South Asia beyond Gandhara and Oceania. Different evidence survives in different regions.

Americas.reason: Teotihuacan and Moche now add selected household, workshop and regional evidence, with original teaching guides and distinct reference histories. The earlier Chavín textile provides a focused annotated comparison rather than a contemporary case or proof of contact. Wider American histories remain selective.

Africa.reason: Expanded Aksum account distinguishes early Adulis exchange, changing royal writing and later excavated inland work. Africa beyond these selected northeast settings remains inadequately covered.

Europe.reason: Roman imperial representation; northern and eastern European communities need later expansion.

West/Central Asia.reason: Expanded Palmyra account separates family memorials, local civic regulation and caravan records. Wider Roman eastern provinces, Parthian/Sasanian histories and diverse households remain limited.

South Asia.reason: Expanded Kushan account separates coin catalogues, chronology disputes and temple maintenance in Bactria. The wider subcontinent, agricultural/household contexts and Buddhist institutions remain selective.

East Asia.reason: Eastern Han and selected tomb models; neighboring societies are not represented equally.

Southeast Asia/Oceania.reason: Đông Sơn material traditions; no Oceanian dossier in this pilot.

investigations.title: Objects, work and exchange
investigations.question: What turns an object into evidence of a connection?
investigations.orientation: Compare a Palmyrene family memorial, Kushan coins and temple records, and Aksumite excavated material. This thematic inquiry crosses different dates and contexts. It is not one traveller’s route, a list of identical economies or proof of direct contact between every stop.
investigations.geography: Separate a city and its named exchange settings, Kushan regional centers and a temple-inscription region, and Aksum’s highland, coastal and inland research contexts. One schematic Palmyra trading-post sequence is qualified; the learning path is not a route.
investigations.limits: Three expanded cases supplement Rome/Han and the existing C4 chapter. Larger regional frameworks, workshop/household histories and independent historical/family acceptance remain incomplete.

investigations.title: Images, spaces and work
investigations.question: How can objects and excavated spaces explain people’s work?
investigations.orientation: Compare Chavín textile making, Teotihuacan household production and distinct Moche object and excavation histories. This inquiry crosses places and centuries; its thematic order does not establish contact, a route or a continuous political tradition.
investigations.geography: Separate the highland centre from the textile’s reported southern-coastal origin. Central Mexican urban evidence and distinct Peruvian valley contexts retain their own locations; no route connects them.
investigations.limits: Two household/production accounts and a focused textile inquiry. Source frames do not replace case intervals; the Tlajinga map combines phases. Wider labor, gender, regional and political histories and human acceptance remain open.

investigations.title: Objects, places and associations
investigations.question: How does a documented place change what an object can tell us?
investigations.orientation: Compare a miniature drum, an architectural model and Ohio earthworks. Visible form, recorded deposits and later surveys answer different questions. Their thematic order establishes no contact, route or common political history.
investigations.geography: Vietnamese locality/complex references and eight modern Ohio property centers retain distinct roles. The Colima model has no precise documented findspot; no route joins these regions.
investigations.limits: Case intervals remain distinct. Later Luy Lâu production extends beyond the drum case. Surveys, restoration and contemporary stewardship retain modern dates; the Vietnam map is selected, not a full Southeast Asian distribution.

packs.title: Communities and institutions in transition
packs.question: How did institutions, beliefs and regional networks change after political transitions?
packs.orientation: Large political labels contain changing communities. Investigate how people made images, shared food, organized learning and built religious environments while political power shifted.
packs.geography: Capitals on the Bosporus, Tigris and in northern China sit beside Mesoamerican vessel traditions, South Asian monastic life and Central Javanese architecture. Chaco’s mid/late-ninth-century building context provides a distinct Southwestern case extending into the next chapter.
packs.limits: Western Europe beyond Byzantium, inland Africa, North America and many smaller communities need fuller treatment. The selected cases do not define one universal medieval stage.

Americas.reason: Maya text/food/rank and earlier Andean/Mexican contexts now include the beginning of Chaco’s regional building history. Most northern regions remain unrepresented.

Africa.reason: Later Aksum context reaches this window; no new dedicated sub-Saharan dossier for these centuries.

Europe.reason: Roman/Byzantine identity, changing political phases and devotional practice.

West/Central Asia.reason: Expanded Abbasid Iraq account separates changing capitals and authority, workshop evidence, ordinary wares and a later manuscript. Wider urban/fiscal/slave labor histories and the full region remain limited.

South Asia.reason: Expanded Nalanda account connects selected translated practices, resources and residential learning, retaining archaeological/conservation phases. The wider subcontinent and institutional history remain incomplete.

East Asia.reason: Expanded Tang/Chang’an account separates government, wards, translation, tomb representation and change. Wider East Asia and rural/tax/military household histories remain selective.

Southeast Asia/Oceania.reason: Borobudur’s Javanese monumental religious environment; island Oceania remains limited in this window.

investigations.title: Spaces, skills and learning
investigations.question: How do institutions organize access and everyday work?
investigations.orientation: Compare access through Chang’an’s gates, skilled production in Abbasid-era Iraq, and living and learning at Nalanda. These selected dates form a thematic inquiry, not a single itinerary, a direct causal sequence or proof of contact among the pictured objects.
investigations.geography: Separate Chang’an’s successive city settings, Baghdad/Samarra/early Basra, and Nalanda from the different textual setting at Tamralipti. Locator maps are approximate; conceptual diagrams are not measured plans or routes.
investigations.limits: Three bounded expansions do not comprehensively cover the wider regions, rural production, social inequalities or every institution. Actual family and independent historical acceptance remain open.

investigations.title: Places, patrons and work
investigations.question: What links making and upkeep to people and institutions?
investigations.orientation: Compare a Maya cup, Borobudur and selected work in Constantinople. Ownership, support and practical tasks need different evidence. These stops organize a comparison across regions; they do not establish contact, a travel route or one shared institution.
investigations.geography: Constantinople, Central Java and distinct Mesoamerican contexts retain separate histories. Cerén is a household comparison, not the cup’s findspot; three Java dots are modern component references, with no route drawn.
investigations.limits: Selected work and support, not complete social histories. All original cases retain their full dates; object, sample, context, photo and modern diagram dates remain distinct. No common patron or contact is inferred.

packs.title: Cities, craft and knowledge in motion
packs.question: How were cities, trade, knowledge, power and everyday life connected?
packs.orientation: Skilled work and learned practices connect the histories of monuments, political institutions and daily life. Move between cities and voyages while asking which connections are demonstrated and which remain hypotheses.
packs.geography: The Sahel, Cambodia, China, the Andes and the Pacific receive new investigations. Byzantine and Abbasid institutions and Nalanda carry earlier histories into this window. Compare Chaco’s Southwest with Cahokia’s Mississippi floodplain; the companion investigation also visits earlier Poverty Point and Ohio Hopewell contexts. Ocmulgee adds a distinct southeastern river/council context, including Muscogee collaboration and revised archaeological dating.
packs.limits: Coverage of European cities outside Byzantium, Central Asian pastoral communities and many Indian Ocean ports is limited. Comparison does not imply direct contact among all selected cases.

Americas.reason: Expanded Inca case distinguishes textile skill, rotating service, resettlement, stores and a particular household excavation. Broader Americas and local labor variation remain selective.

Africa.reason: Expanded Mali case connects ordinary production, older urbanism, oral traditions, pilgrimage and a foreign royal image. Local administration, producers’ voices and wider African coverage remain selective.

Europe.reason: Byzantium’s changing institutions and 1204/1261 phases; other European regions need fuller dossiers.

West/Central Asia.reason: Abbasid continuation and contracted authority; no comprehensive Mongol or pastoral history.

South Asia.reason: Nalanda’s later institutional phases and archaeology.

East Asia.reason: Expanded Song case separates northern/southern government, seasonal lending, markets and ceramic evidence. Wider states, labor outcomes and rural histories remain selective.

Southeast Asia/Oceania.reason: Angkor infrastructure and Polynesian settlement/navigation provide distinct state and non-state inquiries.

investigations.title: Earth, food and gathering in Indigenous North America
investigations.question: How did people make different kinds of community?
investigations.orientation: Four selected settings connect food, skilled work, gathering and long-distance materials across different centuries. They are not stages of one society, and an inquiry crossing dates does not establish a historical route between its stops.
investigations.geography: Follow the Lower Mississippi Valley, Ohio, the San Juan Basin and Greater Cahokia. These cases north of Mesoamerica complement the atlas’s distinct Mexican and Maya histories; none can stand for the whole continent.
investigations.limits: A selective investigation north of Mesoamerica, not a complete precolonial survey. Arctic, Northwest Coast, Plains and many eastern woodland histories remain outside it. Later photographs, surveys and restorations are labeled. Community-authored evidence and scholarly disagreement remain part of the account.

investigations.title: Work, obligation and historical voices
investigations.question: Who supplied the work, and who gets to describe its benefits?
investigations.orientation: Compare a Song fiscal proposal, Mali’s royal image and household production, and Inca textile work and provisioning. The selected dates are a thematic inquiry, not a route, a single causal sequence or evidence of contact among these objects.
investigations.geography: Capital areas in Song China, separate Niger-bend settlements and an Andean household-study region are approximate locators. No object journey, empire border or shared contact route is reconstructed.
investigations.limits: Three bounded expansions leave broader simultaneous-world coverage, regional variation and independent/family acceptance open.

investigations.title: Buildings, food and continuing connections
investigations.question: How can buildings and food help explain communities through change?
investigations.orientation: Compare building, food and material work at Chaco, Cahokia and Ocmulgee. A later plan, a 1907 print and an excavation record answer different questions. Present-day community statements have named speakers and contexts. This order organizes an inquiry; it does not establish contact, a travel route or one shared institution.
investigations.geography: Three distinct North American settings retain their original qualified locators. A Chaco ruin plan and an Ocmulgee feature drawing concern particular buildings; neither supplies a route between the cases or a new surveyed map.
investigations.limits: Selected building, food and material inquiries, not complete societal histories. All full case intervals remain; Ocmulgee’s disputed endpoints remain unknown. Modern depictions, archaeological samples and attributed living relationships have separate dates and evidentiary scopes.

packs.title: Connections, work and unequal power
packs.question: How did connections reshape work, belief, power and resistance?
packs.orientation: Ships joined ports through goods, money, stories and people. These connections were made by artists, translators, sailors and workers as well as rulers. Some were negotiated; others depended on conquest, enslavement and forced displacement. Begin in the 1450–1650 context, then follow selected consequences into the later eighteenth century. A companion investigation turns inland to Ottoman, Safavid and Central Asian cities and follows skilled work into later-eighteenth-century Iran.
packs.geography: Portugal, Benin, Kongo, South Asia, China, Manila, Mexico and Banda belong to different networks. The journey includes the earlier 1497–99 voyage as context and labels a Mexican jar made after 1650. Schematic routes do not establish a particular object’s itinerary. Istanbul/Iznik, Isfahan/New Julfa, Bukhara and the Shiraz political context add distinct West/Central Asian settings; a shared chapter does not merge their governments or identities. Makah Ozette, the Blackfoot hunting landscape at Head-Smashed-In and Hidatsa river villages add distinct northern histories. Southern Ontario and Canandaigua add distinct Wendat and Haudenosaunee investigations.
packs.limits: Selected African, Asian, European and American encounters, with ocean and inland investigations. This is not a complete history of Atlantic slavery, Indigenous resistance, the Indian Ocean, Ottoman Arab provinces, the wider Caucasus or Central Asia beyond the selected Bukhara case. Oceanian perspectives still need fuller treatment.

Americas.reason: Acapulco, Pacific cargoes and later Mexican ceramics; Indigenous and enslaved American experiences need fuller dossiers. Distinct Makah, Blackfoot and Hidatsa investigations add cedar work, communal hunting and village agriculture. Ozette burial estimates remain disputed; the selected hunting context is not the whole site chronology. An ancestral Wendat village and Haudenosaunee treaty diplomacy add northeastern histories. Modeled village bounds, treaty signing and U.S. ratification are different kinds of dates; no common polity or automatic succession is inferred.

Africa.reason: Expanded Benin and Kongo cases explain makers, religious translation and distinct royal evidence. Wider communities, collection histories and trafficking outcomes remain selective.

Europe.reason: Portuguese access and armed expansion; the VOC appears through Banda’s colonial records.

West/Central Asia.reason: Ottoman administration/workshops/markets, Safavid Isfahan and forced Armenian relocation, Bukhara’s urban/bookmaking contexts and later-eighteenth-century Iran now have distinct sourced dossiers. This is not an exhaustive account of Ottoman provinces, the Caucasus, pastoral societies or Central Asia.

South Asia.reason: Expanded Calicut encounter inquiry retains existing ports and intermediaries; broader Indian Ocean economies, local accounts and port histories remain selective.

East Asia.reason: Ming production and Pacific exchange; not a general survey of China, Japan or Korea.

Southeast Asia/Oceania.reason: Banda and Manila represent different roles in ocean networks. Oceania is not covered by a dossier in this pack.

investigations.title: Books, silk and power: West/Central Asia, 1500–1800
investigations.question: How did makers and urban communities work within—and beyond—courtly power?
investigations.orientation: Begin with a book likely copied and painted in different settings, then examine an Ottoman dish and emblem, an Iranian carpet and a 1789 lacquer case. Put skilled work beside patronage, markets and coercion. A luxury object cannot stand in for everyone’s experience.
investigations.geography: Distinct contexts in present-day Türkiye, Iran and Uzbekistan connect artistic production to cities, trade and political power. The manuscript’s Bukhara attribution and the carpet’s workshop location remain qualified; map points do not resolve those uncertainties.
investigations.limits: Four selected contexts within the 1500–1800 navigation frame. Their defined dates are not the lifespans of all relevant empires or peoples. The investigation includes forced Armenian relocation and urban work but cannot recover every maker, purchaser or household.

investigations.title: Makers, interpreters and unequal encounters
investigations.question: Whose knowledge made an encounter possible, and who could choose?
investigations.orientation: Compare an ocean account, an Edo carving and Kongo religious making and royal letters. The selected dates organize a thematic inquiry, not a single causal route or evidence that these particular objects and voyagers met.
investigations.geography: Approximate city and coast locators distinguish Lisbon, Malindi, Calicut, Benin City and Mbanza Kongo. No exact ship track, political border or object findspot is reconstructed.
investigations.limits: Three expansions do not complete Atlantic/Indian Ocean histories or supply independent, family or original-language acceptance.

investigations.title: Makers, patrons and markets
investigations.question: How did makers, patrons and markets organize work?
investigations.orientation: Compare a Ming jar, a Süleiman tughra and a Mughal manuscript folio. Shaping, decoration, writing and translation involved different working relationships. Catalogue identifications, institutional accounts and technical studies supply different evidence. These stops organize a comparison; they do not establish a shared workshop, patron or route.
investigations.geography: Distinct Chinese, Ottoman and Mughal production and court settings retain their original qualified locators. Material or design comparison does not supply a reconstructed route or shared workshop.
investigations.limits: Selected making, commissioning, buying and translation, not complete labor histories. Original case and object intervals remain; reference phases, similar-object records, later market accounts and modern experiments have separate scopes and dates.

investigations.title: Households, books and city work
investigations.question: Whose work supported city life?
investigations.orientation: Compare a manuscript folio, a carpet and a dressing case with separately sourced accounts of teaching, water, correspondence and building. Each object has its own production history. The comparison does not establish contact among these objects, a shared workshop or a route between the stops.
investigations.geography: Separate urban settings retain their source-qualified locators and verbal relationships. No route, neighborhood boundary, object workshop or household location is reconstructed from this comparison.
investigations.limits: Selected letters, making, teaching, endowment, maintenance and political references; not complete urban or household histories. Full case and object intervals remain distinct from the later 1747 letter and the catalogue-described scene absent from supplied Zand views.

investigations.title: Goods, work and coercion
investigations.question: What can particular records tell us about work behind exchange?
investigations.orientation: Compare records of Banda’s 1621 conquest with a separate Pacific registration from 1726. Cultivation, provisioning, shipbuilding and transport involved people working within different relationships. The pictured Mexican jar has its own ca. 1680–1700 catalogue date. These stops support a comparison, not a shared route, a causal sequence or evidence of contact between the cases.
investigations.geography: Banda’s three modern island references and the existing Pacific case locator have different source roles. This comparison draws no sailing track, campaign line, plantation extent, political boundary or connection between the cases.
investigations.limits: The selected stop dates do not replace the complete Manila case 1565–1815 or the exact Banda 1621 case. The jar’s ca. 1680–1700 date, selected 1595/1618/1619/1726 records, separate Banda reference 1599–1630 and public 2021 statement retain their own contexts. A registration is not an arrival receipt, and a colonial intention is not every household’s experience. Original case identities, claims, old comparison meanings and image bytes remain intact.

packs.title: Industry, empire and struggles over the future
packs.question: How did industry, empire, resistance, mass politics, war, decolonization and technology shape ordinary lives?
packs.orientation: Three investigations connect work and machines, political promises, and war and technology. Begin with a photograph or document, then follow the institutions and choices around it. The chapter’s2000 boundary clips the view; it does not end ongoing societies.
packs.geography: Cases span Britain and continental Europe, the Caribbean and United States, Japan, Aotearoa, South Asia and South Africa. Companion inquiries add distinct Arctic, coastal, Plains, Great Lakes, northeastern and southeastern North American settings. Map locators do not reconstruct borders or photographic findspots.
packs.limits: Selective investigations, not a complete modern survey. Latin America beyond Haiti, China’s twentieth century, Middle Eastern national movements, African regions beyond South Africa and post-1960 computing need fuller treatment. War coverage explains major contexts and genocide without cataloguing every campaign.

Americas.reason: Haiti resistance and independence; US child-labor reform evidence. Other regions limited. Northern cases investigate Indigenous work, relocation, clothing, prohibition and community authority. They do not represent all Arctic, Northwest Coast or Plains peoples; the eastern Arctic and many regional histories remain selective. Cherokee printing/removal and an Ojibwe rice-water document add southeastern and Great Lakes perspectives. Eastern Woodlands remains a geographic frame, with many nations and periods still beyond this selection.

Africa.reason: South African transition, constitutional rights and implementation questions; not the whole continent’s decolonization. Ghana adds a sourced independence and early-government inquiry; these cases do not supply a continent-wide modern framework.

Europe.reason: Factory regulation, global war and state persecution, with contextual limits.

West/Central Asia.reason: Soviet Central Asian launch context and Cold War reception; local Kazakh experience and wider regional politics need fuller accounts.

South Asia.reason: Independence, partition, border chronology and ordinary-life disruption.

East Asia.reason: Tomioka’s adapted industrial system, and Japanese/Chinese wartime chronology in the global-war case.

Southeast Asia/Oceania.reason: Te Tiriti texts, consent and signing processes; Southeast Asian decolonization remains limited. Indonesia adds the selected 1945–1950 revolution and constitutional transition, not region-wide decolonization.

investigations.title: Political freedom and the meaning of a promise
investigations.question: Who understood a political promise—and who could exercise it?

investigations.title: Global war, state power and a new signal
investigations.question: How do decisions and institutions connect large events to individual lives?

investigations.title: Arctic, coast and Plains: work, knowledge and belonging
investigations.question: How do different communities sustain life and pass on knowledge?
investigations.orientation: Inspect a carved tool, wooden-household evidence, a hunting landscape, gardens, clothing and a primary title page. Six distinct contexts show how practical work, shared responsibilities and interpretation matter. Similar needs never make these peoples interchangeable.
investigations.geography: Selected places in the Bering Strait, Canadian Arctic, Olympic Peninsula, southern Alberta, Missouri valley and northern Vancouver Island. The inquiry crosses centuries; its sequence is not a documented route or claim of contact.
investigations.limits: Two selected contexts for each of three broad regions. Many Inuit homelands, Thule/Dorset histories, Northwest Coast nations and Plains communities still need fuller treatment. Later photographs, reconstructions, disputed dates and community sources remain explicit.

investigations.title: Eastern Woodlands: communities, knowledge and power
investigations.question: How do places, food and records help people sustain a community?
investigations.orientation: Inspect surviving clay and a reconstruction, look back to a separate Ohio gathering network, then investigate Wendat village work, Haudenosaunee diplomacy, Cherokee printing and Ojibwe rice knowledge. Documents and places record particular histories, not one universal woodland way of life.
investigations.geography: Ocmulgee in the southeast, Ohio earthworks, a Wendat site in southern Ontario, Canandaigua in New York, New Echota and Great Lakes rice waters. The inquiry crosses dates deliberately; it is not an itinerary or an inferred chain of ancestry.
investigations.limits: Selected northeastern, Great Lakes and southeastern histories, with earlier Hopewell context. Many nations and earlier chronological windows still need fuller treatment. Unknown construction dates, modeled ranges, later research figures and qualified photographic metadata remain explicit.

investigations.title: Independence and citizenship, 1945–1997
investigations.question: What changes on a political turning point—and what still has to be built?
investigations.orientation: A focused route through Indonesia, Partition, Ghana and South Africa. Compare different political milestones and their consequences.
investigations.geography: Selected places in South and Southeast Asia and Africa. The map locates inquiries; it does not reconstruct borders or imply a route connecting the four transitions.
investigations.limits: A four-case inquiry, not a complete account of decolonization or a global snapshot of 1950. Other African and Asian experiences, the Americas and Cold War institutions need further work.

investigations.title: Skills, records and protection
investigations.question: How can we distinguish skilled work from effective protection?
investigations.orientation: Compare a factory investigation, mill depiction and reform photograph with their dated records. Different institutions require separate evidence of workers’ protection.
investigations.geography: Tomioka’s four published modern property references identify distinct regional functions. No border, route or shipment is reconstructed.
investigations.limits: Original case dates, retrospective accounts, later laws and the NDL print’s bracketed date remain distinct. No universal conditions, shared legal regime or photograph-to-law causation is established.

journeys.title: What makes a community visible?
journeys.question: Can we recover work, belief and authority from things?
journeys.introduction: Compare a grain account, a tomb wall, reservoirs, jade, public courts and a stone household. These are different windows into early communities, not steps in a universal ladder.

stops.subject: uruk-accounts
stops.title: Information pressed into clay
stops.narrative: Inspect the signs and numerical impressions. Keep the probable grain interpretation separate from a complete translation.

stops.subject: old-kingdom
stops.title: Work and play beside the dead
stops.narrative: Find scenes of offerings and music. Ask why an elite funerary wall selected these activities.

stops.subject: dholavira
stops.title: A city needs water
stops.narrative: Locate the arid island setting. Compare what reservoirs reveal with what the seal’s unread signs cannot yet tell us.

stops.subject: liangzhu
stops.title: Different evidence, different scales
stops.narrative: Inspect the jade’s geometry and then think about waterworks and burials. Do not give a city, culture and artifact one artificial lifespan.

stops.subject: caral
stops.title: A public place across the ocean
stops.narrative: Imagine questions you could ask of platforms and sunken courts. The comparison with Liangzhu implies no historical contact.

stops.subject: skara-brae
stops.title: Bring households into the atlas
stops.narrative: Consider hearths, beds and a tool of uncertain use. Explain which evidence supports a conclusion and what may be missing.

journeys.conclusion: Early communities become visible through many kinds of evidence. Records, monuments and surviving houses illuminate different people and activities. A serious atlas can compare them without ranking their worth or pretending they share one political lineage.

evidence.prompt: Which statement makes the strongest supported distinction?

options.text: Every ancient sign can be translated if we imagine what its maker wanted.
options.feedback: Imagination is not a translation method. The Indus signs remain incompletely read, while even the grain tablet’s interpretation has limits.

options.text: A building, a tablet and a burial object can support different questions about a society.
options.feedback: Their materials, contexts and purposes preserve different information. Compare the questions each can answer.

options.text: Monumental buildings prove that everyone in a community had equal power.
options.feedback: Coordinated work does not establish equality. Differentiated spaces and burials may instead prompt questions about hierarchy.

journeys.returnPrompt: Choose two kinds of evidence. What can each show, and what does each leave difficult to know?

familyEvidence.title: Read a record of grain
familyEvidence.text: The museum interprets this tablet as a probable account of barley and emmer, dated about 3100–2900 BCE. Missing verbs limit a precise reading. Visible marks and a catalogue interpretation supply different kinds of information.
notice: Find a repeated mark.
Separate what you see from the museum’s interpretation.
familyEvidence.claimPrompt: Explain what this tablet might record. What makes a precise reading uncertain?
familyEvidence.returnPrompt: Name another record that could help identify a recipient.
