familyEvidence.feedback: The marks survive; their precise meaning needs interpretation. A probable grain account does not identify every recipient or describe all household work.

journeys.title: Connected worlds, different disruptions
journeys.question: What changed around 1200 BCE—and what did not?
journeys.introduction: Begin before the eastern Mediterranean disruptions, then compare evidence from other regions. This is a regional historical investigation inside a wider world, not one global collapse story.

stops.subject: uluburun
stops.title: One shipment with many materials
stops.narrative: Distinguish objects found together in a wreck from a fully reconstructed route.

stops.subject: hattusha-change
stops.title: A dated stress is not a whole explanation
stops.narrative: Separate a tree-ring drought finding, political transformation and the changing occupation of a capital.

stops.subject: kerma-potters
stops.title: Material can travel without settling identity
stops.narrative: Inspect a Kerma vessel excavated in Egypt. Keep the pot’s context separate from the proposed origin of a person.

stops.subject: shang-ritual
stops.title: A different set of recorded concerns
stops.narrative: Explore ritual writing and skilled casting without imposing Anatolia’s chronology on China.

stops.subject: olmec
stops.title: Look beyond the same network
stops.narrative: Inspect a small ceramic figure and think about how its scale differs from communal monuments.

stops.subject: lapita
stops.title: Connections across an island world
stops.narrative: Ask how dated patterns, settlements and food remains can support different accounts of voyaging.

journeys.conclusion: A network can be demonstrated without knowing every route. A political center can change without all its people vanishing. A dated drought can matter without explaining everything. Elsewhere, other communities faced their own histories and choices.

evidence.prompt: What can the Hittite drought study support?

options.text: A severe environmental stress occurred near the political transformation; direct causation remains unproved.
options.feedback: The authors explicitly preserve that distinction. Other political, social and regional evidence still matters.

options.text: Exactly the same disaster ended every society in the world in 1200 BCE.
options.feedback: The evidence is regional, and other societies had different chronologies. A shared date on an atlas creates no shared cause.

options.text: Every place at Hattusha was occupied and destroyed simultaneously.
options.feedback: The archaeological abstract emphasizes changing areas of occupation and warns against treating the combined plan as one moment.

journeys.returnPrompt: Explain one connection we can demonstrate, one proposed cause we must qualify, and one distant history that should not be folded into the same story.

familyEvidence.claimPrompt: Explain what was measured and what remains unproved about political decisions.
familyEvidence.returnPrompt: Name another source that could test a connection between drought and political decisions.
familyEvidence.feedback: The study supports severe environmental stress near a political transformation. It does not directly measure why leaders acted or prove a single cause.
familyEvidence.title: Read a study summary
familyEvidence.text: Researchers studied tree rings and carbon isotopes in juniper timbers from Gordion. They identified severe drought around 1198–1196 BCE, with ±3-year dating uncertainty. These measurements concern environmental conditions, rather than decisions made at Hattusha.

citations.locator: Printed pp. 719–722: Gordion, dating and causation

notice: Name what was measured and where.
What further evidence would help connect environmental stress with political decisions?

journeys.title: Power, work and whose voice survives
journeys.question: Who could make a message last?
journeys.introduction: Read a palace wall, a ruler’s edicts, a water jar, a royal burial figure and a textile. Ask who made each record and what it leaves silent.

stops.subject: nimrud-palace
stops.title: Enter a royal setting
stops.narrative: Inspect the protective imagery and distinguish the palace from its modern museum arrangement.

stops.subject: ashoka-messages
stops.title: Address people across regions
stops.narrative: Compare two royal messages without turning a similarity into a claim of copying.

stops.subject: athens-water
stops.title: Put daily work in public space
stops.narrative: Look at the handles and painted fountain scene. Separate political rights from participation in everyday work.

stops.subject: taharqo
stops.title: Read a qualified attribution
stops.narrative: Keep probable findspot, royal identity and funerary purpose distinct.

stops.subject: chavin-textile
stops.title: Follow a question instead of inventing a route
stops.narrative: Portable imagery suggests circulation; what evidence would locate this particular journey?

stops.subject: qin-administration
stops.title: A decree meets everyday practice
stops.narrative: Compare an announced standard with excavated administrative documents; uniform rules did not guarantee identical practice.

stops.subject: dongson
stops.title: Hear another material tradition
stops.narrative: Compare skilled bronze making and debated purposes with the evidence encountered so far.

journeys.conclusion: Lasting records are selective. A ruler’s announcement, a work scene and a funerary object preserve different voices. Serious comparison keeps audience, material, dates and uncertainty visible.

evidence.prompt: Which reading best respects the evidence?

options.text: A royal declaration tells us what a ruler announced; its effects need additional evidence.
options.feedback: Purpose and reception are different questions. A surviving statement is strong evidence of a message, not proof of universal compliance.

options.text: Similar images prove that every maker followed the same route.
options.feedback: Similarity alone supplies neither a traveler nor an itinerary. Provenance and dated contexts matter.

options.text: Political exclusion means people did no public work.
options.feedback: The Agora study distinguishes formal rights from the broader evidence of work and presence.

journeys.returnPrompt: Choose a record and name a person whose experience it might leave out.

familyEvidence.title: A palace object in a museum
familyEvidence.text: The museum identifies a protective figure from Ashurnasirpal II’s palace at Nimrud, about 883–859 BCE. Its present museum setting differs from its original room. The surviving carving does not record every person’s response to it.
notice: Describe a feature of the figure.
What does the caption add about its setting?
familyEvidence.claimPrompt: Name the original setting. What further evidence would help establish how a person encountered this figure there?
familyEvidence.returnPrompt: Name a question about its makers or viewers that needs another source.
familyEvidence.feedback: Material, scale and setting can shape a message. The surviving relief does not reveal every maker’s circumstances or prove how all viewers understood it.

journeys.title: The world around 200 CE
journeys.question: At the same time—but connected how?
journeys.duration: 25–40 minutes, or one stop at a time
journeys.introduction: Begin with a building small enough to hold, then travel through families, ports and distant communities. The date is an orientation point: objects retain their actual ranges. We will distinguish a shared moment from evidence of contact.

stops.subject: eastern-han
stops.title: A building for another life
stops.narrative: Look closely before reading. Name one feature you can see and one idea you are inferring. Then investigate why a model might enter a tomb.

stops.subject: roman-world
stops.title: A face of power
stops.narrative: A gem carries the portrait of a woman from Syria in Rome’s ruling family. Compare the scale of an object with the reach of its political message.

stops.subject: palmyra
stops.title: People between distant centers
stops.narrative: Read the names on a family memorial. Follow a sourced network through intermediate cities, and keep the family’s choices separate from the history of every traveler.

stops.subject: kushan-contexts
stops.title: A coin and its limits
stops.narrative: Inspect both sides of the Kanishka coin. Its catalogue date is earlier than our anchor. What does a royal image communicate, and what find evidence would establish circulation?

stops.subject: aksum
stops.title: Highland city, coastal port
stops.narrative: Locate Aksum and the Red Sea. Distinguish a Roman bottle used as a type comparison from an object actually excavated at Aksum. Notice how later monuments complicate a single-year snapshot.

stops.subject: moche
stops.title: Life beyond the same network
stops.narrative: Cross to the north coast of Peru. Investigate irrigation and pottery without drawing a contact line from Eurasia. Then look at Teotihuacan’s different urban setting.

stops.subject: dongson
stops.title: Traditions beyond a royal ribbon
stops.narrative: Count the frogs, consider bronze manufacture and examine the catalogue’s competing explanations. A broad distribution does not establish a single use.

stops.subject: colima
stops.title: Two small buildings, different questions
stops.narrative: Compare with the Han tower. Separate visible form, proposed function and confidence. Choose a supported claim, then save a question to revisit.

journeys.conclusion: Our shared timeline placed distant societies in view without turning them into one connected world. Specific routes and objects supported some connections; comparison helped us ask questions elsewhere. A historical claim becomes stronger when it states its limits.

evidence.prompt: Which claim follows from comparing the Han tower and Colima model?

options.text: Everyone in Eastern Han China lived in a tower.
options.feedback: An elite burial model cannot represent every household. We would need settlement and household evidence.

options.text: The models help investigate buildings, social meanings and possible ritual uses.
options.feedback: This is appropriately limited. The catalogues and curatorial account support these questions while preserving uncertainty.

options.text: Their resemblance proves trade between China and Mexico.
options.feedback: Similarity and overlapping dates establish neither contact nor a route. Evidence for an actual mechanism is missing.

journeys.returnPrompt: What changed in your picture of the world around 200 CE? Name one supported connection and one comparison that does not imply contact.

familyEvidence.title: One model, a wider inquiry
familyEvidence.text: The museum dates this pottery tower to the first–early third century and identifies a burial context. It is a model of architecture, not a surviving occupied home. Its range does not date it precisely to 200 CE.
notice: Point to a feature that resembles a building.
Find the date range in the caption.
familyEvidence.claimPrompt: Describe a building feature. Explain why this model cannot show what every household’s home looked like.
familyEvidence.returnPrompt: Find another dated model before making a comparison.
familyEvidence.feedback: A burial model raises questions about buildings and representation. Another place needs its own evidence; similar dates or shapes do not establish contact.

journeys.title: Institutions, images and the work of continuity
journeys.question: What continues when political power changes?
journeys.introduction: Move among capitals, a cup, a temple and a learning community. Look for changes within long historical labels.

stops.subject: byzantium
stops.title: Roman identity beyond 476
stops.narrative: Read the long frame and its interruptions. Inspect a much later devotional object.

stops.subject: abbasid-craft
stops.title: Craft across changing authority
stops.narrative: Distinguish a dynasty, a capital phase and the date of a bowl.

stops.subject: tang-city
stops.title: A selective image of society
stops.narrative: Explore a capital’s contacts while questioning what an elite burial represents.

stops.subject: maya-vessel
stops.title: A name without a named polity
stops.narrative: Read the difference between ownership, interpretation and a secure findspot.

stops.subject: borobudur
stops.title: Ideas built into a landscape
stops.narrative: Investigate movement and cosmology, then distinguish construction from restoration.

stops.subject: nalanda
stops.title: Learning needs a place to live
stops.narrative: Compare two religious built environments and their surviving construction layers.

journeys.conclusion: Institutions can survive political transitions, but survival does not mean sameness. Buildings, objects and texts preserve different scales of change.

evidence.prompt: Why should Nalanda’s early remains and institutional dates be separated?

options.text: A site can contain earlier activity than the particular institution being investigated.
options.feedback: The detailed synthesis distinguishes the fifth–thirteenth-century institution from earlier remains.

options.text: Any ancient object proves a modern-style university operated from the earliest date.
options.feedback: The kind of institution and the meaning of the earliest archaeological remains need separate evidence.

journeys.returnPrompt: Choose a long historical label and explain one important change inside it.

familyEvidence.claimPrompt: Use the summary to explain why the photograph and the institution need different dates.
familyEvidence.returnPrompt: Find another example where a photograph’s date differs from the history it helps investigate.
familyEvidence.feedback: Earlier archaeology and the dated institution concern different things. A 2023 photograph does not turn conserved remains into one complete ancient moment.
familyEvidence.title: Two dates for different things
familyEvidence.text: UNESCO distinguishes earlier remains at Nalanda from the fifth–thirteenth-century monastic and scholastic institution. This photograph records conserved brick remains in 2023; it does not show every building at one ancient moment.
notice: Find walls and openings in the photograph.
Which date belongs to a photograph, and which range describes an institution?

journeys.title: Cities, craft and knowledge in motion
journeys.question: What kinds of connection can we demonstrate?
journeys.introduction: Investigate a pilgrimage, a modeled figure, water infrastructure, art, cloth and ocean knowledge. Keep different evidence for connection distinct.

stops.subject: mali-networks
stops.title: A journey beyond a wealth story
stops.narrative: Compare oral history, foreign imagery and material evidence.

stops.subject: middle-niger
stops.title: A city need not fit one political model
stops.narrative: Inspect the figure’s posture before naming an emotion or a ruler.

stops.subject: angkor
stops.title: Build beyond the temple
stops.narrative: Put water, roads and farming into the urban landscape.

stops.subject: song-art
stops.title: Ideas can compete within one label
stops.narrative: Explore court and scholarly purposes beside a glazed bowl.

stops.subject: inca-weaving
stops.title: Read technique as evidence
stops.narrative: Compare a regional production argument with the uncertainty of an object’s precise itinerary.

stops.subject: polynesian-voyaging
stops.title: Learn a route through practice
stops.narrative: Separate settlement dating from the broader history of knowledge.

journeys.conclusion: Journeys, techniques, memories and infrastructures connect communities in different ways. Each needs its own evidence. A line on a map can summarize a supported connection; it cannot create one.

evidence.prompt: Which connection is described at the right level of certainty?

options.text: The tunic’s technical features support regional comparison, while its exact individual route remains unknown.
options.feedback: The catalogue makes a technical and regional argument. It does not provide a complete object itinerary.

options.text: One long date range proves an object was made both before and after a conquest.
options.feedback: A date range expresses uncertainty about when it was made, not repeated production of the same object.

options.text: A navigation tradition requires a surviving written map to count as knowledge.
options.feedback: Taonui describes memorized and practiced ways of reading stars, swells and landmarks.

journeys.returnPrompt: Explain one demonstrated connection and one connection that remains a question.

familyEvidence.claimPrompt: Describe a visible pattern. Explain why regional comparisons do not establish this garment’s individual route.
familyEvidence.returnPrompt: Name one record that could help establish the tunic’s individual journey.
familyEvidence.feedback: Technical comparison supports connections among traditions. An individual route still needs provenance or other dated records.
familyEvidence.title: Compare features without inventing a route
familyEvidence.text: The museum compares this tunic’s materials, construction and patterns with highland and coastal traditions. Its broad 1450–1550 date and regional comparisons do not name a weaver or reconstruct this garment’s individual journey.
notice: Point to a pattern you can see.
What would you need to establish this particular garment’s route?

journeys.title: Ocean connections, 1450–1650
journeys.question: Who gained, who made, and who paid for ocean connections?
journeys.duration: 30–45 minutes, or one encounter at a time
journeys.introduction: Follow a route into an ocean that already had merchants and communities. Inspect African ivory, a Mughal manuscript and Chinese porcelain, then ask how patronage, translation, colonial force and resistance produced different kinds of connection.

stops.subject: portuguese-voyage
stops.title: A new route for whom?
stops.narrative: Locate Portugal and Calicut. Explain what changed for European access while preserving the existing lives and commerce of Indian Ocean ports.

stops.subject: benin-ivory
stops.title: African artists picture their visitors
stops.narrative: Look closely at rank, dress and pose. The commission links makers and patrons; do not assume the artist simply copied a European world.

stops.subject: kongo-translation
stops.title: Translation makes new meanings
stops.narrative: Study a crucifix and the history of interpreters. Separate a ruler’s baptism, local practices and the long life of a religious tradition.

stops.subject: mughal-books
stops.title: A story becomes a courtly book
stops.narrative: Observe Krishna sheltering the villagers. Distinguish the production of this painting from the sacred story it represents.

stops.subject: ming-workshops
stops.title: Court design and skilled work
stops.narrative: Inspect the jar’s fish and plants. Compare production and intended audiences with Benin ivory; a material resemblance cannot provide a shipping history.

stops.subject: manila-network
stops.title: An ocean network and its later echoes
stops.narrative: Trace China, Manila and Acapulco. The Mexican jar shown in the dossier is later, around 1680–1700. Use archaeological wreck evidence for the earlier network; keep the chronology visible.

stops.subject: banda-1621
stops.title: Read a company letter against its grain
stops.narrative: The VOC’s surviving account describes policy and resistance. Consider the author’s purpose and the people whose voices are not preserved in this letter. Connections could be coercive, and people contested them.

journeys.conclusion: Ocean connections were made through skilled work, interpretation and political decisions. They also involved conquest, enslavement and resistance. A specific commission, a translation, a wreck and an official letter support different claims. No single arrow can explain all of them.

evidence.prompt: What is a defensible use of Coen’s 1621 letter?

options.text: Treat it as a neutral account of every Bandanese person’s experience.
options.feedback: The author was a company official writing to superiors. His purposes and omissions matter.

options.text: Use it to investigate company policy and resistance, while seeking other perspectives.
options.feedback: The letter supports a limited analysis of decisions and reported resistance; it cannot replace the experiences of those attacked.

options.text: Assume that profitable exchange benefited everyone equally.
options.feedback: The documented killing, enslavement and displacement directly challenge that assumption.

journeys.returnPrompt: Choose two ocean connections. How did their mechanisms, power relationships and surviving evidence differ?

familyEvidence.claimPrompt: Explain whose decisions this report describes and whose perspective you would seek next.
familyEvidence.returnPrompt: Name another perspective you would seek before retelling the event.
familyEvidence.feedback: The letter can reveal company policy and resistance. Its official’s perspective does not replace the experiences of people attacked.
familyEvidence.title: Read a company official’s report
familyEvidence.text: Coen wrote to the Dutch East India Company’s directors on 6 May 1621. The archive’s transcription describes resistance, food and company manpower, including the use of hunger against opponents. An official reported his own decisions to superiors.
notice: Who wrote the report, and for whom?
Whose account would you add before telling the whole history?

journeys.title: Machines, work and who can choose
journeys.question: Who shaped the conditions of work?
journeys.introduction: Compare resistance to coerced plantation labor, regulation, adaptation of machinery and a reform photograph. These are related questions with distinct legal and historical contexts.

stops.subject: haitian-revolution
stops.title: Freedom required struggle
stops.narrative: Distinguish emancipation, its threatened reversal and independence.

stops.subject: factory-reform
stops.title: Look after the law was passed
stops.narrative: Use inspection to test implementation.

stops.subject: tomioka
stops.title: Importing a machine is only a beginning
stops.narrative: Find the local skills and wider supply system.

stops.subject: hine-labor
stops.title: Separate photograph and caption
stops.narrative: Describe what is visible, then consider the competing accounts.

journeys.conclusion: Work changed through resistance, law, institutions, skilled adaptation and campaigning. Mechanization alone does not explain who had freedom, protection or control.

evidence.prompt: What can the Hine image and caption establish most directly?

options.text: A particular photographed setting and Hine’s recorded account of an overseer’s response.
options.feedback: The photograph and caption have different evidentiary roles. Hours, age and prevalence need further records.

options.text: Every child in every factory worked exactly the same hours.
options.feedback: One image cannot establish a universal quantity or experience.

journeys.returnPrompt: Name one change in production and one separate question about power over work.

familyEvidence.title: A photograph and a caption
familyEvidence.text: Lewis Hine made this photograph on 3 December 1908. His caption supplies information and reports an overseer’s denial. The image and written report have different evidentiary roles; age, hours and pay cannot all be read from the photograph.
notice: Describe the person’s position beside the machinery.
Name something the caption adds.
familyEvidence.claimPrompt: Separate one visible observation from one question about age, hours or pay that needs another record.
familyEvidence.returnPrompt: Name a record that could help answer your question.
familyEvidence.feedback: The photograph records a scene; Hine’s caption reports more. Neither one scene nor its caption measures conditions for every worker.

journeys.title: Political freedom and the meaning of a promise
journeys.question: Who understood, shaped and benefited from political change?
journeys.introduction: Read two treaty texts, a border timetable and a constitution. Ask who could participate and how a political commitment reaches everyday life.

stops.subject: tiriti
stops.title: Read both texts
stops.narrative: Preserve consequential translation differences and the process of signing.

stops.subject: partition-1947
stops.title: A new border meets a household
stops.narrative: Keep independence, border announcement and displacement distinct.

stops.subject: south-africa-rights
stops.title: A commitment with duties
stops.narrative: Read a specific right, then ask how implementation could be investigated.

journeys.conclusion: Political statements have audiences, language and consequences. Their texts matter, and so do participation, institutions and lived experience.

evidence.prompt: Which statement respects the distinction between promise and outcome?

options.text: A constitutional right states a commitment; evidence of implementation must be investigated separately.
options.feedback: The legal text is strong evidence of the obligation. It does not itself measure whether everyone can exercise the right.

options.text: A signature proves identical understanding and universal consent.
options.feedback: The treaty record includes differing texts, refusals and uneven opportunities to sign.

journeys.returnPrompt: Choose a promise and explain whose experience would help test it.

familyEvidence.title: Read a commitment — editorial paraphrase
familyEvidence.text: South Africa’s Bill of Rights protects everyone’s equality before the law. It separately gives political rights to citizens, including the right of adult citizens to vote. This is a paraphrase, not the full constitutional wording or a measure of outcomes.
notice: Who holds each right in the paraphrase?
Separate the commitment from evidence of an outcome.
familyEvidence.claimPrompt: Choose one commitment. What later evidence could help test whether a person could exercise it?
familyEvidence.returnPrompt: Read the linked section and compare its exact wording.
familyEvidence.feedback: The text establishes a commitment with particular wording. People’s experiences and later institutional records help test its exercise; the commitment alone does not measure that outcome.

journeys.title: Global war, state power and a new signal
journeys.question: How do decisions and institutions connect large events to individual lives?
journeys.introduction: This non-graphic investigation names persecution and genocide directly. Read with an adult when helpful, and pause whenever you wish.

stops.subject: world-war-one
stops.title: Look beyond one front
stops.narrative: Read a recruiting appeal as persuasion within a global imperial war.

stops.subject: world-war-two
stops.title: Distinguish connected histories
stops.narrative: Keep war chronology, genocide and individual experience visible.

stops.subject: sputnik
stops.title: An achievement with several meanings
stops.narrative: Investigate scientific success and a particular archive of political responses.

journeys.conclusion: Events did not happen by themselves. Institutions and choices connected science, state power, propaganda and violence. People’s lives should not disappear behind either triumphal images or totals.

evidence.prompt: Why does this atlas keep more than one starting date for the Second World War context?

options.text: War in Asia and war in Europe had different chronologies, while the Holocaust has its own 1933–1945 frame.
options.feedback: USHMM distinguishes these connected histories. One regional starting date cannot stand for all of them.

options.text: All regions entered the same conflict simultaneously in 1939.
options.feedback: The source describes Japanese conquest in 1931/1937 before Germany’s1939 invasion of Poland.

journeys.returnPrompt: What does a public image encourage you to see, and what evidence would broaden that view?

familyEvidence.claimPrompt: Choose two dates and explain the different histories they mark.
familyEvidence.returnPrompt: Retell two of these histories with their own dates and meanings.
familyEvidence.feedback: War in Asia, war in Europe and the Holocaust have connected but distinct chronologies. One date cannot stand for all of them.
familyEvidence.title: Read the dates separately
familyEvidence.text: USHMM describes Japan’s 1931 conquest of Manchuria, its 1937 invasion of China and Germany’s September 1939 invasion of Poland. The Holocaust has a distinct 1933–1945 frame. These connected histories do not share one starting date.

citations.locator: German and Japanese Expansion; Invasion of Poland

notice: Put the dates in order, keeping their different meanings.
Explain why one region’s starting date cannot describe all these histories.

journeys.title: Earth, food and gathering in Indigenous North America
journeys.question: How can we investigate community life without making every monument into the same kind of state?
journeys.introduction: Travel across different centuries and landscapes north of Mesoamerica. These are comparisons among distinct communities, not stages in one people’s development or a route connecting all four sites. Notice food, work, gathering and the limits of the surviving record.

stops.subject: poverty-point
stops.title: Start with a meal and a mound
stops.narrative: Inspect heating objects and ask how food preparation belonged to a monumental landscape built by hunter-fisher-gatherers. Individual objects in the later publication are not precisely dated.

stops.subject: hopewell-earthworks
stops.title: Gather without living inside the walls
stops.narrative: Distinguish a ceremonial enclosure from a permanent town. Compare a modern restoration with an 1848 survey; both need interpretation.

stops.subject: chaco-communities
stops.title: Test a connection through a trace ingredient
stops.narrative: Read the cacao analysis as evidence of movement, then separate that result from an exact route or a claim about every household.

stops.subject: cahokia-city
stops.title: Look beyond one monumental view
stops.narrative: Investigate neighborhoods and work, then consider the debate about population after the urban center changed. Compare Cahokia with Chaco without assuming contact or identical government.

journeys.conclusion: Food, skilled work, exchange and gathering took different forms across North America. Monumental building does not require one universal governing system. Changes in a center’s role do not establish the disappearance of a people, and later photographs must be read alongside archaeology and community accounts.

evidence.prompt: Which statement stays within the Chaco cacao study’s evidence?

options.text: Residues in selected Pueblo Bonito vessel fragments support cacao use and ingredient movement, while access and exact routes remain uncertain.
options.feedback: The study selected five samples and detected theobromine in three probable cylinder-jar fragments. Its evidence does not map every intermediary or describe every household.

options.text: The result proves that all Chaco residents drank cacao daily and that we know the precise road it followed.
options.feedback: A small vessel-fragment sample cannot establish universal daily consumption or an exact itinerary.

options.text: Because a city or ceremonial center changed, all related Indigenous peoples must have disappeared.
options.feedback: A building phase, a regional population interpretation and a people’s continuing history are distinct. Pueblo community statements and the Cahokia debate help keep them separate.

journeys.returnPrompt: Choose one object or landscape. State an observation, a supported explanation and one thing it cannot tell you.

familyEvidence.claimPrompt: Name one study finding and explain why it cannot show what every household drank.
familyEvidence.returnPrompt: What additional samples or records could help investigate who had access to cacao?
familyEvidence.feedback: Selected fragments support cacao use and ingredient movement. They do not establish universal access, an exact route or the purpose of every room.
familyEvidence.title: A building photograph and a separate study
familyEvidence.text: A 2009 study tested fragments representing five Pueblo Bonito vessels. Three probable cylinder-jar samples yielded theobromine, interpreted as cacao evidence. This is a selected sample. The architecture photograph is not a picture of the tested fragments or the chemical analysis.
notice: Separate what the photograph shows from what the study measured.
Could these samples establish what every household drank?

journeys.title: Books, silk and power: West/Central Asia, 1500–1800
journeys.question: How did makers and urban communities work within—and beyond—courtly power?
journeys.introduction: Move from Central Asian bookmaking to Ottoman workshops, Safavid Isfahan and later-eighteenth-century Iran. These linked questions do not imply one empire, one identity or a direct route between every object. Follow production, patronage and the people missing from courtly images.

stops.subject: bukhara-books
stops.title: Give the book more than one date
stops.narrative: Separate Sa‘di’s poem, copying likely in Herat and painting probably in Bukhara. Keep the catalogue’s uncertainty visible.

stops.subject: ottoman-workshops
stops.title: Put a dish beside an emblem of power
stops.narrative: Inspect the birds on the Iznik dish, then choose the tughra. Compare material, use and specialized work rather than treating every object as a palace commission.

stops.subject: isfahan-silk
stops.title: Follow labor and forced movement
stops.narrative: Read the carpet as costly craft within a wider silk economy. Bring New Julfa’s 1604 forced relocation into the account, and compare state patronage with the Ottoman case.

stops.subject: zand-iran
stops.title: Keep the later eighteenth century in view
stops.narrative: Open the lacquer case and its additional views. Its date falls after Karim Khan’s death. A practical object and an idealized courtly image do not establish the same facts.

journeys.conclusion: Courts could commission beautiful work while makers also worked for markets and urban institutions. Silk connected farming, skilled production and commerce with coercion and unequal power. A literary painting, official emblem and practical case reveal different things; none can stand alone for everyone’s experience.

evidence.prompt: Which account best respects both the silk evidence and the history of New Julfa?

options.text: Luxury production involved several forms of work, and New Julfa’s later commercial importance does not make the 1604 deportation voluntary.
options.feedback: The workshop account identifies multiple producers and skills. Ghougassian separately documents forced relocation, later settlement and unequal privileges.

options.text: A beautiful carpet proves everyone involved was prosperous and free to move.
options.feedback: An object’s quality does not establish its makers’ freedom or the conditions of every worker. The documented deportation directly challenges that inference.

options.text: The name Polonaise proves the carpet was woven in Poland.
options.feedback: The catalogue explains the older misattribution and identifies Iranian production centers, while leaving this individual carpet’s precise workshop unresolved.

journeys.returnPrompt: Choose one luxury object and explain a chain of work around it. Identify one person or experience the object alone cannot recover.

familyEvidence.claimPrompt: Explain why the carpet and the relocation account answer different questions about work and freedom.
familyEvidence.returnPrompt: Name a source that could reveal one worker’s choices.
familyEvidence.feedback: Later trade cannot make the 1604 deportation voluntary. A carpet does not identify every worker’s freedom or circumstances.
familyEvidence.title: Craft and movement need different evidence
familyEvidence.text: Ghougassian describes forced Armenian relocation in 1604 and settlement at New Julfa in 1605. Later commercial importance does not make that movement voluntary. The carpet shows costly craft; it is not a record of every worker’s freedom.
notice: Describe a feature of the carpet.
Which separate source would you use to explain the forced relocation?

journeys.title: Arctic, coast and Plains: work, knowledge and belonging
journeys.question: How do different communities sustain life and pass on knowledge?
journeys.introduction: Travel across six selected contexts, from a Bering Sea carving to gardens, clothing and community-directed collections. The stops span different centuries and distinct peoples. This is an investigation of shared questions, not an ancient itinerary or a ladder from one way of life to another.

stops.subject: bering-sea-carvers
stops.title: Start with one tool, not a whole people
stops.narrative: Inspect the counterweight. Separate its visible form, the museum’s functional interpretation and the unresolved relationship between object dating and regional chronology.

stops.subject: ozette-makah
stops.title: Ask what mud preserved
stops.narrative: Read Makah accounts of cedar work, oral history and custody. The displayed photograph is later community documentation; the house-burial date remains disputed.

stops.subject: blackfoot-bison
stops.title: Move beyond the moment at the cliff
stops.narrative: Find the work of coordinating a hunt and processing food. Keep a later landscape photograph and a limited cooking experiment distinct from an ancient event.

stops.subject: hidatsa-villages
stops.title: Put gardens and women’s work in the picture
stops.narrative: Investigate growing, storing and exchanging food beside hunting. Compare the village with Ozette: similar needs do not make the communities identical.

stops.subject: inuinnait-sewing
stops.title: Read clothing with its makers’ knowledge
stops.narrative: Begin with named people in a photograph, then read the community-led study of patterns, materials and language. Changing clothes need not mean an ended culture.

stops.subject: kwakwakawakw-potlatch
stops.title: Ask who keeps and interprets belongings
stops.narrative: Separate a ban from the practice it targeted, and publication from community authority. Learn why 1980 is an institutional milestone, not the end of a people or of return efforts.

journeys.conclusion: Hunting, gardening, woodworking, sewing and witnessing drew on distinct systems of skill and responsibility. Material traces establish some facts; community accounts and careful source reading establish others. Similar needs never make these peoples interchangeable, and neither a relocation nor a legal prohibition proves that a culture ended.

evidence.prompt: Which comparison best respects both the material evidence and the community accounts?

options.text: Hidatsa gardens and Makah cedar work sustained different communities; material traces and community accounts answer complementary questions.
options.feedback: The community-authored subsistence guide documents Hidatsa garden/storage work. Makah sources explain cedar techniques and custody. These specific histories support comparison without proving identical institutions or direct contact.

options.text: A photograph of one Arctic outfit or one bison jump can describe how all northern peoples lived.
options.feedback: The photograph names particular people in dancing costume. Plains evidence includes village agriculture as well as communal hunting. Neither image supplies a universal regional identity.

options.text: Once a village moved or potlatching was banned, the people and their knowledge ceased to exist.
options.feedback: The MHA history traces relocation and continuity. U’mista documents potlatching during prohibition and community efforts to recover belongings. Administrative dates are not the lifespan of a people.

journeys.returnPrompt: Choose one northern object or landscape. Keep one observation, one supported explanation and one question that requires another kind of evidence.

familyEvidence.claimPrompt: Name one task from each community. What can the photograph alone leave unknown?
familyEvidence.returnPrompt: Seek a community-authored source about one chosen task.
familyEvidence.feedback: Makah cedar work and Hidatsa gardens concern distinct communities. A later photograph cannot alone establish all their practices or prove contact.
familyEvidence.title: Keep community accounts distinct
familyEvidence.text: A community-authored Hidatsa guide describes women’s gardening and storage. Makah accounts explain cedar work and canoe construction. This later photograph cannot show all those tasks or make the communities one people.
notice: Name the different communities in the source summary.
Which tasks need evidence beyond this photograph?

journeys.title: Eastern Woodlands: communities, knowledge and power
journeys.question: How do places, food and records help people sustain a community?
journeys.introduction: Begin with an ancestral council place, look back to a separate Ohio earthwork network, then investigate a Wendat village, Haudenosaunee diplomacy, Cherokee printing and Ojibwe rice work. These selected histories cross centuries. Eastern Woodlands is a broad geographic frame, not one people, government or path of development.

stops.subject: ocmulgee-council
stops.title: Separate old clay from a new roof
stops.narrative: Inspect the surviving clay and reconstructed shelter, then investigate the revised dating. The reading year is a context, not a settled construction date.

stops.subject: hopewell-earthworks
stops.title: Look back to a different gathering landscape
stops.narrative: Return to an earlier Ohio network. Compare forms of gathering without making Hopewell the founder of every later woodland society.

stops.subject: wendat-laine
stops.title: Let new evidence move a date
stops.narrative: Put village work beside the calibration problem. Two possible date clusters do not mean a village existed continuously between them.

stops.subject: haudenosaunee-canandaigua
stops.title: Ask what a promise establishes
stops.narrative: Separate negotiation, the treaty clauses, U.S. ratification and Onondaga explanations of wampum. Identify the further evidence needed to test a promise.

stops.subject: cherokee-print
stops.title: Read political voice and exclusions together
stops.narrative: Compare printed assertions with the treaty. A national newspaper can document agency, disagreement and unequal rights, while later removal tests the limits of written promises.

stops.subject: ojibwe-manoomin
stops.title: Find the work beyond the camera
stops.narrative: Use Ojibwe accounts to investigate harvesting, finishing and care for rice waters. Keep the archive’s unnamed person and probable location explicit.

journeys.conclusion: Council spaces, village fields, spoken agreements, printed pages and rice waters connected practical work with responsibilities and authority. The evidence is uneven, and the histories are distinct. Neither a revised archaeological date, a printed promise nor forced movement establishes the disappearance of a people. Carry one specific question back to its sources.

evidence.prompt: Which explanation respects both the records and the people whose histories they concern?

options.text: Treaties and newspapers record particular commitments and arguments; investigating their effects requires further evidence.
options.feedback: Canandaigua’s clauses state promises. The Cherokee constitution records both national assertions and exclusions. Neither text proves equal rights, complete consent or successful enforcement for everyone.

options.text: A reconstructed building and an exact-looking date let us recover every ancient decision with certainty.
options.feedback: Ocmulgee distinguishes surviving clay from reconstructed walls and roof. The newer study revises the older date and leaves questions open. A dating model does not recover the words spoken in a council.

options.text: A photograph of rice canoes tells us the full work of every Eastern Woodlands community.
options.feedback: The archive qualifies person and place. Ojibwe accounts explain several harvesting and finishing operations, but one image cannot represent every community, century or food system.

journeys.returnPrompt: Keep an observation, a supported explanation and a question. Revisit this place or record with another type of source.

familyEvidence.claimPrompt: Distinguish the signing date, ratification date and evidence needed to test a promise.
familyEvidence.returnPrompt: Find a later record that could test one promise.
familyEvidence.feedback: Treaty clauses state commitments; later evidence is needed to test performance. Ratification alone establishes neither complete consent nor successful enforcement.
familyEvidence.title: A written commitment needs an outcome inquiry
familyEvidence.text: Canandaigua’s clauses state peace and land commitments. The treaty was signed in November 1794; this U.S. ratification instrument is dated January 1795. Recording and ratifying promises did not by themselves establish how every later official acted.
notice: Name what each date records.
What would help test one promise?

journeys.title: Independence, citizenship and the work after a promise
journeys.question: What changes on a political turning point—and what still has to be built?
journeys.introduction: Follow four investigations in chronological order. They are comparisons of political change, not a claim that one caused the next. Read a proclamation, a border timetable, a stamp and a voting photograph; ask who gained power, who could participate and what remained unsettled.

stops.subject: indonesia-independence
stops.title: A proclamation begins a struggle
stops.narrative: Inspect the signatures and the short text. Use the phases to distinguish the declaration from Dutch recognition and the later unitary state.

stops.subject: partition-1947
stops.title: A political date and a disrupted home
stops.narrative: Follow the independence and boundary-announcement sequence. Use the place study to ask why a national milestone did not settle every family’s security.

stops.subject: ghana-independence
stops.title: New words on an older design
stops.narrative: Find what changed on the stamp and what remained underneath. Then read the debate to identify the powers that changed hands at independence.

stops.subject: south-africa-rights
stops.title: Bind a government to rights
stops.narrative: Move from the 1994 voting photograph to the 1996 constitutional text. Distinguish the right to govern from the rights that constrain government.

journeys.conclusion: A proclamation, a transfer of sovereignty, an election and a constitutional right do different work. Each can change institutions without settling every question of safety, participation or material life. Explain the particular mechanism before comparing outcomes.

evidence.prompt: Which conclusion best uses the evidence encountered on this journey?

options.text: A national independence date establishes when everyone gained equal rights and secure livelihoods.
options.feedback: The documents identify political changes. They do not measure every person’s rights, safety or livelihood.

options.text: Different milestones change different powers; later outcomes need evidence beyond the announcement or image.
options.feedback: The proclamation, stamp, border timetable and constitution let you identify specific changes and ask a separate question about their effects.

options.text: Because these transitions involved institutions, ordinary people played no part in them.
options.feedback: The Ghana account describes organizing networks, and the South African sources discuss public participation. Institutional history also involves people’s work.

journeys.returnPrompt: Choose two cases. Name the power that changed, the evidence for that change and one outcome that needs more investigation.

familyEvidence.title: A declaration and a separate outcome
familyEvidence.text: The proclamation announces independence and addresses a transfer of power. This typed facsimile differs from the handwritten archival draft. The declaration alone does not show who controlled every place afterward.

citations.locator: Printed p. 7: proclamation draft and context

notice: Find the signatures and dated line.
Use this summary when the small scan is hard to read.
familyEvidence.claimPrompt: Explain what is declared. Name a later source needed before claiming control of every place.
familyEvidence.returnPrompt: Compare a declaration with evidence about its implementation.
familyEvidence.feedback: A declaration records an announcement; later evidence tests control and people’s experiences. Independence and equal rights need distinct dated inquiries.

journeys.title: Who did the work? Accounts, reservoirs and rice
journeys.question: What evidence connects everyday work with a city’s organization?
journeys.introduction: Follow three investigations in thematic order. This is a comparison of evidence, not a travel route, a claim of contact or a sequence of stages toward one civilization. Read each source interpretation before deciding what the works reveal about people.

stops.subject: uruk-accounts
stops.title: An account makes selected work visible
stops.narrative: Look at the tablet, then the diagram. Separate an incised sign, a numerical impression and the proposed grain-account reading. List one task an institution might track and one kind of work the record leaves out.

stops.subject: dholavira
stops.title: A water system has components and uncertainties
stops.narrative: Find the well, East/South reservoirs and dashed research area. Explain why excavated structures and radar interpretations use different conventions. Ask what evidence would connect a household to access to water.

stops.subject: liangzhu
stops.title: Materials, farming and unequal status
stops.narrative: Use the landscape diagram and cong photograph to distinguish construction, food production and burial evidence. Then read the reservoir correction. Decide which conclusions concern practical work and which require social interpretation.

journeys.conclusion: Each case connects material work with larger institutions through a different surviving record. Write one supported explanation and one question requiring new evidence. Shared needs do not establish one origin, equal access or a direct connection between these places.

evidence.prompt: Which explanation best fits the supplied evidence?

options.text: The records and works show different kinds of coordination, while household obligations and access need further evidence.
options.feedback: Yes. Match the grain account, excavated reservoirs and water/production landscape to the claims each supports. None supplies a full household census or recruitment record.

options.text: All the Dholavira features in the radar interpretation can be treated as excavated reservoirs.
options.feedback: The proposed structures require excavation. The diagram’s dashed research area must not become a confirmed ancient plan.

options.text: The shared need to organize work proves that writing and cities spread from Uruk to the other two sites.
options.feedback: Functional comparison is not transmission evidence. This route adds no historical contact or causal relationship.

journeys.returnPrompt: Choose two cases. For each, name the practical task, the evidence for organization and one household-level question the source cannot answer.

familyEvidence.title: Grain and the work of recording
familyEvidence.text: The museum reads this tablet as a probable grain account. Recording grain could help organize distribution, but missing verbs limit the exact interpretation. This object does not supply a complete list of households or explain every recipient’s circumstances.
notice: Find repeated and different marks.
Which parts of the explanation depend on interpretation?
familyEvidence.claimPrompt: Explain one practical use for a grain record. Name a question about its recipients that remains unanswered.
familyEvidence.returnPrompt: Compare this record with a water structure using evidence for each.
familyEvidence.feedback: A grain account supports an inquiry into organization. A precise reading, recipients’ identities and their experiences still need evidence beyond the surviving marks.

journeys.title: Institutions, shipments and ritual
journeys.question: How far can a record take us from materials to people?
journeys.introduction: Read a wreck, a capital and ritual objects in thematic order. Their evidence reveals work and power in different ways. This is not a confirmed route between the three cases or a single worldwide collapse story.

stops.subject: uluburun
stops.title: Separate findspot, cargo and proposed origin
stops.narrative: Use the evidence diagram to identify recovered association, laboratory inference and unresolved itinerary. Explain why none is a substitute for the others.

stops.subject: hattusha-change
stops.title: Place a stress within institutions
stops.narrative: Keep the capital’s phases separate from Gordion’s environmental proxy. Ask what would connect a crop stress with a dated institutional decision.

stops.subject: shang-ritual
stops.title: Look at making, then at attribution
stops.narrative: Compare bone and gong, and follow the casting/divination guide. Distinguish visible features, a catalogue attribution and a claim that needs a known findspot or translation.

journeys.conclusion: A secure association does not settle origins; a dated stress does not decide causation; a ritual object does not preserve every participant’s experience. State one supported mechanism and identify the evidence still needed to connect it with particular people.

evidence.prompt: Which claim respects the different records?

options.text: The wreck, proxy and ritual objects support different arguments; each needs contextual evidence to identify particular people, decisions or routes.
options.feedback: Yes. A recovered association, moisture proxy and museum attribution are different kinds of knowledge. Match the inference to the source and preserve its limits.

options.text: The measured drought proves the Uluburun ship sank and Shang society ended in the same worldwide event.
options.feedback: The wreck is earlier, Shang’s conventional endpoint is later, and the drought source cannot establish direct causation even for the Hittite transformation.

options.text: A possible Anyang attribution and a suggested tin source can both be treated as documented excavation findspots.
options.feedback: The documented wreck location is different from an inferred material origin or a qualified museum place attribution. Keep those labels separate.

journeys.returnPrompt: Choose two cases. Name what is observed or recovered, what is inferred about organization, and one new source that could test the inference.

familyEvidence.title: Visible features, qualified attribution
familyEvidence.text: This bronze gong has a spout, handle and worked animal forms. The museum dates it to the thirteenth–eleventh century BCE and gives Henan Province, possibly Anyang. The catalogue does not establish an excavated tomb or named owner.

citations.locator: Description and Artwork Details; qualified place attribution

notice: Find the spout and handle.
Describe an animal form before interpreting its meaning.
familyEvidence.claimPrompt: Use the spout and handle to explain a possible action. What remains uncertain about its owner or findspot?
familyEvidence.returnPrompt: Name a record that could establish a secure find context.
familyEvidence.feedback: Visible features support a discussion of pouring. Cultural attribution and a qualified place are different from documented excavation or identification of an owner.

journeys.title: Rules, messages and public work
journeys.question: Who carried a rule into everyday life?
journeys.introduction: Compare Qin administrative work, Ashoka’s regional messages and Athenian public life in thematic order. These different places and dates are not one political ladder, a travel itinerary or evidence of contact.

stops.subject: qin-administration
stops.title: Test a standard against local records
stops.narrative: Distinguish a measuring device, a prescribed document and an excavated record. Follow the people preparing and processing the materials.

stops.subject: ashoka-messages
stops.title: Connect a message with its audience
stops.narrative: Use the map to keep Girnar, Dhauli and Kandahar evidence separate. Name the work an instruction requires and the local evidence needed to test its results.

stops.subject: athens-water
stops.title: Separate public work from formal power
stops.narrative: Inspect the earlier jar, then read the later civic rules. Explain why supplying water or selling goods did not itself grant Assembly participation.

journeys.conclusion: Rules needed people and material work. A common standard, a royal instruction and a civic eligibility procedure are different institutions. Explain one mechanism, identify whose experience survives and ask what evidence could test the account.

evidence.prompt: Which comparison respects both institutions and ordinary work?

options.text: Records and objects reveal different tasks and powers; announcements, local practice and political eligibility require separate evidence.
options.feedback: Yes. Identify the rule, the people doing the work and the evidence of implementation. A shared question does not erase differences in status or date.

options.text: Publishing a rule proves that every person experienced its promised result.
options.feedback: A decree or instruction preserves a claim. Local records, material use and people’s experience are needed to investigate its effects.

options.text: Anyone shown working in a public place must have held the same political rights.
options.feedback: Water provision, commerce and Assembly participation were different activities. The jar cannot identify each figure’s legal status or turn public work into universal franchise.

journeys.returnPrompt: Choose two cases. Explain who had to do something for a rule to work, and name one source that could test what happened.

familyEvidence.title: A pictured task is not a census
familyEvidence.text: The museum identifies women at a fountain on this water jar, dated about 510–500 BCE. The painted scene represents work. It does not identify each figure’s legal status or measure how everyone in Athens obtained water.
notice: Find the pictured containers and fountain.
Distinguish the jar’s function from the scene painted on it.
familyEvidence.claimPrompt: Describe the work shown. Why can this scene alone not establish each figure’s political rights?
familyEvidence.returnPrompt: Name another source needed to investigate status or water access.
familyEvidence.feedback: The scene makes a task visible. A representation does not supply every person’s status, a household census or a measure of later practice.

journeys.title: Objects, work and exchange
journeys.question: What turns an object into evidence of a connection?
journeys.introduction: Compare a Palmyrene family memorial, Kushan coins and temple records, and Aksumite excavated material. This thematic inquiry crosses different dates and contexts. It is not one traveller’s route, a list of identical economies or proof of direct contact between every stop.

stops.subject: palmyra
stops.title: Begin with named people
stops.narrative: Read the family inscription, then distinguish it from civic tax rules and public caravan commemoration. A name on this memorial does not supply an occupation or journey.

stops.subject: kushan-contexts
stops.title: Separate presentation from upkeep
stops.narrative: Compare a royal coin with the temple-maintenance account. The selected object, earlier commands and surviving records have different dates; a named official is not every worker.

stops.subject: aksum
stops.title: Ask where the object was found
stops.narrative: The excavation photograph shows five coins with different issue dates. Read them with deposit evidence and nearby domestic/craft traces, keeping the earlier port account on its own clock.

journeys.conclusion: Connections become historical explanations through specific practices and evidence: civic regulation, distribution, maintenance, local production and recorded finds. Similar objects or overlapping dates alone do not reconstruct a journey.

evidence.prompt: What further evidence would best support a claim that this named Palmyrene family financed a particular caravan?

options.text: Their memorial and the caravan records belong to the same city.
options.feedback: A shared city supplies context. It does not identify the family’s occupation or participation in a particular journey.

options.text: A dated record identifying these family members and their financial role in that caravan.
options.feedback: The claim names particular people and an activity. It needs evidence linking those people with that activity, read with its date and purpose. The pictured family inscription alone supplies no caravan role.

options.text: Their clothing and banquet look expensive.
options.feedback: A chosen display of resources does not establish how the family earned or invested them. Clothing and a banquet cannot identify a caravan investment.

citations.locator: Trade: caravan inscriptions and trading communities

journeys.returnPrompt: Choose two records. Explain the work or relationship each makes visible, then name evidence needed before drawing a route between their places.

familyEvidence.title: Named people, a separate trade question
familyEvidence.text: The museum describes a Palmyrene family’s funerary relief with named figures and ancestors in an Aramaic inscription. Naming people on a burial marker does not by itself connect those people with a particular caravan.

citations.locator: Description: family inscription and burial marker

notice: Describe how the figures are arranged.
What does naming people add to the record?
familyEvidence.claimPrompt: What dated evidence would connect these named people with one particular caravan?
familyEvidence.returnPrompt: Choose another record and ask what work it can establish.
familyEvidence.feedback: A specific claim needs a record linking the named people with that activity. The family inscription alone supplies no caravan role or route.

journeys.title: Spaces, skills and learning
journeys.question: How do institutions organize access and everyday work?
journeys.introduction: Compare access through Chang’an’s gates, skilled production in Abbasid-era Iraq, and living and learning at Nalanda. These selected dates form a thematic inquiry, not a single itinerary, a direct causal sequence or proof of contact among the pictured objects.

stops.subject: tang-city
stops.title: Begin with a gate
stops.narrative: Trace the conceptual errand, then compare it with the tomb musician. A functional guide and a funerary image answer different questions.

stops.subject: abbasid-craft
stops.title: Read skill behind a surface
stops.narrative: Distinguish visible decoration, production tasks and evidence needed to identify a workshop. Court locations and political control changed.

stops.subject: nalanda
stops.title: Find the work that supports study
stops.narrative: Read the named Nalanda passages. Separate the seventh-century account, an institutional frame and the modern photograph.

journeys.conclusion: Institutions work through particular arrangements: gates, resources, skilled workers, support and teaching. Their stated rules, pictured activities and actual practice need different evidence.

evidence.prompt: What evidence would best test whether residents could actually make the errand shown in the Chang’an diagram after a ward gate closed?

options.text: The diagram shows a straight street.
options.feedback: A street’s shape does not establish permission or actual movement after closing.

options.text: Dated rules about gates together with records or archaeological evidence of actual access.
options.feedback: The claim concerns a particular time and practice. Rules establish intended arrangements; further evidence tests how access worked.

options.text: The tomb figure has detailed clothing.
options.feedback: The figure is evidence of funerary representation. It does not establish a route through a closed gate.

journeys.returnPrompt: Choose one institution. Explain a practical task and who helped perform it, then name evidence needed before claiming everyone had the same access.

familyEvidence.title: A modern guide to a practical constraint
familyEvidence.text: This modern diagram uses a ward gate, public street and market to pose an imagined errand. The cited seminar summary describes gates and curfew. The guide is schematic, not a measured plan or a record of one resident’s actual journey.

citations.locator: Walled wards, gates, curfew and reconstruction limits

notice: Trace the imagined errand to the gate.
Find the boundary that constrains movement.
familyEvidence.claimPrompt: What evidence would test whether a resident could actually pass after the gate closed?
familyEvidence.returnPrompt: Compare an intended rule with evidence about daily practice.
familyEvidence.feedback: A gate and curfew describe intended arrangements. Further dated evidence is needed to test enforcement, exceptions and a particular resident’s access.

journeys.title: Work, obligation and historical voices
journeys.question: Who supplied the work, and who gets to describe its benefits?
journeys.introduction: Compare a Song fiscal proposal, Mali’s royal image and household production, and Inca textile work and provisioning. The selected dates are a thematic inquiry, not a route, a single causal sequence or evidence of contact among these objects.

stops.subject: song-art
stops.title: Follow the proposed timing
stops.narrative: Trace resources before harvest and repayment later. What would you ask a household before accepting the policy’s promised benefit?

stops.subject: mali-networks
stops.title: Look below the royal image
stops.narrative: Describe visible royal signs, then use the account of common pottery to identify work the image omits.

stops.subject: inca-weaving
stops.title: Separate skill from choice
stops.narrative: Find construction features in the garment. Distinguish them from evidence about rotating service, resettlement and provisioning.

journeys.conclusion: Proposals, royal images and finished objects can conceal different parts of work. Add household evidence and distinct voices before judging benefits or choices.

evidence.prompt: Which evidence would best test whether the proposed Song loan helped a particular household?

options.text: The official memorial says the policy would benefit people.
options.feedback: That explains the authors’ justification, not the household’s actual experience.

options.text: Dated local borrowing and repayment records, read alongside that household’s circumstances.
options.feedback: These could test timing, terms, harvest conditions and collection against the promise. Surviving records still need interpretation.

options.text: The Mali map depicts a ruler holding gold.
options.feedback: A foreign royal image cannot establish the outcome of a particular Song loan.

journeys.returnPrompt: Choose one case. Explain a practical task, name the voice describing it, and identify evidence needed before saying the arrangement benefited its workers.

familyEvidence.title: Read a proposal before claiming a result
familyEvidence.text: The modern guide follows the 1069 crop-loan proposal: resources before harvest and repayment later. A policy argument describes an intended arrangement. The arrows do not measure a particular household’s harvest, debt or freedom to participate.
notice: Find when resources arrive and repayment follows.
Keep the proposal separate from a measured result.
familyEvidence.claimPrompt: Name a household record that could test whether this timing and repayment helped.
familyEvidence.returnPrompt: Explain what your chosen record could reveal and still leave unknown.
familyEvidence.feedback: Loan terms, collection records and household accounts could test a proposal against experience. They still need dates, context and interpretation.

journeys.title: Makers, interpreters and unequal encounters
journeys.question: Whose knowledge made an encounter possible, and who could choose?
journeys.introduction: Compare an ocean account, an Edo carving and Kongo religious making and royal letters. The selected dates organize a thematic inquiry, not a single causal route or evidence that these particular objects and voyagers met.

stops.subject: portuguese-voyage
stops.title: Name the necessary work
stops.narrative: Identify a pilot, interpreter and court official. Find the account’s evidence that assistance and coercion could coexist.

stops.subject: benin-ivory
stops.title: Follow a maker’s choices
stops.narrative: Point to carved details and distinguish a patron’s likely audience from unknown instructions or a named maker.

stops.subject: kongo-translation
stops.title: Separate meaning from enforcement
stops.narrative: Compare the crucifix interpretation with Afonso’s earlier proposed inspection rule. Neither proves what everyone believed or what officials enforced.

journeys.conclusion: Objects and accounts show active makers and intermediaries. Their creativity does not erase coercion, and a ruler’s request does not supply every person’s voice.

evidence.prompt: Which work does this guide identify beyond sailing?

options.text: Pilotage and interpretation helped an arrival become possible.
options.feedback: The guide identifies supplies and a pilot at Malindi, then interpreters and a court audience at Calicut. Useful assistance does not prove that everyone could choose freely.

options.text: Everyone involved could choose freely.
options.feedback: The guide explicitly leaves free choice unproven. The journal also records detention.

options.text: The arrow records the exact ship track.
options.feedback: The arrow follows the narrative sequence. It is not a reconstructed sailing course.

journeys.returnPrompt: Choose a task, identify the source that reveals it, and explain what further evidence would help establish the worker’s choices.

familyEvidence.title: Read the tasks in a narrative
familyEvidence.text: The guide follows the journal’s account: supplies and a pilot at Malindi, then interpreters and a court audience at Calicut. The account also describes detention. A narrative sequence is not an exact sailing route; assistance alone does not establish free choice.
notice: Name a task beyond sailing.
Find the place assigned to that task.
familyEvidence.claimPrompt: Explain why the assistance described here does not establish everyone’s freedom to choose.
familyEvidence.returnPrompt: Name evidence that could help establish one worker’s choices.
familyEvidence.feedback: The account identifies useful work and also describes detention. Assistance and coercion need attention together; one narrator does not supply every participant’s experience.

journeys.title: Homes, provisions and renewal
journeys.question: What recurring work kept a place usable, and which records reveal it?
journeys.introduction: Follow three investigations in thematic order: preparing food, renewing built space and maintaining a home. They are comparisons of work and evidence, not a travel route, a claim of contact or stages toward one origin of civilization. Each place retains its own chronology and institutions.

stops.subject: old-kingdom
stops.title: A monument needed recurring provision
stops.narrative: Begin with the relationship between grain, food preparation and people doing work. Keep Giza’s excavated workplaces, the translated crew record and the selected Saqqara chapel wall distinct. A recurring task requires more than a finished monument.

stops.subject: caral
stops.title: An earlier room could enter later construction
stops.narrative: Follow the guide from space through subdivision to fill and renewal. The project describes woven stone-filled bags and changing rooms; it does not supply every builder’s choices or one sequence for all buildings. Compare the material tasks before inferring the same institution.

stops.subject: skara-brae
stops.title: A house required continuing practical work
stops.narrative: Imagine bringing fuel from the entrance toward the hearth in the independently drawn feature guide. Then read how House 1 changed during modern rebuilding. Physical features support practical questions while their present arrangement also has a history.

journeys.conclusion: Preparing food, renewing buildings and maintaining domestic space depended on people, materials and organization. The evidence here makes particular relationships visible without identifying every worker or establishing a common government across these places.

evidence.prompt: How could we investigate the recurring work that kept these places usable?

citations.locator: Printed pp.19 and41 / PDF 21 and43: fill and renewal
Printed pp.67–69: House 1 features and rebuilding

options.text: Match a practical task to its specific record, then test the interpretation with further evidence.
options.feedback: A workplace, construction fill and a described house each support different questions. Their limits help choose a further source rather than erase the work they reveal.

options.text: Treat similar work as proof that one institution governed all three places.
options.feedback: Recurring tasks can be compared across distinct settings. Similarity does not establish shared government, contact or identical labor arrangements.

options.text: Read a modern guide as the exact arrangement experienced by every ancient resident.
options.feedback: The guides are modern and schematic. House phases, later alterations and different records require their own dates and explanations.

journeys.returnPrompt: Choose one task. Explain who or what had to contribute, cite the record that supports it, and name one question needing further evidence.

familyEvidence.title: A practical task in a changing room
familyEvidence.text: HES describes House 1’s hearth, shelving and stone enclosures. Nineteenth-century rebuilding omitted recorded cells; a window is modern. This independently drawn guide uses selected feature relationships. It is not a measured plan or a complete ancient room.
notice: Find the entrance and hearth.
Trace an imagined trip carrying fuel. An adult can read the labels aloud.
familyEvidence.claimPrompt: Explain one task the guide helps you imagine. What evidence would test how people actually used the room?
familyEvidence.returnPrompt: Compare one present feature with a record of its earlier arrangement.
familyEvidence.feedback: Features help explore a practical task. The guide does not identify an actual occupant, exact route, work role or unchanged ancient interior.

journeys.title: Clay, work and local histories
journeys.question: How can clay reveal practical work and connections?
journeys.introduction: Compare heating objects, a small represented body and the making of patterned pottery. Each investigation connects materials with practical work and its own local history. This thematic order is not a travel route, a claim of contact between these places or a single sequence of civilizational stages.

stops.subject: poverty-point
stops.title: A small object could supply stored heat
stops.narrative: Observe the heating-object shapes, then read how the account connects them to cooking. Set that work beside building and maintaining the plaza. The modern terrain image and excavated deposits answer different questions about the place.

stops.subject: olmec
stops.title: A represented body shows a different use of clay
stops.narrative: Look at the figure’s ornaments and modeled details before proposing a social meaning. Its missing excavated findspot matters. Compare a portable figure with earth building and the revised dating of supposed households at San Lorenzo.

stops.subject: lapita
stops.title: A repeated operation could build a larger pattern
stops.narrative: Follow the original modern stamp-action guide. Then distinguish the museum’s plaster cast, ancient ceramic samples and scientific studies of materials, dates and diet. Similar decoration starts an inquiry; it does not recover a canoe’s itinerary.

journeys.conclusion: Clay could supply heat, represent a body or become a useful decorated container. Making and using these forms involved different skills and social settings. Material observations, dated contexts and carefully chosen comparisons explain more than assigning every similar object one use or one origin.

evidence.prompt: What next investigation would best test a ceramic-transfer interpretation?

citations.locator: Published abstract: local and nonlocal temper

options.text: Date a coral tool from the same island.
options.feedback: A well-contextualized dated tool can improve settlement chronology. It does not directly identify the ceramic’s material source or distinguish a carried vessel from local production.

options.text: Compare the sherd’s minerals with local and nonlocal source samples, alongside its dated context.
options.feedback: Material comparison directly tests provenance. Nonlocal fabric can strengthen a transfer interpretation, while movement of raw ingredients remains an alternative to consider; no individual carrier or exact itinerary follows automatically.

options.text: Compare burial protein-isotope values with food baselines.
options.feedback: That is useful for a different question about dietary protein. It does not directly test where the pottery’s clay or temper originated.

options.text: Match decorative bands on a modern plaster cast.
options.feedback: A cast can help compare represented surface detail. Its plaster is not the ancient vessel’s fabric, so it cannot supply that vessel’s clay composition or prove ceramic transfer.

journeys.returnPrompt: Choose one practical task and one proposed connection. Name the evidence that supports each, then choose a further test that would answer the remaining question.

familyEvidence.title: Small actions make a larger pattern
familyEvidence.text: The museum essay describes potters pressing toothed tools into clay before firing. This original modern guide uses a hypothetical tool and pattern to explain that operation. It does not reproduce a recovered ancient tool, motif or vessel. The separate museum photograph shows a modern plaster cast.

citations.locator: Ceramic technique and proposed vessel uses

notice: Find the teeth, the single impression and the repeated marks. An adult can read the labels aloud.
Draw one small paper mark, then repeat it to make a band of your own.
familyEvidence.claimPrompt: Explain how repetition made your pattern. What else would you need before claiming that a pot traveled?
familyEvidence.returnPrompt: Come back to the pattern and add a question about the material or place where the object was found.
familyEvidence.feedback: The guide supports explaining a making operation. Similar marks alone do not date a vessel, establish its material source or identify a voyage; those require different evidence.

journeys.title: Makers, supplies and royal claims
journeys.question: Who made and supplied things for powerful places?
