phases.title: A trading city in a wider setting
phases.text: The Met describes Palmyra’s prosperity and caravan setting by this period. This viewing point is not an exact foundation date.

phases.label: 137 CE
phases.title: A public fiscal decision
phases.text: A council decree and revised tariff address recurring charges. The regulation’s civic scope is distinct from caravan itineraries.

phases.label: Second–third centuries CE: object window
phases.title: The selected family memorial
phases.text: The broad catalogue range does not identify an exact year for carving, commissioning or the deaths represented.

phases.label: 272 CE
phases.title: Aurelian recaptures Palmyra
phases.text: The Getty account distinguishes this siege from the following year’s conflict. The portrait is not evidence of the family’s role in either event.

phases.label: 273 CE
phases.title: Another siege and later habitation
phases.text: A second rebellion and siege damaged the city. The same account describes continued habitation afterward; this is not a date of complete disappearance.

contexts.title: Kushan rule: coin images, temple orders and maintenance

interval.label: First–third centuries CE: selected Kushan frame
interval.note: Analytical orientation, not newly asserted foundation/dissolution dates. Absolute ruler chronology and some inscription readings remain debated.

contexts.summary: Keep an era’s proposed starting point, events described retrospectively, object catalogues and later building works on separate clocks.

phases.label: Possibly c. 104/105 CE
phases.title: A date in an unnamed era
phases.text: Sims-Williams discusses a possible conversion of Dasht-e Nawur’s year 279 and identifies Vima Taktu. The conversion depends on the proposed era and remains conditional.

phases.label: c. 127/128 CE: proposed era start
phases.title: A chronology used for comparison
phases.text: The editor and Berlin catalogue use this revised framework. It does not turn every accession or coin date into an exact settled year.

phases.label: Probably no earlier than c. 132/133 CE
phases.title: The Rabatak record
phases.text: The text remembers first-year events but may refer to year six. A lower bound on the record differs from the date of its narrated commands.

phases.label: Not before c. 158/159 CE
phases.title: Surkh Kotal and water works
phases.text: The editor dates the works’ year 31 in this proposed absolute framework. The inscription itself may be later, and technical readings remain qualified.

contexts.title: Aksum, Adulis and inland work through time

interval.label: First–seventh centuries CE: selected connections and excavated phases
interval.note: A reference window for these sources, not exact founding/abandonment or the full lifespan of Aksum. The original dossier retains its first–eighth-century convention.

contexts.summary: An early port account, fourth-century royal writing and later inland deposits describe different phases. They do not all illustrate 200 CE.

phases.label: Mid-first century CE (viewing anchor)
phases.title: The merchant-oriented account
phases.text: The Periplus discussion places Adulis and inland exchange in this period; the viewing year is not a precise composition date or an imperial border.

phases.label: 200 CE: chapter viewing anchor
phases.title: Keep later evidence dated
phases.text: The chapter opens a changing world. The major stelae and the reproduced excavated coins retain later dates; none is silently assigned to this exact year.

phases.label: Fourth century CE (orientation)
phases.title: Royal writing and changing religion
phases.text: Greek and Ge’ez occur in multiple scripts. The excavation study places Ezana’s conversion broadly in the mid-fourth century while cautioning about its non-elite effects.

phases.label: Late sixth–seventh-century deposits
phases.title: Coins and everyday work
phases.text: The excavation combines coin types, pottery and radiocarbon evidence to interpret later deposits. Armah’s proposed dates have an alternative discussed in the source.

phases.label: Around the mid-seventh century CE
phases.title: Latest dated occupation in this excavation
phases.text: The latest dated charcoal samples inform a phase of habitation. This rounded viewing point does not establish the last resident’s departure or the end of the kingdom.

contexts.title: Chang’an before, within and after the Tang frame

interval.label: Sui rebuilding and Tang capital: selected phases, 581–907 CE
interval.note: A reference window for these sources, not the lifespan of Xi’an or a claim that all fabric dates to 581.

contexts.summary: A rebuilt Sui capital, Tang government, religious translation and later disruptions have separate dates.

phases.label: 581 onward: Sui accession and rebuilding
phases.title: A new capital follows an older city
phases.text: The source places the decision to build a new capital under the Sui; this viewing year marks that transition, not a fully completed city.

phases.label: 618 CE
phases.title: Tang dynastic frame begins
phases.text: An inherited urban and institutional setting precedes the new dynasty.

phases.label: 645 CE
phases.title: Xuanzang returns with texts
phases.text: The return differs from the following work of translation and storage.

phases.label: 652 CE; rebuilding 701–704
phases.title: A pagoda has more than one date
phases.text: A first foundation does not date all the standing structure.

phases.label: Mid-eighth century: orientation
phases.title: Rebellion and weakened authority
phases.text: This viewing anchor locates a major disruption; the dynasty continued afterward.

phases.label: 845 CE
phases.title: Religious persecutions
phases.text: The account describes persecution affecting multiple religious communities. Prior presence did not guarantee lasting security.

phases.label: 907 CE: conventional dynastic endpoint
phases.title: A dynasty ends; a city continues changing
phases.text: This is not Xi’an’s final date or the date of every later monument.

contexts.title: Abbasid-era Iraq: capitals, workshops and changing control

interval.label: 750–1258 CE: selected Iraq-centered phases
interval.note: A teaching frame matching the conventional dynastic case, not uninterrupted uniform sovereignty or the full history of Iraqi cities.

contexts.summary: Baghdad and Samarra, production evidence and a dated manuscript belong to different moments within changing political authority.

phases.label: 750 CE
phases.title: Abbasid rule begins
phases.text: This precedes Baghdad’s foundation.

phases.label: 762 CE
phases.title: Baghdad is founded
phases.text: The new capital concentrates political and cultural activity.

phases.label: 836–892 CE
phases.title: The court at Samarra
phases.text: A capital phase differs from the whole dynastic span and from the selected tenth-century bowl.

phases.label: 945 CE
phases.title: Buyid control of Baghdad
phases.text: Caliphal authority changes; later Seljuq control begins in 1055.

phases.label: 621 AH / 1224 CE
phases.title: A manuscript is copied and illustrated
phases.text: The dated leaf is attributed to Baghdad; this is not a first translation date or observed hospital scene.

phases.label: 1258 CE
phases.title: Mongol sack of Baghdad
phases.text: This endpoint does not retrospectively make earlier political control uniform; later nominal caliphs in Egypt fall outside this case.

contexts.title: Nalanda: institutional history, an account and conserved remains

interval.label: Fifth–thirteenth centuries CE: monastic and scholastic frame
interval.note: Rounded century boundaries; earlier archaeological remains and modern conservation retain separate dates. No exact foundation or destruction year is asserted.

contexts.summary: The institutional frame, seventh-century textual evidence and a modern photograph answer different questions.

phases.label: Fifth century CE: rounded boundary
phases.title: A monastic and scholastic institution
phases.text: UNESCO distinguishes the institutional frame from earlier archaeology at the site.

phases.label: Later seventh century CE: viewing anchor
phases.title: Yijing describes practices
phases.text: This approximate viewing year places selected accounts; it is not a precise observation date for every passage or building.

phases.label: Thirteenth century CE: rounded orientation
phases.title: Sack and abandonment in the broad synthesis
phases.text: The source uses a century-scale account. This viewing point is not an exact destruction date.

phases.label: End of the selected century-scale frame
phases.title: Keep later excavation separate
phases.text: Excavation, conservation and the 2023 photograph are modern episodes, not the medieval institution’s continuation.

contexts.title: Song institutions: northern and southern phases

interval.label: 960–1279 CE: Northern and Southern Song
interval.note: Conventional dynastic frame; distinct neighboring states and changing control remain. It is not the lifespan of all Chinese institutions.

contexts.summary: The two capital phases, a 1069 proposal and an independently dated bowl remain distinct.

phases.label: 960 CE: conventional beginning
phases.title: Northern Song frame
phases.text: The capital setting is Kaifeng; neighboring Liao and later Jin histories remain distinct.

phases.label: 1069 CE
phases.title: Crop loans are proposed
phases.text: A fiscal memorial sets out seasonal lending and repayment. Its intended benefits are not an outcome study.

phases.label: 1127 CE
phases.title: A northern loss and southern court
phases.text: The Jurchen Jin take the northern capital; the Southern Song phase follows. This is not the Mongol conquest.

phases.label: 1279 CE
phases.title: Mongol conquest ends the Southern Song
phases.text: A dynastic endpoint does not end Chinese material work or every institution.

contexts.title: Mali and West African networks: changing scales and voices

interval.label: About 1230–1600 CE: broad exhibition frame
interval.note: Approximate reference orientation, not exact founding/extinction or a fixed empire boundary.

contexts.summary: Older urban histories, Sunjata traditions, a pilgrimage, a foreign image and overlapping later powers have separate dates.

phases.label: Early thirteenth century: approximate anchor
phases.title: A Mali political frame
phases.text: Sunjata traditions concern beginnings; urban work at Jenne-jeno has a much older history.

phases.label: 1324 CE: Cairo pilgrimage anchor
phases.title: Mansa Musa travels via Cairo
phases.text: This is a dated episode, not the origin of regional networks or a measured fortune.

phases.label: About 1375 CE: conventional atlas date
phases.title: Mali pictured in Majorca
phases.text: A foreign royal image is made later than the pilgrimage; attribution remains qualified.

phases.label: Later fifteenth century: orientation
phases.title: Overlapping Songhay power
phases.text: The exhibition’s Songhay frame overlaps later Mali histories; this anchor is not an exact transfer of every settlement.

phases.label: About 1600 CE: selected endpoint
phases.title: A reference window ends
phases.text: The broad display frame does not mean all institutions, communities or memories suddenly disappear.

contexts.title: Inca labor and authority: garment, state and colonial account

interval.label: Fifteenth century–about 1615: selected institutional and source window
interval.note: Rounded early boundary and later manuscript endpoint; not the empire’s exact lifespan or the tunic’s manufacture range.

contexts.summary: Imperial work, a 1450–1550 garment range, Spanish invasion and later Indigenous criticism answer different questions.

phases.label: 1450–1550 CE: catalogue range
phases.title: The tunic’s broad date begins
phases.text: This date belongs to a material attribution; it does not supply an individual maker or exact political phase.

phases.label: Around 1500 CE: viewing anchor
phases.title: Roads, work and stores
phases.text: A rounded orientation for institutions described in these sources, not the foundation year of every road or store.

phases.label: 1530s: Spanish invasion and rupture
phases.title: Colonial conditions change the setting
phases.text: The viewing anchor orients the invasion period; the garment’s broad date does not determine whether it was made before or after it.

phases.label: 1550 CE: catalogue range ends
phases.title: An object range ends
phases.text: This is not the disappearance of Andean weaving or Indigenous communities.

phases.label: About 1615 CE
phases.title: Guaman Poma’s colonial critique
phases.text: A later Indigenous manuscript addresses exploitation and reform, rather than witnessing every preconquest workshop.

contexts.title: Benin court, makers and Atlantic encounters

interval.label: Fifteenth–seventeenth centuries: selected court and encounter window
interval.note: Rounded orientation, not the kingdom’s foundation or ending; later collection history is discussed separately.

contexts.summary: Court production and Atlantic encounters have a broader frame than one export saltcellar.

phases.label: Fifteenth century: rounded orientation
phases.title: An established court and its makers
phases.text: The court and craft traditions predate the selected saltcellar. This anchor is not an exact foundation year.

phases.label: Fifteenth–sixteenth centuries: broad contact frame
phases.title: Expansion and traded materials
phases.text: Portuguese trade joined a changing court economy. The anchor is not the first contact’s exact date.

phases.label: About 1525–1600: catalogue range
phases.title: The selected saltcellar
phases.text: Its dated attribution belongs to one object inquiry; no named commission is established.

phases.label: End of selected seventeenth-century window
phases.title: A teaching frame ends
phases.text: Benin’s court and artistic histories continue beyond this boundary.

contexts.title: Kongo Christianity: translation, royal claims and disagreement

interval.label: 1491–1706: selected religious and political episodes
interval.note: The baptism and Kimpa Vita episodes bound this reference window, not the lifespan of Kongo or its Christianity. The dossier retains its open ending.

contexts.summary: Baptism, letters, religious teaching and later conflict are distinct source episodes.

phases.label: 1491 CE
phases.title: Nzinga Nkuwu receives baptism
phases.text: The royal episode does not establish universal or permanent adoption.

phases.label: July and October 1526
phases.title: Afonso writes about trafficking
phases.text: Distinct complaints and proposed inspections do not prove effective protection.

phases.label: 1624 CE
phases.title: Portuguese–Kikongo teaching text
phases.text: A bilingual catechism belongs to continued translation, not the start of every local religious practice.

phases.label: 1645 CE
phases.title: Capuchin missions arrive
phases.text: A later missionary setting should not be projected onto the 1491 baptism.

phases.label: 1706 CE
phases.title: Kimpa Vita is executed
phases.text: Conflict over a later religious movement ends this selected window; Kongo Christianity continues.

contexts.title: Indian Ocean encounters: voyage and later conquest

interval.label: 1497–1510: selected voyage and later Goa episode
interval.note: A short sequence, not the beginning of Indian Ocean commerce or the whole Portuguese presence.

contexts.summary: Existing ports, a 1497–1499 voyage and a later conquest have separate histories.

phases.label: 1497 CE
phases.title: Departure from Portugal
phases.text: This begins the selected voyage, rather than maritime exchange between continents.

phases.label: 1498 CE
phases.title: Malindi and Calicut encounters
phases.text: Pilotage, negotiation, coercion and interpretation feature in the participant’s account.

phases.label: 1499 CE
phases.title: The voyage frame ends
phases.text: A return date does not settle the later history of these ports.

phases.label: 1510 CE
phases.title: Portuguese conquest of Goa
phases.text: A later military episode, distinct from the first voyage and Calicut audience.

contexts.title: Old Kingdom institutions, provisioning and changing service

interval.label: c. 2649–2130 BCE: selected Old Kingdom orientation
interval.note: Uses the current Met essay’s convention, not the lifetime of Egypt or the date of the chapel wall. The wall remains c. 2465–2389 BCE; Giza construction support and later cult service belong to their own phases.

contexts.summary: Royal building and funerary service required continuing material and administrative work; institutions and political relationships changed across the period.

phases.label: Dynasty 3, c. 2649–2575 BCE: period convention
phases.title: Monuments and funerary institutions
phases.text: The Met frames Djoser’s Saqqara complex within a changing royal and elite funerary landscape. This orientation is earlier than the selected chapel wall.

phases.label: Dynasty 4, c. 2575–2465 BCE: broad frame
phases.title: Construction needs provision
phases.text: Giza settlements and the late-Khufu logbook reveal distinct kinds of support work. A period anchor does not date one continuous crew or identify Merer’s team with the excavated settlement.

phases.label: c. 2465–2389 BCE: selected wall’s catalogue range
phases.title: An elite chapel and ongoing service
phases.text: The Saqqara wall depicts offerings and activities within commemoration. Its purpose and present arrangement differ from an excavated workplace and from a contemporary crew’s administrative entry.

phases.label: Later Old Kingdom: Dynasty 6 begins c. 2323 BCE in Met convention
phases.title: Repair, reuse and changing authority
phases.text: AERA describes renewed cult buildings and settlement reuse. The Met discusses increasing provincial officials’ prominence and debated political change. Neither source supports one uniform ending for every place.

citations.locator: Dynasty 6 and end of Old Kingdom

contexts.title: Caral-Supe: settlement, food and renewed buildings

interval.label: c. 3000–1800 BCE: selected settlement and building sequence
interval.note: Broad orientation follows UNESCO. The phase labels adapt the 2005 project scheme; anchors are not exact construction dates for every building or universal political transitions. The case retains its complete original interval and alternative 1900 BCE endpoint.

contexts.summary: A settlement landscape changed through construction, enlargement and renewal. The 2005 project scheme offers one phased account, rather than a recovered timetable for every household.

citations.locator: PDF p. 15, printed p. 13: cultural-process scheme

phases.label: About 3000–2600 BCE: 2005 project scheme
phases.title: Settlements and public spaces grow
phases.text: The project groups settlement growth and substantial public building within this broad early phase. The anchor is not one founding year.

citations.locator: PDF p. 15, printed p. 13: cultural-process scheme

phases.label: About 2600–2300 BCE: 2005 project scheme
phases.title: Buildings and their relationships are redesigned
phases.text: The scheme describes remodeling and the addition of circular plazas. Its political interpretation is not an independently established date of state formation.

citations.locator: PDF p. 15, printed p. 13: cultural-process scheme

phases.label: About 2300–2100 BCE: two grouped project subdivisions
phases.title: Enlargement and further remodeling
phases.text: This editorial phase groups the project’s 2300–2200 and 2200–2100 subdivisions; it does not erase their separate labels in the source.

citations.locator: PDF p. 15, printed p. 13: cultural-process scheme

phases.label: About 2100–1800 BCE: 2005 project scheme
phases.title: Later renewal, covering and ending
phases.text: The project places renewed construction, the covering of some components and abandonment within its final broad phase. No single terminal event is asserted.

citations.locator: PDF p. 15, printed p. 13: cultural-process scheme

phases.label: End of this selected UNESCO orientation
phases.title: A teaching window ends
phases.text: UNESCO’s development range ends here; the existing case also records the Peruvian orientation’s different 1900 BCE endpoint. Neither is a precise date for every last activity.

contexts.title: Skara Brae: households and a changing landscape

interval.label: 3300–2440 BCE: selected archaeological orientation
interval.note: The left edge is the atlas’s display boundary, not a foundation date. The modeled beginning of earlier activity, within 3360–3160 cal BCE, can precede it. Occupation was interrupted; modeled final boundary 2545–2440 cal BCE is not one exact end year. The original case remains c. 3180–2500 BCE with its full conflict note.

contexts.summary: Standing houses gather several Neolithic phases and modern conservation changes. Earlier cereal evidence, changing passages and nearby monuments require their own contexts.

citations.locator: Skara Brae and the Braes of Ha’Breck

phases.label: Modeled beginning within 3360–3160 cal BCE; display edge 3300 BCE
phases.title: Evidence beneath the surviving houses
phases.text: Phase 0 cereal material precedes the main standing settlement. The 3300 marker is an atlas display boundary within a source uncertainty range, not a dated founding event.

citations.locator: Skara Brae and the Braes of Ha’Breck: underlying Phase 0

phases.label: Modeled beginning boundary 2920–2885 cal BCE
phases.title: Earliest surviving house phase begins
phases.text: HES reports a range for the beginning of the earliest houses that survive today. It is not the complete duration of a house or a precise year for every wall.

phases.label: Apparent interruption associated with 2870–2760 cal BCE
phases.title: A discontinuous sequence
phases.text: The report identifies an apparent interruption, possibly associated with sand. Boundary uncertainties overlap; they are not exact nonoverlapping reign-like periods.

phases.label: Renewed occupation modeled within 2840–2685 cal BCE
phases.title: New houses and remodeling
phases.text: New structures and altered older houses form a later phase. Passages also changed over time; some acquired roof slabs during occupation rather than belonging to one original complete plan.

phases.label: Modeled ending boundary 2545–2440 cal BCE
phases.title: Later village use ends, later activity remains
phases.text: This modeled boundary spans the retained case’s approximate 2500 BCE endpoint. Later traces and modern excavation are separate histories; no single sudden disaster is established here.

contexts.title: Gulf Coast communities and changing centres

interval.label: c. 1800–400 BCE: selected settlement and regional-centre frames
interval.note: A teaching window combining the 2020 San Lorenzo construction scheme with INAH’s conventional La Venta peak. It is not one continuous polity or one universal sequence. The original c. 1200–400 BCE case interval and the figure’s separate 1200–900 BCE catalogue range remain unchanged.

contexts.summary: Selected construction phases at San Lorenzo and a different monumental setting at La Venta broaden the small-object inquiry. Their source conventions remain visible rather than becoming one origin story or exact political succession.

citations.locator: San Lorenzo and La Venta paragraphs

phases.label: c. 1800–1400 BCE: San Lorenzo project’s Arenas phase
phases.title: Earlier settlement and prepared floors
phases.text: The 2020 account groups earlier settlement and building evidence within this construction phase, before the retained dossier’s starting date. It is not an origin date for all Olmec communities.

phases.label: c. 1400–1200 BCE: San Lorenzo project’s Terrazas phase
phases.title: Earth building enlarges the settlement
phases.text: The source describes substantial filling and residential terrace construction. Its approximate phase labels do not identify every builder or establish one labour-recruitment system.

phases.label: c. 1200–1000 BCE: San Lorenzo project’s BAV phase
phases.title: A source-specific peak-phase scheme
phases.text: The project assigns this interval to its later construction phase. INAH instead uses a conventional 1200–900 BCE San Lorenzo peak; the conventions are recorded separately rather than silently harmonized.

phases.label: c. 800–400 BCE: INAH’s conventional La Venta peak
phases.title: A different monumental setting
phases.text: INAH places La Venta’s peak here. Platforms and buried greenstone offerings belong to a different centre; this range is neither its complete occupation nor proof of an exact political transfer from San Lorenzo.

citations.locator: After about 900 B.C.; In fact, the growth of La Venta

phases.label: End of this selected frame
phases.title: Material histories continue elsewhere
phases.text: Doyle describes continued sculpture and ceramic production at centres including Tres Zapotes after La Venta’s monumental phase. This teaching endpoint does not date the disappearance of a people.

citations.locator: Large stone sculpture at La Venta paragraph

contexts.title: Lapita island communities and changing pottery

interval.label: c. 1500–400 BCE: selected island sequences and later Tongan change
interval.note: A teaching frame across different islands, not one polity or continuous voyage. The broad Bismarck orientation differs in precision from site-specific models. Later Tongan ceramic change extends beyond the unchanged c. 1500–500 BCE case. Cal BP denotes years before 1950; BCE equivalents are rounded. Regional phases overlap.

contexts.summary: Pottery production, coastal provisioning and dated settlement evidence reveal different parts of island community history. A change in ceramic practice is not the end of a people, while each island retains its own sequence.

citations.locator: Abstract; Context; Discussion: latest phase boundary

phases.label: Around 1500 BCE: broad regional orientation
phases.title: Bismarck communities and the pottery complex
phases.text: The institutional synthesis places Lapita emergence in the Bismarcks. This marker does not identify one starting village, a first-ever inhabitant or an exact founding year.

phases.label: Broad 1100–800 BCE expansion window
phases.title: Different settings in Remote Oceania
phases.text: The regional account describes movement toward Fiji and West Polynesia through several generations. Settlement, food procurement and introduced resources varied; not every island began the same economy at once.

citations.locator: Lapita in Remote Oceania: migration window, coastal settlement and food

phases.label: Around 900–750 BCE: rounded orientation to Tongan site models
phases.title: Tongan island groups have their own dated sequences
phases.text: The 2015 analysis places early Tongatapu occupation before expansion to other principal groups, with overlapping first-settlement estimates for Ha’apai and Vava’u. Site samples and probability levels require their own explanation; no crew’s itinerary is reconstructed.

phases.label: Around 750–400 BCE: selected later Tongan context
phases.title: Plainware continues after decorated pottery
phases.text: Undecorated ceramics continued in the Tongan sequence. The 2018 authors argue that manufacture had ceased by about 400 BCE. That latest bound is contextual follow-through beyond this case, not a universal Pacific endpoint or established cause of change.

citations.locator: Abstract; Discussion: maximum 2700–2350 cal BP phase interval

contexts.title: Poverty Point: building, provisioning and maintaining a place

interval.label: Main-site orientation, c.1700–1100 BCE
interval.note: Selected NPS/Louisiana main-complex frame, not the lifespan of a people or the full regional archaeological tradition. Broad phase anchors do not precisely date every earthwork. The booklet rounds Mound A to 1350 BCE on p. 4 and 1300 BCE on p. 10; recent scholarship debates the pace of the whole complex. Earlier Jaketown and later Mound D have their own histories outside this frame.

contexts.summary: A large earthwork landscape depended on earthmoving, food, materials and continuing care. Different mounds, sampled deposits and later surface alterations require distinct histories.

citations.locator: Printed pp. 4, 10–13 and 17: sequence, different mounds and upkeep
The chronology of the Poverty Point site

phases.label: Around 1700 BCE: selected early earthwork orientation
phases.title: Mound B and earlier activity
phases.text: The state account places the beginning of Mound B around this time. Building involved prepared ground and successive layers. This is a selected mound history, not one founding day for the entire community.

phases.label: Across the main occupation, c.1700–1100 BCE
phases.title: Ridges, plaza and continuing work
phases.text: People occupied and changed a landscape of mounds, ridges and open space. The plaza required filling low areas and controlling gullies. This broad orientation does not settle the debated timing of all ridge construction or assign every feature to one moment.

citations.locator: Printed pp. 4 and 17: sequence and plaza upkeep
The chronology of the Poverty Point site

phases.label: Later second millennium BCE: approximate Mound A orientation
phases.title: Peak, platform and ramp have a sequence
phases.text: The booklet uses approximate 1350 and 1300 BCE orientations in different passages and distinguishes the peak, platform and connecting ramp. A rapid episode proposed for one part is not a single measured duration for every earthwork.

citations.locator: Printed p. 4 and pp. 10–11: Mound A and its parts
Overview; The chronology of the Poverty Point site

phases.label: Around 1200 BCE in the state sequence
phases.title: Mound F belongs to the later main-complex story
phases.text: The booklet places Mound F late in its Late Archaic sequence. This is different from Mound D, built around 700 CE long after the main frame; similar-looking surface features need not share a date.

citations.locator: Printed pp. 4 and 13: Mounds F and D

phases.label: End of the selected main-site frame, c.1100 BCE
phases.title: A teaching boundary does not end Indigenous history
phases.text: The retained frame bounds this inquiry. Later building, land use and archaeological research remain part of the place’s history, rather than extending every old object to one continuous period.

citations.locator: Printed p. 13: later Mound D and nineteenth-century land use

contexts.title: Kerma: a Nubian capital, production and changing relationships

interval.label: c.2500–1500 BCE: selected Kerma urban history
interval.note: A selected regional reference, separate from the complete unchanged c.2050–1500 BCE case and the beaker’s c.1802–1640 BCE date. Archaeological phase conventions differ between the project and museum sources. The broad endpoint orients later political transition rather than dating one exact destruction event. No continuous Kerma-to-Taharqo polity is implied.

contexts.summary: Households, craft installations and political/religious buildings make work and institutions visible across a changing Nubian capital.

citations.locator: Présentation; La ville antique de Kerma

phases.label: Around 2500 BCE: broad urban foundation frame
phases.title: A city and its institutions develop
phases.text: The city account places foundation around 2500 BCE. The earlier Pre-Kerma agglomeration has its own evidence; direct settlement continuity remains unproved.

phases.label: Around 2050–1750 BCE: project Middle Kerma convention
phases.title: Walls and institutional space
phases.text: The project table associates this phase with fortifications, palaces and princely tombs. These are broad archaeological assignments, not an exact schedule for each building.

phases.label: Around 1750 BCE onward: differing Classical frames
phases.title: Expansion and monumental institutions
phases.text: The project associates Classic Kerma with expanded defences, temples and royal tombs and ends it around 1480 BCE. The Met’s Classical range instead ends around 1550 BCE. The selected beaker retains its own 1802–1640 BCE catalogue range.

phases.label: Around 1500 BCE: reference endpoint and later transition
phases.title: Political control changes across a wider interval
phases.text: This is the selected teaching boundary, not a single exact conquest date. The project distinguishes a final transition around 1480–1450 BCE; the Met places Egyptian campaigns within its broader 1550–1070 BCE entry, with southern control by about 1450 BCE.

contexts.title: A palace through changing Assyrian government

interval.label: Selected ninth–seventh-century contexts, 883–612 BCE
interval.note: A reference frame around the Northwest Palace and later administration, not the complete life of Kalhu or an imperial border. Selected phase anchors have gaps; they do not establish a continuous universal sequence. The case remains 883–859 BCE.

contexts.summary: Making a palace, staging royal authority, administering people and sustaining practical work left different evidence. Later letters and alterations belong to their own dates.

citations.locator: Managing the palace; Behind the scenes; After Assurnasirpal

phases.label: 883–859 BCE: the selected reign
phases.title: Ashurnasirpal’s palace setting
phases.text: Building and royal display establish the selected ninth-century case. The recurring inscription represents the king’s rebuilding, conquest and settlement claims.

phases.label: Around 732 BCE: an editorial proposed date
phases.title: A later reign in the palace archive
phases.text: The catalogue assigns SAA 19 006 to Tiglath-pileser III’s reign; its more precise date, about 732 BCE, is proposed rather than written on the tablet.

citations.locator: Date metadata and Room ZT4 archive provenance

phases.label: The 670s BCE: a later alteration
phases.title: Selected alterations in the 670s
phases.text: Robson’s account describes removal of sculptures from the West Suite under Esarhaddon in the 670s. This later work helps explain why an excavated plan is not a single original interior.

citations.locator: After Assurnasirpal: Esarhaddon and dismantling in the 670s BC

phases.label: 612 BCE in the project account
phases.title: Sack and institutional rupture
phases.text: The project account places the sack of Kalhu in 612 BCE after continued use of palace offices and stores. This endpoint concerns the selected palace context; it does not claim all later settlement disappeared.

contexts.title: Kushite and Egyptian power: temples, skilled work and royal claims

interval.label: c. 747–656 BCE: selected Dynasty 25 orientation
interval.note: Uses the 2026 Sanam article’s approximate Dynasty 25 frame, not the whole history of Kush or a continuous unchanged state. The retained case remains Taharqo’s c. 690–664 BCE reign. Kawa’s c. 680 BCE temple/shrine, individual shabti dates and the broadly dated Sanam workshop answer different questions. The workshop is not assigned an exact year or wholly to this reign; its ceramic discussion includes broader seventh–sixth-century parallels beyond this frame.

contexts.summary: Kushite rulers linked power in Egypt and Nubia with temple building, ritual service and the organisation of people and materials. Royal inscriptions, surviving objects and excavated production remains reveal different parts of those institutions.

citations.locator: Introduction: Dynasty 25 frame, Taharqo and temple institutions; workshop dating discussion, PDF p. 10
Description and Artwork Details: reign, material and probable Nuri attribution
Information sheet pp. 1–3: c. 680 BCE temple/shrine and service

phases.label: c. 747 BCE: approximate beginning of the selected dynastic frame
phases.title: Kushite kingship extended into Egypt
phases.text: The Sanam article places Piankhy’s conquest of Egypt within the beginning of Dynasty 25, which it dates approximately 747–656 BCE. This convention frames changing political relationships across the Nile valley; it is not an exact date for every conquest, settlement or temple. The later Taharqo figure belongs to one reign within that wider history.

citations.locator: Introduction: Piankhy, Dynasty 25 and the c. 747–656 BCE frame

phases.label: c. 690–664 BCE: Taharqo’s retained reign interval
phases.title: A king commissioned and presented institutions
phases.text: The Met dates the selected granite figure to Taharqo’s reign. At Kawa, inscriptions described a king providing people and resources for a temple; Hallmann discusses his claim to have sent crews, skilled craftspeople and an overseer while he remained in Memphis. A royal assertion of provision is different from a builder’s account of the work.

citations.locator: Printed p. 132 / PDF p. 163: mediated discussion of Kawa IV lines 21–22

phases.label: Around 680 BCE: the museum’s Kawa building orientation
phases.title: Temple service joined materials, images and repeated tasks
phases.text: The Ashmolean places the Kawa temple and shrine around 680 BCE. Its teaching account links skilled building to the shrine’s offering imagery and priests’ care for the divine statue. The published date is a broad building orientation; it does not date each carving, each worker’s service or the manufacture of the Met’s shabti.

citations.locator: Information sheet pp. 1–3: building, shrine imagery and divine-statue service

phases.label: c. 656 BCE: end of the selected Egyptian dynastic convention
phases.title: One dynastic boundary does not date every institution
phases.text: The Sanam article ends its Dynasty 25 convention around 656 BCE, after the selected Taharqo reign. Its faience-workshop evidence has its own broad ceramic chronology and is not reduced to a single king’s lifetime. Compare that excavated production context with a reign-attributed granite figure and a probable Nuri origin, keeping the different materials, dates and levels of certainty visible.

citations.locator: Introduction: dynastic frame; The Sanam Temple faience workshop, PDF pp. 10 and 13
Description and Artwork Details: date, material and probable Nuri

contexts.title: Chavín: a highland centre and portable images

interval.label: Selected source frames, c.1500–200 BCE
interval.note: An orientation spanning differing centre/tradition conventions and the selected later textile, not one state’s lifespan. UNESCO’s Description gives 1500–300 BCE, its Brief Synthesis 15th–5th centuries BCE; the older Met chronology labels highland Chavín 1000–500 BCE. Neither replaces the complete unchanged 400–200 BCE object case. Phase dates below are attributed approximate points, not a newly modeled building sequence.

contexts.summary: Stone buildings, galleries and carved images made Chavín de Huántar a highland ceremonial centre. Portable objects support comparisons across media and places, while each object keeps its own date and provenance.

phases.label: Around 950 BCE in the Met’s 2004 chronology
phases.title: A carved image within the centre
phases.text: The museum places the Lanzón’s erection within the temple around this time. This is its approximate reference date, not a date for the textile.

phases.label: Around 850 BCE in the Met’s 2004 chronology
phases.title: Pilgrimage and specialist making
phases.text: Its account describes pilgrims and resident artisans producing several media. It does not identify the makers of this surviving fragment.

phases.label: Around 500 BCE in the Met’s 2004 chronology
phases.title: A changing monumental setting
phases.text: The museum describes declining Chavín power and changes at northern centres. Its convention is not proof that all related images or communities ended together.

phases.label: Fourth–third centuries BCE: the selected catalogue range
phases.title: This fragment has its own date
phases.text: The current catalogue assigns this cloth a later range. It does not locate its production at the highland centre or document a journey from there.

contexts.title: Teotihuacan: building a city and organizing neighborhood work

interval.label: c.100 BCE–650 CE: selected urban and neighborhood reference
interval.note: Selected teaching frame, not a lifespan or uniform polity. The case remains c.100 BCE–800 CE. The 650 edge lies within Barnes’s reduced-population period (600–800), not a collapse/abandonment date. Monuments, neighborhoods, samples and mask keep separate dates.

contexts.summary: Monuments and apartments developed at different times. Household production, shared spaces and changing construction explain urban organization without supplying a recovered list of rulers.

citations.locator: The Tlajinga District and Its Neighborhood Center; Complexes 2 and 4

phases.label: Around 100 BCE: broad city chronology begins
phases.title: A broad frame is not the date of every building
phases.text: Barnes uses approximately 100 BCE–800 CE for Teotihuacan. This selected reference begins with that broad convention; it does not assign the later apartments or surviving mask to the first year.

phases.label: Around 100–250 CE: major monumental building
phases.title: Monuments and streets organize public space
phases.text: Barnes places major monumental construction in this interval. The orderly layout allows questions about coordination, but a single original master plan remains one interpretation rather than a demonstrated construction schedule.

citations.locator: Introduction; City Layout and Monumental Architecture: master-plan alternatives

phases.label: Around 250–550 CE: apartments and local urban expansion
phases.title: Household space becomes central to the urban account
phases.text: Barnes’s broad apartment-building range differs in scale from the Tlajinga report’s local transition to dense apartment occupation around the mid-third century. Compounds 17 and 18 preserve evidence of craft, domestic space and links to the street. These are selected excavated settings, not a complete household census.

citations.locator: The Tlajinga District and Its Neighborhood Center: local settlement transition
Compounds 17 and 18; grid alignment, courtyards and drains

phases.label: Around 550 CE: burning of core monuments
phases.title: A changed center does not identify its destroyers
phases.text: Barnes reports burning by unidentified people around this time. The event does not by itself establish its cause, the people responsible, or an immediate end to life in every neighborhood.

phases.label: After 600 CE: reduced population within a longer history
phases.title: Occupation continues beyond the main monumental phase
phases.text: Barnes describes markedly reduced population during 600–800 CE. The selected reference stops at 650 within that broader interval; the complete case continues to 800. Neither endpoint means that a people disappeared.

contexts.title: Moche regional societies: valleys, skilled work and changing coordination

interval.label: c. 100–850 CE: selected object and regional histories
interval.note: A selected teaching frame, not the beginning/end of one Moche kingdom. The start orients the selected bottle’s broad second–fifth-century attribution; it is not an exact year of manufacture or cultural origin. The complete case remains 1–800 CE. Huacas de Moche Phase IV, La Capilla’s 650–740 frame and San José de Moro’s broader 650–850 frame retain separate scopes. Castillo and colleagues use 700–800 for their selected Late Moche discussion. The endpoint does not terminate every regional community.

contexts.summary: River valleys supported different Moche communities. Archaeological traces of making, domestic work and local coordination explain institutions that cannot be recovered from decorated vessels alone.

citations.locator: Printed pp. 183–190: local sequence and work
Abstract; Death in the Moche world and San José de Moro

phases.label: Second–fifth centuries CE: the selected snake bottle’s broad date
phases.title: A vessel has its own horizon
phases.text: The museum attributes the snake bottle to the second–fifth centuries. This broad object range supplies the beginning of our selected orientation, not a founding event. Its regional attribution is Moche, but the catalogue does not identify an excavated valley or workshop. The seated figure retains a separate 200–500 CE range.

phases.label: c. 400/450–700/800 CE: Chapdelaine’s local Phase IV frame
phases.title: Compounds join production and domestic work
phases.text: Chapdelaine describes the later Huacas de Moche occupations through a broad local Phase IV frame. Compounds, workshops and grinding/storage evidence reveal practical urban activities. His continued occupation sequence challenges a rapid abandonment around 600 CE. This local ceramic chronology does not supply a universal sequence for every northern valley.

phases.label: 650–740 CE at La Capilla; 650–850 at the wider ceremonial center
phases.title: A northern place has a different sequence
phases.text: In the Jequetepeque region, Muro Ynoñán examines La Capilla’s changing monumental spaces within San José de Moro. His building frame is narrower than the site’s broader elite cemetery and ceremonial history. These independently dated northern contexts cannot be assigned to the selected museum bottles merely because all are called Moche.

citations.locator: Abstract; Death in the Moche world and San José de Moro

phases.label: Around 800–850 CE: compare the sources’ selected endpoints
phases.title: Regional change does not end on one date
phases.text: Castillo and colleagues discuss a selected San José de Moro Late Moche frame of 700–800 CE; Muro uses a broader 650–850 ceremonial frame. Read those conventions beside the retained case’s 800 CE endpoint. They organize different evidence and questions, rather than demonstrating one simultaneous collapse across the north coast.

citations.locator: Death in the Moche world and San José de Moro

contexts.title: Đông Sơn traditions: selected find, use and production contexts

interval.label: c.700 BCE–600 CE: selected traditions and later production evidence
interval.note: Source-qualified teaching frame, not one continuous polity or universal drum chronology. The 2014 museum archaeological-culture scheme ends in the first/second centuries CE; later Luy Lâu production has a separate third–sixth-century interpretation. The complete miniature case stays c.500 BCE–300 CE, including its original note and precision. Later manufacture does not extend or redetermine that case.

contexts.summary: A shared bronze form enters different local settings. Find associations, later uses and production remains help distinguish those histories without drawing one state or a demonstrated movement route.

phases.label: Seventh–sixth centuries BCE: museum early-stage convention
phases.title: A broad archaeological frame precedes the miniature’s range
phases.text: The 2014 museum account identifies an early stage in varied upland, midland and delta settings. This attributed convention supplies orientation; it neither establishes a precise founding year nor dates the selected miniature to this stage.

phases.label: Fifth–third centuries BCE: museum middle-stage convention
phases.title: Regional settings and particular objects need separate dates
phases.text: The museum describes an extension into river and delta settings during its middle stage. Its broad scheme does not override the separate c.third–second-century-BCE date assigned to Ngọc Lũ in the 2013 object record, or the selected miniature’s wider catalogue interval.

phases.label: Second/first centuries BCE–first/second CE: museum late convention
phases.title: Different deposits supply local histories
phases.text: The source’s late-stage wording overlaps centuries rather than fixing one transition year. Phú Chánh’s official drum date and its wood results are different kinds of evidence; the excavation report calls the site about 2,000 years old. These conventions do not establish an exact shared year of use.

phases.label: Third–sixth centuries CE: later Luy Lâu production evidence
phases.title: Manufacture has a later reference of its own
phases.text: The 2024 preliminary field account associates mould and casting discard with Six Dynasties material. This later production interpretation extends beyond the case endpoint 300. The 2016 report separately distinguished typological dating from an approximately fourth-century associated layer. Neither identifies the Met miniature’s workshop.

citations.locator: Artwork Details: Date and regional attribution

contexts.title: Western Mexico: architecture, offerings and regional communities

interval.label: c. 300 BCE–400 CE: selected western Mexican funerary context
interval.note: Uses López Mestas’s 2026 Late Preclassic/Early Classic orientation, not the lifespan or borders of one Colima state. The selected model’s complete case remains 200 BCE–200 CE; its 2015 essay caption ends at 300 CE. Regional shaft-tomb conventions, an excavated first-century-CE Huitzilapa context and the undated creation of modern photographs answer different questions. The endpoint does not end every western Mexican funerary practice.

contexts.summary: People made architectural miniatures and prepared funerary places within varied western Mexican communities. A possible vessel lid, regional offering traditions and a documented excavation reveal different parts of that work.

phases.label: Around 300 BCE: beginning of the selected regional frame
phases.title: Shared mortuary forms did not require one state
phases.text: López Mestas describes western Mexican communities through a 300 BCE–400 CE orientation. Her account connects elaborate mortuary practices with different styles and autonomous villages or small chiefdoms. This is a regional interpretation of social relationships, not a founding date, common constitution or political border for everyone called Colima.

citations.locator: Opening regional frame; stylistic variation and political organization paragraphs

phases.label: 200 BCE–200 CE: the selected model’s catalogue range
phases.title: An object carries its own dating question
phases.text: The current Met record attributes this ceramic model to Colima and gives a broad 200 BCE–200 CE range. The date does not identify its maker, excavated tomb or precise year of manufacture. Roof, stair and platform can be observed in the supplied photograph while the proposed incense-burner-lid function remains an interpretation.

phases.label: First century CE: the separately excavated Huitzilapa tomb
phases.title: An excavation supplies an association
phases.text: The 1996 excavators report radiocarbon clustering in the first century CE at Huitzilapa, in central Jalisco. The 2006 organic-study abstract reports an averaged/calibrated date around 74 CE through that earlier study and describes six interments in two chambers. These are site-specific findings; the original laboratory tables were not consulted, and no object route or Huitzilapa origin is assigned to the Colima model.

citations.locator: Publisher abstract: reported approximate date and interments

phases.label: 200 CE and 300 CE: two published endpoints for the same model
phases.title: Keep a discrepancy visible
phases.text: The current catalogue ends the selected model’s range at 200 CE. The opening caption in Pillsbury’s 6 November 2015 essay ends it at 300 CE. This atlas retains the current catalogue interval and records the older alternative. Neither endpoint dates the end of a people or all shaft-tomb offerings.

phases.label: Around 400 CE: end of this selected regional orientation
phases.title: A teaching frame is not a universal ending
phases.text: The selected reference follows the 2026 essay’s regional endpoint. The INAH Colima account has its own wider shaft-tomb orientation and a local Comala convention of 200–400 CE. These differing scopes should remain identified, rather than being merged into a single rise-and-fall story or used to redate the museum object.

contexts.title: Ohio gathering and earthwork construction

interval.label: Selected wider orientation, c.100 BCE–500 CE
interval.note: Broader orientation follows the approximate 100 BCE–500 CE span of the Hopewell religious movement in Logan York’s 2023 article; Newark Earthworks Center’s archaeological-culture FAQ uses approximately 100 BCE–400 CE. Those are attributed conventions with different scopes, not a state’s lifespan or dates for every structure. The entire selected dossier interval remains byte-for-byte 1–400 CE.

contexts.summary: Households provisioned themselves while communities built, used and changed shared earthwork places. Different source frames and one sampled wall date help locate those activities without making every enclosure contemporary.

citations.locator: Logan York, p. 5A: broader 100 BCE–500 CE movement convention
FAQ: approximately 100 BCE–400 CE archaeological-culture convention

phases.label: Around 100 BCE: start of a broader source frame
phases.title: A wider orientation keeps its source
phases.text: York’s 2023 article describes a Hopewell religious movement approximately 100 BCE–500 CE. The Newark Earthworks Center FAQ uses approximately 100 BCE–400 CE for its archaeological-culture convention. These are attributed frames with different scopes, not a founding date or one people’s complete lifespan.

citations.locator: FAQ: What is the Hopewell Culture?

phases.label: 1–400 CE: selected Mound City frame
phases.title: Buildings, gatherings and later mound additions
phases.text: NPS places Mound City construction within this broad interval. Its account describes a ceremonial building and clay floor, deliberate dismantling and earthen additions. The relative order does not supply numeric dates for individual operations; possible repeated gatherings remain qualified.

phases.label: Around 300 CE: one reported Hopeton wall estimate
phases.title: A sampled wall has a narrower dating question
phases.text: The NPS account of 2001–02 investigations associates burned logs in one trench with initial construction of one Hopeton enclosure wall around 300 CE. The reported estimate does not date all walls or every Ohio earthwork. Original laboratory and calibration details were not supplied on the consulted page.

citations.locator: Ongoing Research: wall trenches and burned-log estimate

phases.label: 400 CE: end of the selected NPS case frame
phases.title: A teaching bound does not end Indigenous presence
phases.text: The selected NPS inquiry ends at 400 CE, while the wider context records York’s convention through approximately 500 CE. Neither endpoint establishes that every structure stopped being used together or that Indigenous people disappeared. Modern survey, restoration and contemporary statements are separately dated evidence outside these ancient phases.

contexts.title: Constantinople: portable images and harbour work

interval.label: 843–1204 CE: a selected Middle Byzantine reference frame
interval.note: Follows Brooks’s Middle Byzantine convention, with the substantive urban inquiry bounded to ninth–eleventh-century evidence. This is not a new lifespan or territorial boundary for Byzantium: the complete original case remains 330–1453, including Latin rule in Constantinople during 1204–1261. Earlier timber evidence may predate this reference frame; a phase marker is not a precise construction, sinking or production year.

contexts.summary: An ivory panel and separately excavated ship timbers reveal carving, fitting, joining and repair in a working capital. Object interpretation, archaeological context and political change answer different questions.

citations.locator: Ivory images in the tenth–eleventh centuries

phases.label: 843: images return after the second iconoclastic episode
phases.title: A period convention follows a contested practice
phases.text: Brooks distinguishes image controversies in 726–787 and 815–843 and describes the reintroduction of images in 843. Icons appeared in different materials and settings, while their relationship to sacred subjects was debated. This boundary organizes a reference period; it does not mean every image, viewer or workshop followed one uninterrupted practice.

citations.locator: Definition of Iconoclasm; Icons after Iconoclasm

phases.label: Late ninth–early tenth centuries: YK14’s pottery-layer context
phases.title: One wreck has several chronological questions
phases.text: The excavators initially associated YK14 with pottery dated to the late ninth or early tenth century. Wood dating and a timber likely associated with the ship suggested construction in the first half of the ninth century, potentially before this reference begins. Fitted planks and repeated repairs belong to its material history. The marker 900 is an approximate orientation to the reported context, not an exact construction, repair or sinking year. No cargo or ballast was recovered.

citations.locator: Printed pp. 53–55; Table 2, p. 47: YK14 chronology and repairs

phases.label: Mid-tenth century: the selected ivory panel
phases.title: Carving makes a portable devotional image
phases.text: The Met dates accession 17.190.44 to the mid-tenth century and attributes it probably to Constantinople. Its central panel has carved figures and an openwork architectural frame; missing wings once made a triptych. Probable private devotional use is the catalogue’s interpretation. The atlas retains the existing 925–975 search envelope, without treating 950 as a known manufacture year or identifying an original household, carver or workshop.

citations.locator: Description; Artwork Details: Date and Geography

phases.label: Tenth–eleventh centuries: ivory images and other objects
phases.title: One medium served more than one purpose
phases.text: Ryder discusses ivory religious images alongside secular caskets and varied forms of assembly. The broader medium connects material supply with skilled making and use. It does not identify this panel’s source tusk, assembly materials, patron or labour arrangement. The marker 1000 locates the author’s broad production discussion; it is not a dated output total or a new date for the selected icon.

citations.locator: Tenth–eleventh-century production, religious images and secular caskets

phases.label: 1204: Latin rule interrupts the Constantinople capital story
phases.title: Political change does not supply one cultural endpoint
phases.text: Crusaders took Constantinople in 1204. Brooks distinguishes Latin rule there until 1261 from Byzantine centres elsewhere, followed by the return of Byzantine rule to Constantinople. This ends the selected Middle Byzantine reference convention, not all making, religious practice or Roman self-identification. The full case continues to the 1453 capture of Constantinople and retains its qualification about other territories.

contexts.title: Central Java: religious buildings, stories and support

interval.label: Eighth–tenth centuries: selected construction and relief-study frames
interval.note: Teaching frame combines UNESCO’s eighth–ninth-century monumental construction with Santiko’s attributed ninth–tenth-century cultural frame for Karmawibhangga interpretation. These overlap rather than form universal successive stages. They do not extend the complete 700–900 case, date every relief or establish a continuous polity, universal itinerary or an exact end of use. Modern conservation/community sources are explicitly later reading, not ancient phases.

contexts.summary: Stone galleries, religious narratives and support for upkeep are different parts of a religious landscape. Source-specific dates and interpretations help explain their relationship while leaving individual patrons, households and visitors incompletely known.

citations.locator: Brief synthesis: construction and associated monuments

phases.label: Eighth–ninth centuries: broad construction frame
phases.title: A hill, carved galleries and upper platforms
phases.text: UNESCO places monumental construction broadly in these centuries under the Syailendra dynasty. Square terraces and circular upper platforms organize a building around a natural hill. The source’s broad frame supplies orientation rather than exact beginning and completion years for each part.

citations.locator: Brief synthesis: location, construction and form

phases.label: Ninth–tenth centuries: one study’s cultural frame
phases.title: Religious narratives represented in local settings
phases.text: Santiko’s abstract interprets Karmawibhangga through religious-text comparison and Javanese cultural adaptation, using a ninth–tenth-century frame. This is a study-specific interpretive setting, not a new construction date or an independently verified date for every depicted building.

phases.label: 842: an attributed land-and-upkeep interpretation
phases.title: Religious support enters an inscription account
phases.text: BorobudurPedia connects Tri Tepusan, Sri Kahulunan and land privileges for a religious foundation with Borobudur. This modern institutional interpretation is kept distinct from a complete primary translation, a securely named founder or proof of collected revenue. It does not derive from the different Kayumwungan edition’s two consulted English stanzas.

contexts.title: Classic Maya courts, makers and households

interval.label: Selected Classic-period orientation, c. 250–900 CE
interval.note: Follows Doyle’s broad Classic-period ceramic/courtly frame across varied communities, not one state or the lifespan of Maya peoples. The selected cup keeps its entire 600–800 CE case. Cerén and Ik’ are separately sourced comparisons; neither supplies this cup’s findspot, workshop or recovered route.

contexts.summary: Potters, artists, patrons and households connected made objects with food, representation and exchange. A named owner’s cup and separately documented household and painter contexts reveal different scales of that work.

citations.locator: Classic Period, c. 250–900 paragraph; production and diplomatic-gift paragraphs

phases.label: Around 250 CE: beginning of the selected source frame
phases.title: A broader ceramic and courtly orientation
phases.text: Doyle describes the Classic period approximately 250–900 CE, with artists developing varied painted vessels and possible royal sponsorship. This is a scholarly orientation, not a founding date or proof that all makers worked for courts.

phases.label: 600–800 CE: the selected catalogue object range
phases.title: A cup with its own date and ownership reading
phases.text: The museum assigns this vessel to the seventh–eighth centuries. Its ownership text and imagery support a specific elite-object inquiry, while maker, exact production year and polity remain unidentified in the consulted record.

citations.locator: Artwork Details; Description ownership and polity paragraphs

phases.label: A separate Cerén context: c. 600 in UNESCO; c. 660 in 2020 abstract
phases.title: Household work preserved by volcanic burial
phases.text: UNESCO’s Description dates burial approximately 600 CE and its synthesis describes seventh-century preservation; the 2020 botanical abstract uses approximately 660 CE. These source conventions remain distinct. Preserved domestic materials support a separate farming and provisioning comparison, not a findspot for the cup.

phases.label: Around 755 CE: a separate Ik’ dish attribution
phases.title: A named patron and an attributed painter
phases.text: The Princeton exhibition caption attributes dish y1993-19 to Mo?-n Buluch Laj and names patron Yajawte’ K’ihnich. The place is Ik’a/Motul de San José or vicinity. This source-qualified comparison does not identify the selected cup’s maker or court.

phases.label: Around 900 CE: end of the selected Classic frame
phases.title: An orientation ends; Maya peoples continue
phases.text: The reference ends with Doyle’s selected Classic-period frame. It does not make regional political changes simultaneous, terminate all ceramic practices or end the history of Maya peoples. Modern publications, acquisition and photography belong outside these ancient phases.

citations.locator: Classic-period frame and concluding political-change convention

contexts.title: Chaco communities: building, provisioning and circulation

interval.label: Selected Pueblo-period orientation, c.700–1300 CE
interval.note: Uses the NPS Pueblo-period archaeological convention as orientation, not the beginning/end of Pueblo peoples or one government. The complete original 850–1250 case and Pueblo Bonito’s narrower 850–1150 construction frame stay unchanged. Food, building and regional interpretations overlap; modern preservation, 1850 recording and the 2025 council statement are later evidence, not ancient phases.

contexts.summary: Great houses, smaller habitation compounds, food practices and constructed alignments supply different scales of evidence. Their relationships can explain work without choosing one complete political model or ending living cultural ties at a display boundary.

citations.locator: Opening period convention; Architecture and Subsistence

phases.label: c.700–1300: an archaeological period convention
phases.title: Smaller habitation and storage spaces enter the frame
phases.text: The NPS Pueblo-period account describes smaller habitation compounds alongside later great houses, with storage rooms, pithouses, outdoor shelters and additions. This broad material convention is not a founding year, universal household sequence or the origin of present-day Pueblo communities.

phases.label: c.850–1150: Pueblo Bonito’s staged construction frame
phases.title: A building changed over generations
phases.text: NPS places Pueblo Bonito’s planned construction in stages across roughly three centuries. Rubble cores, faced masonry and varied spaces involved different materials and tasks. These broad dates do not identify every room’s construction, workers or occupants, or extend one building’s chronology to the full regional system.

phases.label: c.1000–1125: stylistic dating of the earlier cacao-study samples
phases.title: A small material sample answers a particular food question
phases.text: The retained 2009 study consultation records five vessel-fragment samples, three positive probable cylinder jars and stylistic dates around 1000–1125. This supports a limited ingredient-use inference; the marker 1000 is not a known drinking event, an absolute wall date, a universal menu or an exact import route. The earlier 27 October consultation remains dated.

citations.locator: Prior consultation: sample selection, results and stylistic dating

phases.label: 1100s–1200s: changing construction and regional roles
phases.title: Reorganization continues beyond a monumental centre
phases.text: NPS describes slower new construction and changing regional roles in these centuries, with migration and connections to other places. The marker 1150 is an approximate orientation, not a single collapse event. Neither the selected regional case’s 1250 edge nor this reference’s 1300 edge ends Pueblo peoples or their continuing relationships with Chaco.

citations.locator: Changes in the 1100s/1200s and continuing connections

contexts.title: Cahokia: neighborhoods, making and material evidence

interval.label: Selected neighborhood and making evidence, c. 1050–1200 CE
interval.note: A bounded inquiry from the inherited urban reorganization orientation around 1050 through the copper paper’s attributed workshop context around 1200. It is not a new city lifespan, common ethnic identity or end of making. The complete original case remains 1050–1400. Soil evidence covers a broader span; the later population-proxy debate, 1907 print and modern community accounts keep their own dates.

contexts.summary: Homes, public buildings and craft debris help reveal urban relationships. Unfinished copper and a local soil test connect particular materials with particular questions, without making one photo or proxy a complete history of the city and its people.

citations.locator: Retained 27 October scope: urban reorganization around 1050
Printed p. 1728: attributed c.1200 workshop context

phases.label: Around 1050: the inherited urban-investigation orientation
phases.title: Settlement includes more than a monumental core
phases.text: The retained Illinois source scope places organized earthmoving and urban reorganization around 1050. A later ISAS research summary describes homes interspersed with public and religious buildings in the East St. Louis precinct. These are specific places within Greater Cahokia, not a border around every Mississippian community or proof of one household form.

citations.locator: Retained 27 October scope: urban core and reorganization

phases.label: Late eleventh century: neighborhoods being created and reconfigured
phases.title: A building pattern needs an interpretation
phases.text: Betzenhauser and Pauketat compare architectural diversity, density, placement and craft-production debris in neighborhoods at Cahokia and East St. Louis. Their abstract asks how to distinguish homes from other occupational zones and interprets social and religious organization. The marker 1100 orients the reported late-eleventh-century frame; it is not an exact construction year, count of residents or recovered household roster.

phases.label: Around 1200: an attributed Mound 34 workshop context
phases.title: Small unfinished pieces reveal a working process
phases.text: The 2011 copper paper attributes a workshop-house context to the early Moorehead phase around 1200 through previous field reports. Its eight studied pieces came from old excavation backdirt. Metallographic observations and modern comparisons support an interpretation of repeated hammering and annealing; they do not date each piece precisely or identify a named worker. This ends the selected evidence frame, not city life or Indigenous history.

contexts.title: Ocmulgee: public buildings and a changing settlement history

interval.label: Selected post-1000 public-building and Middle Plateau inquiry, to 1715
interval.note: A source-qualified research frame for selected buildings and settlement evidence, not an Earthlodge construction/use interval. The study situates its inquiry after about 1000; 1715 is a documented trading-house boundary used for the Middle Plateau model, not the end of every Ocmulgee community or Muscogee history. The original disputed null/null case and both original alternatives remain intact. Modern excavation, reconstruction and community publications belong outside these phases.

contexts.summary: Built gathering places, household work and retained archaeological collections support different inquiries. Dating particular samples changes explanations of construction and occupation, while living Muscogee relationships are not reduced to the presence or absence of one archaeological layer.

phases.label: Around 1100: an approximate interpretation for Council Chamber 2
phases.title: Another public building enters the comparison
phases.text: The authors discuss Council Chamber 2 as approximately contemporary with the Earthlodge, while its model remains imprecise. This is a separate building and an attributed model interpretation; it is not a new start date for the Earthlodge or proof that every public building was used together.

citations.locator: Results: Council Chamber 2; Discussion: The Earthlodge and Public Buildings

phases.label: After about 1160: a timber constraint, not a completion date
phases.title: A retained roof timber revises the familiar chronology
phases.text: The selected roof-wood model places cutting sometime after about 1160. Preserved rings and their analysis constrain this material; they do not identify the day people finished the room. The authors retain a possible earlier structure from other observations and cane evidence.

citations.locator: Results: Earthlodge; Discussion: The Earthlodge and Public Buildings

phases.label: 1324–1415 at 68%: a modeled maize-sample range
phases.title: A short-lived sample tests a claimed occupation gap
phases.text: Middle Plateau maize sample UGA 61307 has a reported modeled range of 1324–1415 at 68% and 1315–1425 at 95%. The authors could not resolve its double peak. This sample challenges a simple abandonment story in that area; it does not recover a settlement census or date use of the Earthlodge.

phases.label: 1715: a documented boundary for one modeled area
phases.title: A trading-house history helps constrain earlier features
phases.text: The study uses the recorded destruction of the Macon Trading House in 1715 as a boundary for the Middle Plateau analysis. It describes relocation to other sites in the valley. This is not a disappearance date for people, a universal end of use or a newly reconstructed route.

citations.locator: Understanding the Broader Occupational History; Results: Middle Plateau

contexts.title: Ming ceramics: court orders, private kilns and changing demand

interval.label: Selected production changes within the Ming period, 1368–1644
interval.note: Uses conventional dynastic boundaries to orient selected institutional changes, not the beginning/end of Jingdezhen pottery, private enterprise or makers’ lives. Reign ranges, an order for related jars and this object’s mid-sixteenth-century attribution remain distinct. A 1608 imperial-kiln stoppage is a reported institutional event, not the end of all production. Later Qing restart alternatives are outside this frame.

contexts.summary: Court models, inspection, private contracts and several markets connected different kinds of work. Their relationships changed; an object’s fine decoration does not establish its precise commission, maker or buyer.

citations.locator: Conventional Ming dates and final decorative-arts paragraphs
Early and late Ming production paragraphs

phases.label: Early Ming: official production within a wider ceramic economy
phases.title: Court supply depended on particular production arrangements
phases.text: The marker begins the conventional Ming period, not a precisely dated workshop foundation. The National Palace Museum identifies both Longquan and Jingdezhen in early official supply, then describes court models, supervision and selected products. These are institutional relationships, not a statement that every ceramic was made for the ruler.

phases.label: Jiajing period, 1522–1566: connected official and private work
phases.title: An order could cross the boundary between kiln organizations
phases.text: The CUHK account places allocation of court orders to capable private kilns in the Jiajing period when imperial capacity was insufficient. This broad reign marker does not date a specific contract or identify who made the selected jar. Its catalogue retains a mid-sixteenth-century attribution and a separate inherited search envelope.

citations.locator: Thriving Country of China: court orders

phases.label: 1542: a written reference to jars with related pond scenes
phases.title: A dated order is evidence for related production, not this jar’s batch
phases.text: The Met cites contemporary records for jars with similar pond decoration in 1542. That catalogue-mediated reference belongs beside the material object, but does not make accession 17.127.2 a securely identified member of that order. No original Chinese order or complete factory ledger was consulted here.

phases.label: 1608: a reported stoppage of imperial operations
phases.title: A particular institution’s change did not end skilled production
phases.text: The Palace Museum exhibition reports that imperial-kiln operations ceased in 1608 and describes flourishing private production afterward. This is an attributed institutional account, not a shutdown of every kiln or an end of Chinese ceramic culture. The conventional 1644 boundary ends this selected Ming frame; makers and production have later histories.

contexts.title: Ottoman makers: signatures, workshop remains and markets

interval.label: Selected maker and market evidence, 1549–seventeenth century
interval.note: Begins with the separately inscribed 1549 lamp and groups selected sixteenth-century objects, seventeenth-century tile comparisons and a traveler’s 1670s market account. The 1700 edge is a century-level orientation, not a kiln closure, end of making or polity boundary. The complete original 1500–1755 case, both selected object ranges and the later 1748–55 building example remain separate. Modern photographs, archaeological publication and laboratory replication have their own dates.

contexts.summary: A named decorator, an official emblem, a painted dish and production remains reveal different parts of skilled work. Markets and commissions could overlap without assigning every maker to a palace or every object to one known workshop.

citations.locator: Date, production place and Curator’s comments
B.1: mediated Covel account of the 1670s

phases.label: 1549: a name on a separate lamp
phases.title: An inscription makes one decorator visible
phases.text: The British Museum records AH 956/1549, Iznik and Musli in its account of the lamp’s inscription. The supplied translation identifies a painter. This dated comparison gives one maker a name without assigning the selected, unsigned Met dish to him or recovering everyone involved in preparing and firing the lamp.

phases.label: c.1555–60: the selected tughra’s catalogue range
phases.title: Drawing and illumination make an official emblem
phases.text: The Met distinguishes a specialist drawing the standard form from an illuminator decorating certain imperial documents. The marker begins the selected emblem’s approximate catalogue range, not every document’s issue date or the moment the tughra form was invented.

citations.locator: Visible date; description of specialist roles

phases.label: c.1575–90: the selected dish’s catalogue range
phases.title: Material and design belong to a particular vessel
phases.text: The painted stonepaste dish retains its Iznik attribution and approximate production range. Its round border and plant ornament can be observed, but the museum record does not name its buyer or original occasion of use. Broader design exchange does not recover this vessel’s itinerary.

phases.label: Seventeenth century: production remains and building comparisons
phases.title: Unfinished tiles connect a product to making
phases.text: The excavation authors compare six tile finds with seventeenth-century buildings in Istanbul. Kiln debris, firing equipment and unfinished pieces support production questions. The 1600 marker orients a century-level comparison; it does not date every kiln, identify all workers or link the selected Met dish to one excavated context.

phases.label: 1670s: a traveler’s market account, mediated by a later course
phases.title: A buyer’s setting enters the evidence
phases.text: The Ashmolean teaching course excerpts John Covel describing a weekly market, local ceramic materials and vessels in use. This is a particular observer’s account, not a workshop census. Neither his judgments nor a later economic synthesis supplies every potter’s earnings or a single universal course of decline.

citations.locator: B.1: Covel excerpt and introductory framing

contexts.title: Mughal book projects: making, translation and changing patrons

interval.label: Selected manuscript-project orientation, c.1562–1617 CE
interval.note: A selected project frame from the V&A’s approximate Hamzanama production convention to a separately catalogued 1616–17 Razmnama patronage example. It does not replace the complete 1556–1605 Akbar case, the selected folio’s visible ca.1590–95 date or its inherited 1565–1620 numeric search envelope.
