Translation, illustration, copying, a preface and sacred narrative time are different clocks. Court workshops do not represent every reader or religious community.

contexts.summary: Successive commissions brought translation, writing and painting together. Changing projects and patrons connect the selected folio to a longer bookmaking inquiry without assigning one team, audience or political effect to every surviving page.

phases.label: c.1562–1577: an approximate production convention
phases.title: A large illustrated project brings specialists together
phases.text: The V&A places the Hamzanama project approximately within these years while acknowledging contradictory contemporary volume counts and unstated exact dates. It describes writing, calligraphy and painting as related work. This is another manuscript project, not the selected Harivamsa folio or its recovered team.

phases.label: 1582: the commission reported in the catalogue
phases.title: A Sanskrit epic enters a Persian translation project
phases.text: The British Library catalogue dates Akbar’s commission of the Mahabharata’s Persian translation to 1582 and the first illustrated Jaipur copy to c.1585–86. Commission, translation and a later manuscript copy are not one date; neither dates the epic’s narrated events.

phases.label: 1585: a change in principal residence
phases.title: The court atelier is associated with Lahore
phases.text: The Met’s essay describes Akbar adopting Lahore as his principal residence in 1585 and places the royal atelier first at Fatehpur Sikri, then Lahore. The selected painting’s own catalogue still says probably Lahore. A court move does not convert that qualified attribution into a proven findspot or a precise itinerary.

citations.locator: Fatehpur Sikri/Lahore and royal atelier paragraphs

phases.label: 1587: the preface discussed by Pye
phases.title: Translation is framed through imperial religious authority
phases.text: Pye interprets Abu al-Fazl’s dated Razmnama preface as linking inquiry into religious truth with Akbar’s sovereign authority. This is an interpretation of an elite text, not measurement of universal agreement or a date when one fully formed policy began.

phases.label: c.1590–95: the selected folio’s visible catalogue date
phases.title: A Harivamsa story is made visible in paint
phases.text: The Met dates the selected Krishna/Govardhan folio approximately to 1590–95. The V&A separately places completion of the Harivamsa’s Persian translation around 1590, with illustrations added. These accounts do not identify an exact day, all stages of this leaf or the historical date of a sacred event.

phases.label: 1616–17: a different copy and named patron
phases.title: A courtier supports a later illustrated book
phases.text: A separately catalogued Razmnama folio belongs to a 1616–17 project for Abd al-Rahim, a commander and literary patron. It shows patronage continuing beyond the Akbar case. Its patron, painter and page history are not transferred to the selected Harivamsa.

contexts.title: New Julfa: forced settlement, work and surviving family records

interval.label: Selected New Julfa records, 1604–1747; final letter is later comparison
interval.note: A frame for selected events and differently dated records, not a community’s lifespan or a political boundary. The complete Isfahan capital-phase case remains 1598–1722. The 1747 family letter is explicitly later than that case; a seventeenth-century carpet, an individual firm’s records and modern source publications have separate dates.

contexts.summary: Coerced movement and unequal households belong beside skilled making and commercial coordination. Dated records reveal particular people and relationships, without supplying one experience for all Armenians or identifying the selected carpet’s makers.

citations.locator: Origin, settlement, and population; Society and administration

phases.label: 1604: destruction and forced movement from Old Julfa
phases.title: Commercial importance followed coercion
phases.text: Ghougassian describes the destruction of Old Julfa and forced Armenian relocation during the Ottoman–Safavid war. Later privileges or prosperity do not make the movement voluntary. The account distinguishes the circumstances of merchants from those of other deportees; no settled mass-deportation total is supplied here.

phases.label: 1605: settlement begins at New Julfa
phases.title: A new quarter required buildings and everyday work
phases.text: The Iranica account places the beginning of New Julfa’s settlement in early summer 1605 on the southern bank of the Zayandarud. Houses and churches formed part of a community built after forced movement. This date is distinct from the conventional 1597–98 capital transfer and does not date every surviving building.

citations.locator: Origin, settlement, and population: early summer 1605
Isfahan as the Safavid Capital: gradual development

phases.label: 1655–1659: a later movement of Armenian artisans
phases.title: Settlement did not end state-directed displacement
phases.text: Ghougassian identifies later expulsions of Armenian artisans from Isfahan and movement toward New Julfa in 1655–1659. This is a different episode from the 1604 deportation. It should not be merged into one journey or made the assumed biography of every craft household.

phases.label: 1656: funds pooled in one family firm
phases.title: A particular business joined capital and travelling agents
phases.text: Tajiryan’s selected account dates the Girach-Mirman brothers’ pooling of funds in New Julfa to 1656. It describes partnerships between capital holders and travelling agents, coordinated through commercial information. This particular gem-trading firm is not evidence for every household’s organization or a transaction involving the Doria carpet.

citations.locator: Family-firm paragraph; Commenda Contracts and Agents

phases.label: 1700: a translated letter negotiates turquoise prices
phases.title: Information was part of commercial work
phases.text: The paper presents a 1700 exchange between Herapet di Martin and Amirbēk di Vardan about the price and availability of turquoise. It exposes a practical disagreement, rather than a smooth, automatic flow of goods. The supplied translation does not establish a carpet shipment, complete route or the behavior of all merchants.

phases.label: 1747: a later family letter, outside the atlas case interval
phases.title: A household message adds another perspective on separation
phases.text: The UCLA account supplies passages from Anna Khatoon’s letter to her husband, a textile merchant, including family news and a request for his safe return. Its rendered date is 9 August 1747. This is a later comparison with the 1598–1722 case, not an eyewitness account of 1604 or a voice representing every woman.

contexts.title: Bukhara: making books and sustaining urban institutions

interval.label: Sixteenth–seventeenth-century bookwork and urban institutions
interval.note: Century-level orientation for selected manuscript work, restored teaching spaces, foundations and water infrastructure; not the city’s or a polity’s lifespan. The complete original 1500–1785 case and the selected folio’s ca.1525–35 range remain separate. Building ranges and restoration years do not recover a timetable for every teacher, maker or water worker.

contexts.summary: Books, classrooms, markets and reservoirs required continuing work. A painted folio, architectural descriptions and records of endowed property reveal different tasks and interests within a changing city.

citations.locator: Selected sixteenth/seventeenth-century building and restoration passages

phases.label: 1530s: a probable painting setting
phases.title: A copied text acquires a painted reception
phases.text: The Met places the manuscript’s painting probably in Bukhara in the 1530s, after likely copying in Herat. The decade marker is an orientation within the retained ca.1525–35 catalogue range, not a recovered manufacture year. The much older poem and modern photograph keep their own dates.

citations.locator: Description; visible date and qualified geography

phases.label: 1535–36: Mir-i Arab construction
phases.title: Teaching gains another built setting
phases.text: The architectural account dates Mir-i Arab to 1535–36. It belongs to a city with older teaching institutions, rather than the invention of learning there. This range does not establish an exact opening day, a complete curriculum or every student’s experience.

phases.label: 1585: restoring an older madrasa
phases.title: Continued use can require repair
phases.text: The Ulugh Beg madrasa was built in 1417, outside this reference frame, and restored in 1585. Its described courtyard, cells, classroom and mosque connect education to material spaces. Restoration is a separate event from the building’s first construction.

citations.locator: Ulugh Beg madrasa: plan description and restoration

phases.label: 1619–23: the Lab-i Hauz complex
phases.title: Water storage joins institutions and public space
phases.text: The architectural synthesis groups a khanaqah, madrasa and reservoir within a 1619–23 building range. The marker uses that range’s later edge. It does not reconstruct every canal connection, worker or resident’s right to draw water.

phases.label: 1671: a foundation known through a written record
phases.title: An endowment can outlast its buildings
phases.text: McChesney cites a document for Ay Padshah Bibi’s madrasas and water tank in 1671 among works no longer surviving as buildings. His account connects physical provision to endowed resources, while leaving the original deed and its precise obligations for further consultation.

citations.locator: Monuments and public works: Ay Padshah Bibi

contexts.title: Shiraz and changing rule: a selected Zand political sequence

interval.label: Selected political orientation, 1747–1794 CE
interval.note: Selected milestones from Perry’s account, beginning with Nader Shah’s assassination and ending with the last Zand ruler’s defeat. This reference does not replace the complete 1751–1794 case or date all Iranian life, lacquer production or the selected object’s use. Authority changed and had territorial limits; the frame is not a uniform national border.

contexts.summary: Karim Khan made Shiraz a residence and building center within a contested political landscape. His death preceded the selected lacquer case by ten years. The later succession provides orientation without assigning the case to a ruler, purchaser or workshop city.

citations.locator: Opening chronology; Karim Khan; succession to 1794

phases.label: 1747: a political rupture
phases.title: Nader Shah’s death precedes the Zand convention
phases.text: Perry begins Karim Khan’s rise within the struggles following Nader Shah’s assassination. This earlier reference point explains the selected sequence; it does not move the case’s preserved 1751 starting boundary.

citations.locator: Opening account of 1747 and Karim Khan’s rise

phases.label: 1751: the dynastic convention begins
phases.title: The title wakil represents authority
phases.text: Perry’s dynastic account uses 1751–1794 and describes Karim Khan’s adoption of the title wakil rather than shah. A deputy’s title did not eliminate executive power, campaigns or limits to the territories under his authority.

citations.locator: Karim Khan, the Wakil: title and limits of rule

phases.label: 1765–1779: residence at Shiraz
phases.title: A court, commercial work and building gather in one city
phases.text: Perry dates Karim Khan’s residence at Shiraz to these years and describes the citadel, mosque, gardens and covered bazaar, merchants and artisans. This urban context does not identify the manufacturing place of a case catalogued only as Iranian.

citations.locator: The Wakil at Shiraz, 1765–79: residence and urban work

phases.label: 1779: Karim Khan dies
phases.title: Succession changes the political setting
phases.text: Karim Khan’s death was followed by struggles among Zand successors. The selected case’s catalogue date, 1789, belongs to this later period; no surviving ownership record was established in this consultation.

phases.label: 1789: separate political and object dates
phases.title: Lotf Ali Khan’s accession and a dated case
phases.text: Perry dates Lotf Ali Khan’s rule from 1789; the Met separately dates Muhammad Baqir’s case 1204 AH/1789 CE. Their shared year supplies chronology, not evidence that this ruler commissioned or owned the case.

phases.label: 1794: the selected dynastic endpoint
phases.title: The last Zand ruler is defeated
phases.text: Perry ends the dynastic convention with Lotf Ali Khan’s defeat and execution. This political endpoint does not establish when a case ceased to be used or when a craft tradition ended.

citations.locator: Lotf Ali Khan’s defeat and execution in 1794

contexts.title: Pacific exchange: a wreck, shipbuilding and a later Mexican jar

interval.label: Selected exchange and work records, 1565–1726
interval.note: An orientation for selected evidence, not the full trade’s duration or a universal voyage. The complete original case remains 1565–1815. The 1595 wreck, separate 1618/1619 official accounts, ca. 1680–1700 Mexican jar and a 1726 registered consignment are different records. The reference ends with that selected registration, not the trade’s endpoint.

contexts.summary: Commodity movement depended on ships, materials and people. A particular interrupted voyage and official reports make some work visible; a later Mexican jar belongs to a different episode within the longer exchange history.

citations.locator: Title convention and short route/cargo account

phases.label: 1565: the retained trade convention begins
phases.title: A long commercial frame contains different episodes
phases.text: The Met essay and Point Reyes collection account use the 1565–1815 convention. This opening marker does not identify a particular cargo or make every journey follow an identical track. The selected reference stops earlier than the complete case.

phases.label: 1595: the San Agustín voyage is interrupted
phases.title: A wreck and village finds give a particular context
phases.text: The San Agustín, sailing from the Philippines toward Mexico, wrecked at tamál-húye, present-day Drakes Bay. Written accounts and objects recovered in Coast Miwok village contexts support a bounded inquiry. They do not turn the much later selected jar into wreck cargo or establish one exact route for the whole trade.

phases.label: 1618: a governor reports burdens of royal shipbuilding
phases.title: A colonial report links ships to fields and communities
phases.text: Fajardo’s letter of 10 August 1618 describes workers drawn from cultivation, harsh conditions and contributions from their communities. His contrasting claim about consenting labor concerns smaller private ships for regional navigation. It is an official’s argument about royal service and cost, not a survey of every worker or a proof that instructions changed conditions.

citations.locator: Fajardo letter: royal and private shipbuilding passages

phases.label: 1619: Pineda’s report, as editorially attributed
phases.title: Craft tasks and unpaid labor appear together
phases.text: The edition attributes Pineda’s report to [Mexico? 1619]. It identifies woodcutting, carpentry, mast-making and smithing, while reporting pay arrears and people leaving. The report covers ships, galleys and defense; it does not provide one galleon’s complete crew or prove that its wage schedules were paid.

citations.locator: Pineda: heading; Those who cut these woods; And because, they have; smiths

phases.label: ca. 1680–1700: a separate Mexican jar
phases.title: The selected object belongs to a later material history
phases.text: The Met dates accession 11.87.36 to approximately 1680–1700 and identifies Mexican tin-glazed earthenware. This is later than the 1595 wreck and remains distinct from imported Chinese porcelain. The catalogue does not identify its particular buyer, contents or voyage.

citations.locator: Artwork Details: Date, Geography, Medium and Object Number

phases.label: 1726: a particular registered consignment
phases.title: A named ship’s record gives a more specific connection
phases.text: Caño Ortigosa and Lee study the Santo Cristo’s register dated at Cavite on 26 June 1726 for a voyage to Acapulco. Their discussion follows Julián Ignacio’s entry for lacquered furnishings, ceramics described as Japanese and personal belongings. The registration does not identify this Mexican jar or establish every good’s precise origin, route, sale or successful delivery.

citations.locator: PDF 4 note 5; PDF 14: Julián Ignacio discussion

contexts.title: Banda: trade, coercion and continuing communities

interval.label: Selected trade and displacement evidence, 1599–1630
interval.note: A selected reference around the unchanged 1621 event case, not the beginning or end of Bandanese history. The final marker is a dated colonial observation of communities in Kei, not their first existence. The separate 2019 and 2021 sources concern modern language, remembrance and public claims; they are not eyewitness accounts of 1621.

contexts.summary: Monopoly required more than a contract: control of land, food and labor changed lives. Surviving communities continued work, relationships and remembrance beyond the campaign.

phases.label: 1599: Dutch visitors enter an existing trading society
phases.title: A trading port precedes the company’s monopoly
phases.text: Mostert and Manuhutu describe the first Dutch visitors paying port dues and exchanging goods for nutmeg and mace. This encounter did not create Bandanese commerce or establish a monopoly in practice.

phases.label: 1609: occupation and fortification intensify conflict
phases.title: Company trading claims acquire military force
phases.text: The National Archives account places the occupation of Neira and construction of a fort in the escalation toward conquest. Treaties and company claims must be distinguished from the choices and trading practice of the communities targeted.

phases.label: 1621: removal, hunger and enslavement
phases.title: The event case examines a policy of forced displacement
phases.text: The archive presents the council’s removal decision of 24 April and Coen’s report captioned 6 May. Its account characterizes the campaign as genocide. These records expose official purposes and resistance; they do not supply the full experience of those attacked or one settled casualty count.

citations.locator: Genocide: 24 April decision; 6 May report and modern Dutch renderings

phases.label: 1622: persecution and forced work continue
phases.title: The campaign’s consequences exceed one year
phases.text: Mostert and Manuhutu trace renewed persecution and forced transfers after 1621. Their account connects plantation production with the cultivation and processing knowledge of enslaved Bandanese people. The 1621 case date is not an endpoint for these consequences.

phases.label: 1630: a colonial encounter records a community in Kei
phases.title: Displacement is not disappearance
phases.text: The PALA account reports that VOC visitors encountered Bandanese people in the Kei region in 1630. It also describes continuing diaspora trade and political initiatives. The record is evidence of presence at that encounter, not a precise migration route, founding date or complete family history.

contexts.title: Textile work, schooling and inspection: selected 1833–1836 records

interval.label: Selected statute and enforcement evidence, 1833–1836
interval.note: This reference is an evidence sequence around the unchanged case, not industrialization’s lifespan or a claim that all factories changed together. The Act’s passage and commencement provisions are different dates. Quarry Bank provides broader background; the Science Museum’s catalogued 1927 machine is later and is not placed within these phases.

contexts.summary: A rule needed people, records and institutions to operate. These selected sources distinguish covered work, statutory obligations, an inspector’s investigation and contested evidence of results.

citations.locator: Lesson PDF, printed p. 9, Source 1 transcript

phases.label: 1833: the Act is passed
phases.title: 29 August dates a statute, not completed workplace change
phases.text: The Act names powered textile processes and regulates children and young persons through restrictions, schooling, certification and inspection. Its exceptions and commencement provisions matter. Its title does not turn it into a ban on all child work or a complete protection for every worker.

citations.locator: PDF 1: title/date and clause I; selected provisions

phases.label: 1834: selected provisions begin; others are phased
phases.title: The date of passage differs from implementation dates
phases.text: Clauses I and VII specify 1 January 1834 for their restrictions; clause VIII phases further age coverage over later months and contains a silk proviso. These are statutory instructions, not a measured series of compliance. The draft does not replace their detail with one universal daily-hours number.

citations.locator: PDF 1, clause I; PDF 3, clauses VII–VIII

phases.label: 1836: Parliament debates enforcement and alteration
phases.title: Reports become evidence in a contested political decision
phases.text: On 9 May, speakers disputed the law’s operation and a proposed change. Hindley quoted Inspector Howell describing instances of benefit, especially reduced night work; other speakers raised household earnings and practical difficulties. A parliamentary argument is not a neutral national compliance survey.

phases.label: 1836: an inspector describes a particular investigation
phases.title: A reported complaint requires evidence about what followed
phases.text: The institution dates the Taylor, Ibbotson & Co. extract to 1836. The inspector reports questioning boys, looking at a time book and intending punishment. The selected transcription does not provide ages, every break, the book’s findings or a completed penalty; it cannot alone measure all workplaces.

contexts.title: Silk work: learning, adaptation and the limits of protection

interval.label: Selected mill, training, storage and legal changes, 1872–1916
interval.note: A selected source frame from Tomioka’s opening to Factory Act implementation, extending four years beyond the Meiji period. It is not the mill’s operating lifespan or the beginning/end of Japanese industrialization. The earlier 1863 farmhouse and a later 1917 worker recollection are explicitly contextual comparisons. The original exact October 1872 case remains unchanged. Memoir writing/publication, modern scholarship, heritage listing and digitization have separate dates.

contexts.summary: Imported machinery depended on trained hands, local materials and people raising silkworms. Learning and technical change could coexist with restrictive working arrangements and incomplete legal protection.

phases.label: October 1872: the model mill opens
phases.title: A new mill uses established regional skills
phases.text: French machinery and advice met Japanese building work and an existing sericultural region. Opening the mill did not create the whole production system in one year or determine every employee’s later experience.

phases.label: 1874: trained workers teach at another mill
phases.title: Learning can travel through people
phases.text: The NDL places Wada Ei(ko)’s departure from Tomioka in July 1874 and subsequent teaching at Saijō, later Rokkōsha. Nakamura and Molteni discuss material changes at that separate Matsushiro mill through her later recollection. This is not an account freshly written during the visit or a reconstruction of Tomioka’s equipment.

phases.label: 1884: Takayama-sha becomes a school
phases.title: Controlling a living crop requires practice
phases.text: Students learned sericulture through practical rearing. Ventilation, warmth and humidity mattered to silkworms before cocoons reached a reel. The school’s date is distinct from the mill’s opening and from Tajima’s earlier 1863 farmhouse.

phases.label: 1905: Arafune’s first storage units operate
phases.title: Storage changes the timing of work
phases.text: Keeping eggs cool delayed hatching. Labels and catalogues helped staff return egg cards when needed. These early twentieth-century facilities did not exist at the mill’s 1872 opening, and their later functional association is not a mapped shipment itinerary.

phases.label: 28 March 1911: Factory Act promulgation
phases.title: Making a law and applying it have different dates
phases.text: The National Archives distinguishes the 1911 law from its later implementation. Protective provisions had a defined initial scope, rather than instantly covering every person working with silk.

phases.label: September 1916: implementation begins
phases.title: Protection needs evidence of how it works
phases.text: The law came into force after a five-year delay. Nakamura and Molteni describe exceptions affecting silk-reeling and evidence of continuing long hours in Nagano. This is a qualified regional comparison, not a finding that every Tomioka shift violated or complied with the law.

contexts.title: Photographic investigation, child-labor rules and enforcement in the United States

interval.label: Selected campaign and federal-administration frame, 1904–1918 CE
interval.note: An orientation frame from the NCLC’s founding through a particular federal act’s operation and constitutional reversal. It preserves the selected case’s complete 3 December 1908 interval. The 1921 report publication and 2019 institutional interpretation are later evidence clocks, not extensions of this frame. This is neither the beginning of all US labor organizing nor the end of child labor.

contexts.summary: Investigators made working conditions visible through photographs, captions, reports and exhibits. Enforcing age and hour rules required different work: checking evidence, issuing certificates and inspecting workplaces. A campaign, a statute and its administration answer different questions.

citations.locator: Background and Scope; The Photo Captions

phases.label: 1904: the institutional founding date
phases.title: An organization assembles a reform campaign
phases.text: The Library of Congress dates the NCLC’s founding to 1904. Its collection account describes investigation and publicity aimed at working children’s conditions. Founding one organization is not the origin of every labor campaign or proof that all families shared its program.

phases.label: 3 December 1908: the catalogued photograph date
phases.title: A particular mill scene enters a documented series
phases.text: The selected catalogue caption places the spinner at Mollahan Mills, Newberry, and reports the overseer’s denial. A separate group caption from that mill is also dated 3 December 1908. Related records allow comparison without making either picture a census, a verified age record or the same view.

citations.locator: Existing photo; indexed caption title, Hine 358 / nclc.01451

phases.label: 1913: a change in Hine’s NCLC role
phases.title: Photographs circulate through exhibits as well as print
phases.text: The collection account dates Hine’s promotion to head of the exhibits department to 1913. It describes photographs circulating in reports, publications, slide shows and displays. These uses explain intended audiences and publicity work; they do not measure each viewer’s response.

citations.locator: Background and Scope: distribution and exhibits

phases.label: 1 September 1916: approval of a particular act
phases.title: Congress links product shipment to age and hour conditions
phases.text: The Keating-Owen Act restricted interstate or foreign shipment of specified products made under prohibited child-employment conditions. It authorized inspections and provided for certificates. Its enactment was a legal step with a defined reach, not a direct result established for this single photograph or proof of compliance.

phases.label: 1 September 1917: the act takes effect
phases.title: Age evidence becomes an administrative task
phases.text: The Children’s Bureau report identifies this effective date. Its certificate discussion explains why trustworthy age evidence and coordination with state systems mattered. The report distinguishes those administrative arrangements from simply printing an age rule.

phases.label: Spring 1918 inspections; 3 June constitutional decision
phases.title: Inspection findings and a court ruling change the inquiry
phases.text: The report records underage employment and certificate gaps in a defined South Carolina inspection sample before the act was declared unconstitutional on 3 June. It also records later investigations under other authority and longer hours at the South Carolina factories revisited. This is a particular observed sequence, not proof that every protection or inspection ceased.

contexts.title: Communal work and the later interpretation of a Blackfoot hunting landscape

interval.label: Selected later-hunting frame and later source/heritage dates, 1700–2008
interval.note: The opening retains the atlas’s selected c.1700–1850 inquiry; it does not establish the first hunt. Later phases date heritage recognition, a photograph’s publication and an archaeological book, not continued hunting through 2008. The much longer site chronology and its interruption remain distinct; seasonal tasks are not assigned invented calendar years.

contexts.summary: Preparing and coordinating a hunt, processing materials and storing food connected a cliff with camps and household work. Community-authored teaching, a modern landscape view and archaeological interpretation supply different kinds of evidence across different dates.

citations.locator: Brief synthesis:long site history and interruption

phases.label: c.1700: opening of the selected atlas inquiry
phases.title: A teaching boundary, not an origin
phases.text: This opening inherits the dossier’s bounded later context. UNESCO describes a much older hunting landscape with an extended interruption; no particular eighteenth-century hunt or continuous identity of all earlier users is dated here.

citations.locator: Brief synthesis:long chronology and interrupted hunting

phases.label: c.1850: UNESCO’s later use boundary for this site
phases.title: A site endpoint does not end a people’s knowledge
phases.text: UNESCO gives an approximate 1850 endpoint in its site-use description. The community teaching accounts explain continuing cultural knowledge; this site boundary is not the end of Blackfoot people, all bison hunting or every community’s history.

phases.label: 1981: World Heritage inscription
phases.title: Recognition is a later institutional event
phases.text: The interpretive-site history and UNESCO identify 1981 inscription. This dates heritage recognition, not construction of drive lanes or the beginning of community care for the landscape.

phases.label: 2005: publication of the landscape photograph
phases.title: A modern surface view has a particular source history
phases.text: Commons records UM’s own photograph uploaded 17 July 2005 and a public-domain dedication. The picture is a later view, not a photograph of a hunt; camera metadata is not independent verification of an exact exposure date.

phases.label: 2008: publication of Brink’s archaeological study
phases.title: An experiment tests a question about processing
phases.text: Brink’s chapter 7, printed pp. 195–198, distinguishes a modern grease-processing experiment from a recovered ancient meal. Its cattle bones and modern tools remain part of its method, rather than disappearing from the explanation.

contexts.title: Hidatsa gardens, village relocation and continuing knowledge

interval.label: Selected village, recollection and displacement records, 1600–1954
interval.note: Big Hidatsa’s original c.1600–1845 case remains exact. Later Like-a-Fishhook recollections, 1917 publication, 1953 dam completion and 1954 relocation belong to this separate reference. Different villages have distinct occupations; no continuous occupation of one place or end of Hidatsa people is implied.

contexts.summary: Women’s cultivation, houses and storage supported households and exchange. Disease, relocation and government projects changed the settings in which people carried this knowledge; later records do not become direct witnesses to every earlier village.

citations.locator: Village & Relocations; Elbowoods & Garrison Dam Relocations

phases.label: c.1600: selected Big Hidatsa occupation begins
phases.title: One village has its own frame
phases.text: NPS places establishment of Big Hidatsa around 1600. Neighboring Awatixa villages have different histories; this is not the beginning of Hidatsa people or all cultivation in the region.

phases.label: 1837: epidemic and village reorganization
phases.title: A trading region also carried danger
phases.text: MHA’s selected history describes the smallpox epidemic and subsequent consolidation of village survivors. NPS connects the epidemic with river travel. The accounts do not supply one identical household experience or a precise mortality total adopted here.

phases.label: 1845: Like-a-Fishhook established upriver
phases.title: Relocation did not end community knowledge
phases.text: MHA identifies Núeta and Hiraacá establishing Like-a-Fishhook. This changes the place of residence and the case’s village frame; it does not end gardening, family relationships or Hidatsa identity.

phases.label: 1917: publication of a woman’s mediated agricultural account
phases.title: Remembered gardens are later evidence
phases.text: The University of Minnesota book presents Maxi´diwiac’s recollections through Goodbird’s interpretation and Wilson’s editing. The foreword describes 1912 recording and later corrections. Her Like-a-Fishhook memories are not a direct transcript of earlier Big Hidatsa life.

phases.label: 1953: Garrison Dam completed, in NPS’s account
phases.title: River engineering changed the conditions of life
phases.text: The NPS account describes the dam and flooding of reservation land despite tribal objections. The construction milestone is separate from MHA’s date for completed relocation the following year.

phases.label: 1954: relocation completed, in MHA’s account
phases.title: Displacement disrupted bottomland households
phases.text: MHA describes families moved from fertile bottomlands, communities dismantled and people scattered across new tracts. Its account places relocation completion in fall 1954. These losses do not authorize a story that the communities vanished.

contexts.title: Kwakwaka’wakw witnesses, prohibition and particular returns

interval.label: Selected law, community institution and return records, 1884–2003
interval.note: The complete original 1884–1980 case remains unchanged. Later returns in this reference do not move its endpoint, establish that every belonging returned or date the origins of potlatch. The 1884 amendment and 1885 commencement are distinct; 1980 opening and a particular 2003 return are separate events.

contexts.summary: Witnesses, family work and care for belongings give potlatch its consequences in the public explanations selected here. Prohibition, confiscation and return changed circumstances without making government or museum custody the sole authority over community knowledge.

citations.locator: Start and End of the Potlatch Ban

phases.label: 1884: amendment in U’mista’s history
phases.title: A law targets an institution
phases.text: U’mista dates the amendment to 1884. This is a government action against an existing practice, not the beginning of potlatch or evidence that people stopped participating.

phases.label: 1885: law takes effect in Living Tradition’s account
phases.title: Commencement is a different date
phases.text: Living Tradition gives 1 January 1885 for the prohibition taking effect. The two dates answer different questions about the legislation.

citations.locator: The Start of the Potlatch Ban

phases.label: 1921: Dan Cranmer’s Village Island potlatch
phases.title: A particular gathering and later prosecution
phases.text: The community history places Dan Cranmer’s potlatch at Village Island and describes prosecutions and confiscation afterward. The title page published in the same year is a different document, not a record of that gathering.

phases.label: 1922: surrender and detention in the community accounts
phases.title: Belongings were taken under pressure
phases.text: The public accounts connect coerced surrender of belongings with sentences after the potlatch. Vera Newman and Chief Bill Cranmer describe particular family experiences and the pressure exerted. Their statements do not become an identical experience for every family.

citations.locator: Impact transcript and named speaker captions

phases.label: 1951: prohibition removed
phases.title: A legal change does not instantly repair harm
phases.text: Living Tradition dates the removal to 1951; Barb Cranmer describes the continuing fear and the time needed to feel secure participating openly. The legal milestone and family confidence are different changes.

citations.locator: The End of the Potlatch Ban

phases.label: 1974: U’mista Cultural Society formed
phases.title: Return requires organized negotiation
phases.text: The Society’s history dates its formation to 22 March 1974. The return account describes families and communities planning institutions to house belongings; this is not proof that all return negotiations were already completed.

phases.label: 1980: U’mista opens
phases.title: A home for care, language and history
phases.text: U’mista opened in November 1980. The public return page identifies family members with returned belongings at that opening, while the wider account describes decisions about where family treasures would be held.

phases.label: 2003: a particular headdress return in the source caption
phases.title: Return histories continue beyond the case
phases.text: The public caption records Chief William T. Cranmer with Aube Elléouët on 23 September 2003 and says she returned a headdress surrendered by Chief Sam Scow in 1922. This is one documented return account, not a complete chain of custody or the end of repatriation.

citations.locator: Chief William T. Cranmer and Aube Elléouët, 23 September 2003

contexts.title: War damage, negotiation and the material work of peace

interval.label: Selected war-to-ratification frame, 1779–1795 CE
interval.note: A selected window connecting dated destructive orders, the treaty and its separate U.S. ratification. It is not the founding, ending or complete history of the Haudenosaunee. The whole 1794–1795 case interval stays unchanged. The 1989 custody account and undated present Nation accounts are later evidence clocks outside this frame.

contexts.summary: Destroying crops and homes threatened the work sustaining communities. Negotiation addressed land, peace, supplies and complaint procedures. Putting agreements into practice required further actions that the written treaty alone cannot establish.

citations.locator: Creation date and Contains: treaty and ratification

phases.label: 31 May 1779: instructions target settlements and crops
phases.title: Read an order as an intended action
phases.text: Washington instructed Sullivan to destroy settlements, ruin crops and prevent further planting. The letter establishes this program; Powless’s separate Onondaga account describes damage and displacement. The order is not itself an inventory of completed destruction.

phases.label: 11 November 1794: treaty commitments are recorded
phases.title: Peace includes land, material support and redress
phases.text: The treaty records peace and land acknowledgments, provision for continuing purchases and skilled work, and a complaint procedure. These are commitments with specified roles, rather than proof of all later conduct.

citations.locator: Articles I–III,VI,VII and dated signature block

phases.label: 21 January 1795: a separate U.S. ratification
phases.title: One archival recto carries distinct dated actions
phases.text: The archive identifies the incorporated 1794 treaty and an instrument signed by Washington and Randolph on 21 January 1795. The document’s opening heading does not move the negotiations into 1795 or make ratification evidence of complete performance.

citations.locator: Contains entry; full recto and lower ratification

contexts.title: Printed government, coercion and renewed publication

interval.label: Selected constitution-to-renewed-newspaper frame, 1827–1844 CE
interval.note: A selected sequence from the 1827 constitution through the Advocate’s 1844 establishment in Tahlequah. The whole original 1821–1839 inquiry remains unchanged. Neither end dates Cherokee nationhood, language, printing or the end of enslavement. The 1828 April photograph, February first-issue transcription and 1832 reprints retain separate issue dates.

contexts.summary: Print carried laws, practical staffing concerns and disagreement to readers. Forced removal disrupted lives and government without ending publication or nationhood; the renewal of institutions did not create equal rights for everyone.

citations.locator: Publication heading and July 1827 adoption; Article III
Conflicts with Georgia; Forced Removal and Reunification, including1844 Advocate
Slavery in Cherokee Nation;1839 timeline entry

phases.label: July 1827: a written constitution
phases.title: National authority includes political exclusions
phases.text: The later first-issue transcription identifies a constitution formed at New Echota in July 1827. It describes national land and divided government while restricting office and voting by sex, freedom and ancestry.

citations.locator: Adoption heading; ArticlesI–III, especiallyIII sections 4 and 7

phases.label: 1828: separate newspaper issues
phases.title: Preserve publication and object identities
phases.text: The February 21 first-issue transcription carries the constitution. The unchanged supplied photograph identifies the April 10 title portion, vol. 1 no. 8; it is not the February first issue and has an unknown later photographic-reproduction date.

citations.locator: Retained catalogue scope; actual unchanged masthead

phases.label: September/October 1832: staffing and publication are debated
phases.title: The newspaper contains different speakers
phases.text: Boudinot’s dated letter discusses assistance and a vacancy. A separate correspondent debates how to seek Ross’s views, while an October reprint urges continued publication. These pieces are distinct from a single uncontested editorial voice.

citations.locator: September 15 issue: letter and separate September 7 reply
October 6 issue: Christian Soldier attribution and comment

phases.label: 1835: contested treaty authority
phases.title: Signatures are not universal consent
phases.text: The Cherokee Nation’s historical account states that New Echota signatories lacked authority under Nation law. The account distinguishes their act from the position of the majority who opposed relinquishing their homelands.

citations.locator: Conflicts with the State of Georgia

phases.label: 1838–1839: forced removal
phases.title: Political pressure becomes coercive movement
phases.text: The Nation’s account describes U.S. troops enforcing removal. Its public Freedmen history includes people enslaved by Cherokee citizens in this forced movement. No single route or uniform legal position is inferred for everyone.

citations.locator: Forced Removal, Internal Conflict, and Reunification

phases.label: 1839: reorganization without universal equality
phases.title: Political continuity includes continuing conflict
phases.text: A new constitution reorganized the Nation after removal and earlier western migration. The public Freedmen history records continuing racial inequality. The date does not mark the end of internal conflict or slavery.

citations.locator: Reunification under a new constitution; persistent disputes

phases.label: 1844: the Cherokee Advocate is established
phases.title: Publication resumes in a changed setting
phases.text: The Cherokee Nation’s account identifies the bilingual Advocate in Tahlequah alongside rebuilt institutions. It is evidence of continued publication, not proof that removal’s consequences or political exclusions were resolved.

contexts.title: Manoomin work, selected treaty evidence and intertribal care

interval.label: Selected U.S. treaty, separate photograph and stewardship frame, 1837–1984 CE
interval.note: The bounds connect an 1837 U.S. treaty and the 1984 creation of GLIFWC; they do not date manoomin’s origins or all Ojibwe history. The whole original bracketed [1913] photographic case remains unchanged. Its probable Ontario setting is separate from the U.S. ceded territories; neither treaty jurisdiction nor a legal identity is assigned to the unnamed person. Later public accounts/brochure have their own dates and scopes.

contexts.summary: Gathering, finishing and caring for rice waters involve knowledge and repeated work. A treaty clause, an archival photograph and an intertribal institution document different aspects of that history without making every Great Lakes community one legal or political setting.

citations.locator: Actual catalogue: bracketed date and probable Ontario location
Opening1984 institutional account and reserved rights

phases.label: 29 July 1837: a particular treaty names gathering wild rice
phases.title: Retained rights concern specified places and parties
phases.text: Article 5 addresses hunting, fishing and gathering wild rice within the ceded territory. GLIFWC explains that the Ojibwe retained rights rather than receiving the origin of those rights from the United States. The text does not identify the later photograph’s setting or prove every implementation.

citations.locator: Article 5; Article 6 and dated close, printed p.492

phases.label: Catalogued [1913]: a separately situated photograph
phases.title: One archival scene leaves questions open
phases.text: LOC assigns the bracketed date and a probable Ontario location. The person is unnamed and the exact lake unknown. The picture does not transfer the U.S. treaty’s geography or legal framework to this person.

phases.label: 1984: GLIFWC is created
phases.title: An institution supports continuing tribal responsibilities
phases.text: GLIFWC’s account dates its creation to 1984 and describes resource assessments and stewardship supporting member tribes. The brochure also identifies rice-bed protection and enhancement from that year. This dates an institution, not the beginning of Indigenous knowledge or care.

contexts.title: Bering Strait objects and archaeological date ranges

interval.label: Selected catalogue and regional research ranges, 300–1250 CE
interval.note: A comparison of differently scoped and overlapping published ranges, not the lifespan of one people or a resolved single regional chronology. The Met object remains catalogued 300–500 CE. The later proposed Old Bering Sea range does not individually redate it. The modern Kawerak interviews occurred in 2019 and are outside this archaeological reference frame.

contexts.summary: An individual catalogue attribution, a type-site account and a regional radiocarbon argument organize evidence at different scales. Their ranges overlap without establishing one succession of peoples or states.

citations.locator: Explicit 500–900 CE range and type-site explanation

phases.label: 300–500: the individual object’s catalogue range
phases.title: A date attached to a particular carving
phases.text: The Met assigns accession 2019.456.17 to Old Bering Sea III and dates it 300–500 CE. This is the retained object attribution; it is not a newly inspected radiocarbon measurement or a beginning/end for all carving in the region.

phases.label: 500–900: the NPS Birnirk comparison
phases.title: A type-site helps archaeologists compare tools
phases.text: NPS uses this explicit range for Birnirk near present-day Utqiagvik. Its account describes house mounds and comparisons among tools. A type-site supplies an archaeological reference, not this Met object’s recorded findspot or a political boundary.

citations.locator: Visible site body and explicit range

phases.label: 650–1250: a proposed Old Bering Sea florescence
phases.title: A regional argument changes the chronological question
phases.text: Mason and Rasic’s published abstract proposes this later range after marine-carbon corrections to existing regional assays; it also places earlier related contexts at 300–600. The proposal and the catalogue attribution remain separately reported. Neither fixes the date of every surviving carving.

contexts.title: Ozette: exposure, collaboration and community custody

interval.label: Selected exposure and excavation-start frame, winter 1969–70 to April 1970
interval.note: A modern research/custody frame from the Makah museum account, not a date for the houses, the whole excavation, the cultural center’s founding or the village’s life. The original disputed burial estimates remain c. 1560 or 1700, and the reported 500±50 BP is not silently converted. The c. 1910/copyright 1911 photograph is different later evidence.

contexts.summary: The museum’s account connects exposed wooden belongings with a collaboration initiated through the Tribe. Makah oral history and the decision to keep the collection on the reservation matter to how this material is interpreted.

citations.locator: Complete visible Ozette Archaeological Site body

phases.label: Winter 1969–70: storm exposure
phases.title: A bank slump exposed preserved wooden material
phases.text: MCRC describes a storm exposing belongings at the village site. A hiker contacted the Makah Tribe, and the Tribe contacted Washington State University. This modern exposure is not the ancient burial event or the beginning of Makah knowledge of the place.

phases.label: April 1970: collaborative excavation began
phases.title: Study and care followed the community’s connection to the site
phases.text: The museum dates the excavation’s start to April 1970. Its account places oral history alongside recovered evidence and states that the Tribe kept the collection on the reservation. It gives no exact museum-founding date here; that later institution is not silently assigned to April 1970.

citations.locator: Excavation start, oral history and collection custody

contexts.title: Inuinnait clothing: seasonal work, new supplies and teaching

interval.label: Selected represented periods and community research, 1880s–2019
interval.note: A bounded frame following selected community-directed exhibit periods and the separately dated 2017–19 research workshops, not the beginning/end of Inuinnait clothing or people. The original case remains the Southern Party window 1913–16. The photograph’s exact exposure is unknown and its 1922 publication date remains separate. Reconstructed garments were made in modern workshops rather than in the periods they represent.

contexts.summary: Preparing skins, choosing supplies and teaching patterns made clothing an ongoing practical task. The community exhibit explains material changes alongside outside pressures and continued making by Inuinnait.

phases.label: 1880s: a represented clothing and seasonal-work frame
phases.title: Land, harvest and making were connected
phases.text: The community exhibit links winter sea-ice sealing and summer caribou/fish harvests with the materials of clothing. Its selected 1880s account describes copper/bone needles, sinew thread and skins. The displayed parka was researched and made much later; 1880 is not its actual manufacture date.

phases.label: 1913–16 observations; photograph published in 1922
phases.title: An expedition record names two people
phases.text: The report’s Southern Party window frames the selected case. Plate I names Ikpakhuak and Higilak in dancing costume. Publication and fieldwork context do not independently establish the exposure’s exact date or location, and the photograph does not identify who sewed these particular garments.

citations.locator: Retained title-page scope; actual Plate I; archive metadata

phases.label: 1930s: the exhibit traces changes beginning in the 1920s
phases.title: Purchased materials entered clothing work
phases.text: The exhibit connects fox-fur exchange and trading posts with cotton covers, wool linings and steel tools. These selected changes concern access, work and choices; they do not mean every household adopted the same garment at one moment.

citations.locator: English body: exchange, materials and tools

phases.label: 1950s: settlement pressures and new supplies
phases.title: Making continued amid imposed changes
phases.text: PI/KHS describes government-directed changes in housing, work and schooling alongside continued hunting/fishing in outpost camps. Its clothing account includes ready-made supplies and hand-crank sewing machines. This attributed period account does not recover an identical experience for every family.

citations.locator: English body: government decisions and clothing

phases.label: 2017–19: researching, sewing and teaching
phases.title: Elders and learners made an exhibit for the future
phases.text: Mary Avalak, Mabel Etegik and Annie Atighioyak led the sewing program. Participants researched five historical parkas, prepared hides, made patterns and sewed modern reconstructions while documenting language and supporting new making for family and friends.

citations.locator: Creating Patterns of Change and Objects bodies

contexts.title: Saint-Domingue and Haiti: emancipation, work and political authority

interval.label: Selected revolutionary decisions and records,1791–1804
interval.note: A phased source inquiry, retaining the complete original case interval unchanged. The boundaries connect an uprising to independence, not the lifespan of Haitian people or a completed transition to equal land, work or political rights. Later recognition/debt and 1825 comparisons are not incorporated without separate verified sources.

contexts.summary: Resistance, provincial emancipation, military allegiances, constitutional work rules and independence were distinct changes. Their surviving records expose authority and practical stakes without recovering every cultivator’s experience or one uniform revolutionary intention.

phases.label: 1791: uprising in the northern plantation region
phases.title: Resistance did not begin everywhere in the same way
phases.text: Manigat distinguishes the northern uprising from different struggles and alliances in the West and South. Enslaved people acted within changing military and political circumstances; a later independence outcome does not prove one identical starting program.

phases.label: 1793: provincial emancipation measures
phases.title: Local struggle preceded the metropolitan decree
phases.text: The parliamentary account places Sonthonax’s northern proclamation on 29 August, followed by Polverel’s measures in other provinces. English Heritage’s brief overview instead says September for the northern measure. The discrepancy is retained in source notes; the provincial decisions are not collapsed into the separate 1794 decree.

citations.locator: Selected renewed scope; compressed northern chronology

phases.label: 1794: the French Convention decrees colonial abolition
phases.title: A rule still required political and military support
phases.text: The institutional account describes deputies from Saint-Domingue reaching the Convention and the 4 February abolition decision. A decree changes the formal legal claim; it does not itself document implementation in every place or remove the military threats that followed.

citations.locator: Le débat: delegation and Convention decision

phases.label: 1797: Louverture’s letter to Vincent
phases.title: A formerly enslaved leader defended a particular allegiance
phases.text: The catalogued 21 October letter seeks Vincent’s advocacy with the Directory, challenges racist allegations and affirms attachment to France. It is a particular leader’s argument, not proof that every formerly enslaved person agreed or that independence was already a fixed 1791 objective.

phases.label: 1801: abolition and controlled cultivation in one constitution
phases.title: Status, labor and government power were different questions
phases.text: Articles 1 and 3 retain a French connection while prohibiting slavery. Articles 14–16 insist on cultivation and authorize police regulation of cultivators’ movement. Article 28 grants Louverture life tenure. These provisions do not certify voluntary work, actual revenue shares or equal political participation.

phases.label: 1804: independence proclaimed at Gonaïves
phases.title: An official act also organized authority
phases.text: The Acte’s dateline is 1 January. Its assembled generals renounce France. The separately studied printed packet also authorizes Dessalines’s life governorship. An official declaration and a new allocation of state power do not amount to a direct record of every household’s freedom or consent.

contexts.title: Te Tiriti: negotiation, asserted authority and early enforcement

interval.label: Selected negotiations and early colonial conflicts, 1840–1846
interval.note: A bounded frame from the first signings through the Northern War, not the Treaty’s lifespan, the whole colonization of Aotearoa or a common outcome for all iwi and hapū. The original exact 1840 case interval remains unchanged. Earlier He Whakaputanga, later land institutions, twentieth-century inquiries and a 2025 speech have separate dates. The close of this frame does not end Māori authority or continuing disputes.

contexts.summary: Making copies, interpreting words and gathering marks did not settle how authority would work. Crown proclamations and subsequent enforcement need evidence distinct from the signing record.

citations.locator: Northern War findings in official release

phases.label: 5–6 February 1840: discussion and the first signing
phases.title: An agreement is heard, debated and marked
phases.text: Rangatira heard the Māori text and verbal explanations at Waitangi before the first signatures on 6 February. Supporting and opposing speeches concerned authority, land and relations with newcomers. A later complete text does not preserve every spoken assurance.

citations.locator: Initial discussions; proposed Treaty; first signatures

phases.label: March–April 1840: different sheets and regional decisions
phases.title: One English sheet does not stand for every signing
phases.text: The Waikato-Manukau sheet is in English. Its first signing date is uncertain; an 11 April witness note is distinct from a 26 April Manukau signing. Some rangatira signed while Te Wherowhero declined. Neither choice describes every Waikato or Ngāti Whātua position.

phases.label: 21 May 1840: Hobson proclaims sovereignty
phases.title: The Crown announces a claim before circulation ends
phases.text: The proclamation asserts British sovereignty over the islands while sheets are still circulating. Ōnuku’s 30 May signing followed this announcement. A proclamation records what the Crown claimed; it does not establish every community’s consent or prove the promises were fulfilled.

phases.label: Early September 1840: the recorded signing process ends
phases.title: Absence and refusal remain part of the record
phases.text: The source records a final signing near Kāwhia on 3 September. The sheets did not reach every community, and some rangatira refused. The end of collecting marks was not an agreement on every interpretation or a referendum of all inhabitants.

phases.label: 1844–1846: disputes and the Northern War
phases.title: Enforcing authority changes people’s lives
phases.text: Hōne Heke and his followers challenged British authority by cutting the flagstaff at Kororāreka. Armed conflict followed. The Tribunal’s later Te Raki inquiry found serious Crown breaches in this period, including attacks on pā and kāinga and harm to non-combatants. These are district-specific historical findings, not a story of one uniform Māori response.

contexts.title: Satellite projects, observation and institutions: selected 1955–1958 records

interval.label: Selected satellite planning, launch and institutional responses, 1955–1958
interval.note: A bounded reference inquiry around an exact 1957 event, not the lifetime of Sputnik 1 or a complete 1945–1991 Cold War account. The registry’s broader institutional framework remains open. Later webpage editions, archive catalogues and anniversary exhibits are source-publication clocks, not ancient/event phases.

contexts.summary: An international scientific program gave satellite work a shared timetable while state priorities organized funding, secrecy and competition. A proposal, a completed launch and later arguments about observation or institutions establish different things.

phases.label: 1955: a public US satellite program for the IGY
phases.title: A common scientific timetable also became competitive
phases.text: NASA’s account dates the White House satellite announcement to July 1955 and the Vanguard selection to September. These are program decisions before the launch; the IGY itself ran from July 1957 through December 1958.

phases.label: January 1957: Korolev requests a simpler project
phases.title: A plan names organizations and a hoped-for date
phases.text: The 5 January proposal requests April–June launches, coordination across ministries and a radio/optical tracking system. The launch actually occurred in October. Proposed work and completed work must be checked against different records.

phases.label: October 1957: launch, announcement and observation
phases.title: One event entered several institutional arguments
phases.text: The 4 October launch is distinct from the Pravda announcement catalogued for 5 October and the 29 October Commons debate. The debate records both observation work and disagreement over national priorities, without standing for all British responses.

phases.label: 1958: new US institutions; IGY continues
phases.title: Institutional changes followed rather than defined the launch
phases.text: NASA’s timeline distinguishes the July Space Act, NASA opening in October and the IGY ending in December. These later decisions belong to the reference frame; the case retains its exact 1957 launch interval.

contexts.title: War decisions, correspondence, work and selected aftermath

interval.label: Selected decision, work and aftermath records,1914–1919
interval.note: The original whole 1914–1918 case is preserved.1919 belongs to selected retrospective administration and cemetery-care records, not a universal extension/end of fighting. The regional cases have their own intervals; source publication/transcription dates do not become wartime events.

contexts.summary: A European crisis involved contested government decisions, followed by mobilization through states and empires. Selected regional records make communication, civilian work, coercive recruitment and household consequences visible without making them one experience.

phases.label: 1914: decisions debated in public
phases.title: One government’s arguments are contested
phases.text: In the 3 AugustCommons discussion, Grey sets out the government’s position and MacDonald challenges the case for intervention. These are situated public arguments, not all diplomacy or a referendum of every population drawn into war.

phases.label: 1916: selected letters and factory records
phases.title: Mobilization reaches different kinds of work
phases.text: Named Indian correspondence and Birtley planning/factory records reveal different practical settings. Their shared war years do not establish a common journey, meeting or causal chain between the people described.

phases.label: 1917: recruitment and a separate public appeal
phases.title: Power and persuasion have different forms
phases.text: The selected South Nyeri research examines coercive recruitment. The existing USposter is a separate 1917 appeal to women. Neither source stands for the people or choices in the other setting.

phases.label: 1918: original major-war endpoint
phases.title: One timeline boundary does not settle every aftermath
phases.text: The conventional major-war interval remains 1914–1918. Regional fighting, movement and political consequences did not all begin or stop together; later care and administrative records have their own dates.

phases.label: 1919: selected work of recording and care
phases.title: Aftermath appears in particular documents
phases.text: Debauche’s care letter and Watkins’ retrospective report answer different questions after the selected wartime years. They cannot establish every household’s outcome or completion of all requested work.

contexts.title: Different war and persecution chronologies, 1931–1945

interval.label: Selected Asian and European war/persecution frame, 1931–1945
interval.note: A comparative orientation, not a new interval for world-war-two, one universal war start or a single policy imposed on all regions. The whole original 1933–1945 case remains intact.

contexts.summary: Japanese conquest, European warfare and the Holocaust have connected histories with different beginnings. Read regional institutions, people and records within their own dates.

citations.locator: German and Japanese Expansion; Invasion of Poland; Defeat of Germany; Defeat of Japan

phases.title: Japan invades Manchuria
phases.text: USHMM locates this conquest in September 1931; it precedes the later European war.

phases.title: The Holocaust’s persecution frame begins
phases.text: USHMM uses 1933–1945 for the evolving persecution and murder of European Jews. The original dossier keeps this frame.

phases.title: War expands in China
phases.text: The museum dates Japan’s invasion of China proper to July 1937.

phases.title: Germany invades Poland
phases.text: The museum places the start of World War II in Europe at Germany’s 1 September 1939 invasion.

phases.title: Different surrender dates
phases.text: Germany’s defeat in May and Japan’s formal surrender in September are distinct events within 1945.

citations.locator: Defeat of Germany; Defeat of Japan

contexts.title: Middle Niger settlements: food, craft and changing places

interval.label: Selected archaeological phases, approximately 400–1400 CE
interval.note: A selected frame for excavated settlement evidence, not the whole lifespan of Middle Niger communities or of Jenné-jeno. Earlier occupation reaches the third century BCE in the 1981 extract; later people and places continued. The original thirteenth-century object interval remains separate. Neither site chronology nor modern acquisition dates establish this unprovenanced figure’s findspot or purpose.

contexts.summary: Food production, exchange, building and furnace work connected settlements whose uses changed through time. The evidence invites comparison between forms of urban organization without supplying this figure’s missing biography.

phases.label: Approximately 400–950: changing uses within the settlement
phases.title: Places for living, work and burial
phases.text: The report places cemetery/ritual areas in selected sectors during Phase III, approximately 400–950. Later house-floor burials have a different distribution. These excavated patterns are not a recovered setting for the Met figure.

citations.locator: PDF pp. 4–5: Phase III and IV uses

phases.label: Approximately 750–1100: an urban high point
phases.title: A town within a settled landscape
phases.text: The 1981 article’s extract describes Jenné-jeno’s urban apogee in this range, alongside other large settlements. Staple foods and exchange belong to this account of urban growth; the clay figure is dated later.

citations.locator: Exposed Extract: chronology and staple products

phases.label: After approximately 1200: a proposed change in settlement focus
phases.title: Testing a relationship between two places
phases.text: Cores in Djenné yielded no pottery earlier than approximately 1000–1200. The excavators propose a relationship between its growth and Jenné-jeno’s decline after 1200, explicitly requiring more work. A preliminary sample does not establish the foundation date of every neighborhood.

citations.locator: PDF p. 3: preliminary coring and hypothesis

phases.label: By approximately 1400: the reported end of occupation at Jenné-jeno
phases.title: A site ending is not a people disappearing
phases.text: The excavators use abandonment by 1400 for this site. That boundary does not end the history of the region or date every object attributed to it. Djenné’s different occupation history remains a separate inquiry.

contexts.title: Settlement of Aotearoa: dated evidence and navigation knowledge

interval.label: Selected settlement-dating window, c. 1250–1300 CE
interval.note: A source-qualified archaeological orientation, preserving the separate complete case interval unchanged. The dated phases below locate published model windows, not recovered canoe departures, an exact first landing, one Great Fleet, or the lifespan of Māori identity. Modern practice, teaching and research-publication dates remain outside this medieval frame.

contexts.summary: Dated materials help investigate settlement, while attributed accounts of practiced knowledge explain navigation and its transmission. Their evidence and dates can be compared without turning a statistical range or modern sailing achievement into one recovered ancestral itinerary.

citations.locator: The date debate: Reaching New Zealand
PDF pp. 2–3: Timing of Polynesian Arrival; p. 7: HPDs

phases.label: 1250–1275: a published North Island model window
phases.title: A range belongs to an analysis
phases.text: Bunbury, Petchey and Bickler’s 2022 analysis places North Island settlement in a modeled 1250–1275 window. Its standard reporting uses 68% highest-probability-density intervals. The phase marker orients that attributed window; it does not identify a named canoe or make 1250 an exact landing.

citations.locator: PDF p. 2: Timing of Polynesian Arrival; p. 7: Bayesian Analysis

phases.label: 1280–1295: a separate South Island model window
phases.title: Different materials do not become one voyage
phases.text: The same study reports a South Island window of 1280–1295. The older 2008 rat-and-seed analysis inferred introduced-rat arrival around 1280 using a different evidence stream. These remain attributed findings, not a crew’s exact travel time or a route between two landfalls. The broader orientation around 1300 does not end voyaging or Māori history.

citations.locator: PDF pp. 2–3: settlement and rat-proxy discussion

contexts.title: Aegean centres and British farms: different Bronze Age settings

interval.label: c. 1900–1100 BCE · selected European settings
interval.note: A teaching frame connecting separately dated evidence, not the lifespan of one society. Cretan palaces, mainland Greek centres and British farms did not share one government or one collapse. Britain’s broader museum periodization is c. 2300–800 BCE. The Uluburun link offers a dated cargo comparison; it does not identify that ship’s origin or destination.

contexts.summary: Around 1900 BCE, centres such as Knossos and Phaistos concentrated work, goods and record keeping on Crete. Mainland Greek workshops and palaces later provide a different set of records and objects. In Britain, farms, fields and round houses belonged to another settlement pattern; metal tools coexisted with stone and flint. These settings let us ask who organized production and how materials moved, without turning an Aegean palace history into the history of every European community.

citations.locator: Paragraphs beginning Around 1900 B.C.; With the palaces; Much of the first half
Mainland centres, workshops, commerce and Linear B paragraphs
Bronze Age overview, first three paragraphs

phases.title: Cretan centres and records
phases.text: The museum dates the establishment of major Cretan palaces to around 1900 BCE. Administrative clay records and concentrated craft activity help explain their institutional role; agricultural redistribution remains a proposed function.

citations.locator: Around 1900 B.C.; With the palaces; The scripts

phases.title: A mainland Greek cultural frame
phases.text: The selected museum overview begins its Mycenaean frame around 1600 BCE. Mycenae, Tiryns, Thebes and Athens are named centres. Vessels found far away support circulation of goods; they do not reveal every trader or the route of one voyage.

citations.locator: Opening chronology; mainland centres; Wide-ranging commerce

phases.title: A Cretan destruction horizon
phases.text: Archaeological destruction on Crete is placed around 1450 BCE in the consulted account. The source leaves responsibility uncertain. This date should not be merged with later mainland destruction or used as a universal end to European exchange.

phases.title: Different settings around the snapshot date
phases.text: The mainland account describes destruction and decline in the late thirteenth century BCE. The British overview instead describes a much longer Bronze Age sequence of farms, field divisions and deposited objects. Comparing these accounts does not establish synchronized change or an identical cause.

citations.locator: Period heading; settlements, landscape divisions and deposition

contexts.title: Kuk: drainage and cultivation in New Guinea

interval.label: c. 2400–450 BCE · selected Phase 3 evidence
interval.note: Rounded orientation for the Phase 3 sequence, not proof of cultivation in every field in every intervening year. The published early range is 4350–3980 calibrated years before 1950 (about 2400–2030 BCE); the late range is 2700–2400 (about 750–450 BCE). This is a highland New Guinea setting, not a history of all Southeast Asia or Oceania.

contexts.summary: At Kuk in the upper Wahgi Valley, buried ditch networks show people altering wet ground for cultivation. Archaeologists distinguish early and later drainage episodes and compare Kuk with other highland sites. Draining soil could make land usable, but the surviving cuts do not name the workers, settle their land rights or reveal every crop. This agricultural history should be read alongside, rather than absorbed into, the later island settlements associated with Lapita pottery.

citations.locator: The choice of Kuk; calibration convention; Table 1.2 and notes
Phase 3 subphases; Tables 13.1–13.2; The emergence of ditches in highland New Guinea

phases.title: Early Phase 3: a dated range
phases.text: The early ditch-network range is approximately 2400–2030 BCE. The opening year is a rounded edge of that range, not a known day when ditch digging began.

phases.title: Later drainage evidence
phases.text: The table places a later subphase around 750–450 BCE. The interval between the published subphases must not become a fabricated continuous list of annual events.

phases.title: An archaeological boundary, not the end of a people
phases.text: The selected late range ends here. The authors distinguish later phases and warn that other sites lack enough evidence to establish the same pattern of abandonment. Changing a field system does not by itself establish the disappearance of a community.

citations.locator: Regional processes: cessation at Kuk and limits at other sites

What does a new political settlement promise, and what must be investigated afterward?
How do institutions and choices turn conflict into mass violence?
How does technical change depend on organized work?
What does coordinated earthmoving show, and what remains uncertain?
How can archaeology test explanations of gathering and change?
How do patrons, markets and unequal power shape craft?
How do changing patrons affect books and decorative arts?
How do tools and clothing carry skilled knowledge?
How do surviving belongings relate to community knowledge and authority?
How do communities coordinate food, work and seasonal knowledge?
What can a public building and a village reveal about collective life?
How do words and records carry political responsibilities?
How do material work and knowledge connect across generations?
How do royal images, work claims and excavated production answer different questions about authority?
What can different materials and find contexts tell us about skilled work and institutions?

orientations.title: Supe Valley: public buildings and the work of feeding people
orientations.question: How can buildings and food traces tell different parts of a community’s history?

summary.title: Coast and valley
summary.text: Caral’s platforms and circular courts place collective building beside a less visible history of food production. Coastal Áspero offers a second setting in the Supe Valley. Comparing them connects monumental spaces with the plants people used, without assuming that every household had the same diet or role.

citations.locator: Brief synthesis: platforms and recessed circular courts

sections.title: Provisioning leaves several kinds of evidence
sections.text: The dental-calculus study recovered plant starches from nine people at Áspero and one at Caral. These traces bring food use into an account otherwise dominated by large buildings. The authors consider exchange as one possible explanation for access to some plants. Starch presence is not a measure of the calories supplied by a crop.

citations.locator: Abstract; Discussion: exchange and limits of starch ubiquity

sections.title: Buildings accumulated over time
sections.text: Caral’s urban plan and ceremonial architecture developed over centuries within the broad 3000–1800 BCE frame. A visitor’s view gathers different building episodes. The arrangement supports questions about organized work, but cannot by itself tell us who assigned tasks, whether people volunteered, or how work varied between households.

citations.locator: Brief synthesis, criterion (ii), Integrity and Authenticity

orientations.perspectives: Builders and food producers left material traces, not a complete set of personal accounts. A small sample of human remains cannot speak for all valley residents.
orientations.scope: A coastal–inland comparison within the Supe Valley, not an account of every American community. Burial samples and building phases have their own dates within the wider site frame.

activity.prompt: Use the account above to choose evidence for two questions: what plants some people consumed, and how public gathering spaces were arranged. What could neither source tell you?
activity.response: Starches address plant use; platforms and courts address spatial arrangement. Neither supplies every household’s diet or a named worker’s explanation of their obligations. Explain the mismatch rather than treating the two sources as interchangeable.

snapshots.text: Around 2400 BCE lies within Caral’s broadly dated development. Platforms and circular gathering spaces orient us to the Supe Valley’s built landscape. They do not establish the same layout or activity in every year; the linked coastal food study has separately dated burial contexts.

orientations.title: Nile communities: building, supply and different centres of power
orientations.question: What had to happen around a monument to keep people working?

summary.title: Giza, Saqqara and Kerma
